question_text: A 55-year-old, otherwise healthy man, presented with rapid onset of severe chest wall pain. A moderately calcified 4 cm posterior paravertebral mass was diagnosed by CT scan. It did not invade neural foramina. A VATS resection for a presumed neurogenic tumor was planned, but during operation a mass with prominent neovascularity and evidence of proximal rib invasion is observed (see figure). The most appropriate next steps are to
critique:
While about two-thirds of mediastinal tumors are benign, the presence of symptoms increases the likelihood of malignancy to two-thirds. While masses of the posterior mediastinum are most commonly benign neurogenic tumors, this patient's rapid pain onset is a clue that the tumor may be atypical. CT and MR scans can diagnose a benign nerve sheath tumor with reliability. Therefore, in cases with typical presentations, a preoperative image-guided biopsy is often avoided because it can cause considerable discomfort. Planning in this case might have been better with a preoperative FNA biopsy, particularly if it showed ganglion and spindle cells suggestive of a ganglioneuroma. In clinical practice, however, technical problems or tumor characteristics like necrosis or calcifications may cause inconclusive results. Intraoperative judgment in this case considers the tumor's gross appearance, paravertebral location and rib adhesion/invasion. Calcification increases the likelihood that this is a Malignant Tumor of Nerve Sheath Origin (MTNSO). Such tumors have also been called malignant schwannomas, malignant neurofibromas, or neurogenic fibrosarcomas. MTNSOs are more common in patients who have systemic neurofibromatosis but they can occur sporadically. Two malignant tumors that arise from the sympathetic ganglion cells, neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma, are also in the differential diagnosis of lesions in this region. However, both of these malignancies typically occur in children less than 5 and 10 years of age, respectively. Staging of sympathetic ganglion tumors includes: Stage 1 (encapsulated); Stage 2 (locally invasive); Stage 3 (extension across midline or with lymph node metastases); and Stage 4 (distant metastases). The calcified nature of this malignancy makes immediate frozen section diagnosis difficult. Calcification also reduces the chance that it is an unusual malignancy like Ewing's sarcoma for which neoadjuvant chemotherapy might be indicated to improve results.

For all of these discussed neoplasms, complete surgical resection with wide margins is the best therapy. Little is known about the safety or long-term outcomes of thoracoscopic resections for such unusual tumors, but VATS techniques are evolving rapidly. In the meantime, open resection is preferred. Adjuvant radiation therapy can be used for close or involved margins and, if available, brachytherapy techniques may be considered. The final pathology in this case showed osteosarcoma of the proximal rib that mimicked the working diagnosis of atypical neural tumor. It was appropriately treated by the same method of resection.

question_text: A 70-year-old woman had a left radical mastectomy and radiation therapy for breast cancer 20 years ago. Aortic valve replacement through a median sternotomy was done eight years ago. A chest wall lesion is shown in the photographs. The best management is
critique:
Radiation therapy is integral to multidisciplinary treatment for breast cancer, but it can have long-term complications. Radiation necrosis of the chest wall, seen here, provides a formidable challenge to the thoracic surgeon. Collaboration with a plastic surgeon is often prudent, and principles for managing chest wall radionecrosis, necrotizing infections, or complex malignant lesions include: (1) removal of all necrotic, devitalized and irradiated tissue; (2) avoidance of prosthetic materials for reconstruction if infection is present; and (3) coverage of the wound with well-vascularized soft tissue. The best solution for a patient must be based on individual considerations.

In this case it was possible to resect all necrotic tissue down to the chest wall but entry into the pleural cavity was avoided. A myocutaneous flap was utilized for soft tissue coverage. Muscle flap selection is largely dependent on the location of the chest wall defect. Two of the most commonly used muscles are the latissimus dorsi and the pectoralis major. The ipsilateral pectoralis major muscle in this patient was removed during the radical mastectomy years before. The past breast/chest wall irradiation would have rendered the ipsilateral pectoralis muscle an unacceptable tissue flap in any case. The arc of rotation of the contralateral pectoralis major muscle is inadequate. The composite figure shows a cadaver prep of a latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap based on the thoracodorsal neurovascular pedicle. This robust tissue flap can be mobilized with an adequate arc of rotation to permit transfer to the upper anterior chest wall. The created posterior soft tissue defect can be successfully skin grafted. An intraoperative photograph of this patient with the flap tacked into place is shown.

title: chest wall; trauma; flail chest; associated injuries
question_text: A 52-year-old woman was involved in a motor vehicle collision. She was breathing spontaneously. During transport to the hospital, she was noted to have a plate of right anterolateral chest wall including portions of ribs three through six that moved in with inspiration and moved out with exhalation. During full trauma evaluation in the emergency department, which of the following associated injuries is most likely?
critique:
Flail chest injury is defined as fracture of two or more ribs in two or more places, which results in an isolated, unstable segment of chest wall. This flail chest wall segment moves paradoxically with respiration (in with inspiration). The direct force required to produce such an injury places the patient at high risk for associated intrathoracic and upper abdominal injuries. While each listed choice is possible, underlying pulmonary contusion is most common.

Effective pain management is critical to facilitate effective cough, deep breathing, and early mobility (if not limited by other injuries). Elaborate tape strapping and chest wall immobilization techniques were formerly popular for these injuries, but paradoxical chest wall motion is seldom severe enough to prohibit adequate spontaneous breathing if pain is resolved. For patients who require mechanical ventilation, consideration should be given to early tracheostomy to optimize clearance of tracheobronchial secretions and to minimize the risk of pneumonia. Operative chest wall stabilization procedures in selected patients have been championed by some surgeons to enhance ventilation efficiency, decrease pain, and shorten the duration of required ventilator support. Severe underlying pulmonary contusion, however, has been cited as a contraindication to early chest wall stabilization.

question_text: Concerning lung cancer pathogenesis, which of the following is true?
critique:
As the field of cancer genetics advances, more is known about the specific genetic alterations that cause both non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Perhaps the most studied oncogene in lung cancer is Ras. Mutations in K-Ras occur in approximately 30% of all lung adenocarcinomas and 15% of all NSCLCs. However, Ras mutations are almost never noted in small cell lung cancer. P53 deletion is also a common event in non-small cell lung cancer. P53 mutation is much more common in the tumors of non-smokers than those of smokers.

A rapidly growing field of inquiry into tumorigenesis is that of promoter methylation. CpG "islands" are areas of increased density of the dinucleotide sequence cytosine-phosphate diester--guanine. They form stretches of DNA up to several thousand base pairs long. In humans there are about 45,000 CpG islands, mostly found at the 5' ends of genes and are largely unmethylated. Methylation of CpG-rich areas in promoters effectively "turns off" expression of downstream genes and may silence protein expression despite a heterozygous genotype. This phenomenon has been identified at genetic loci for the tumor suppressors p16 and APC, among others. Recently, tumors of non-smokers have been demonstrated to be more often positive for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations than for other oncogenes. This finding may have implications for treatment as targeted inhibitors of EGFR have shown considerable therapeutic efficacy in these patients.

question_text: Prior to the National Lung Screening Trial (2002-2007), computed tomography-based lung cancer screening studies demonstrated
critique:
Lung cancer screening was controversial after the publication of these two studies. Because lung cancer currently kills approximately 160,000 people per year, an appropriately performed screening study should demonstrate a disease-specific mortality advantage. However, an effective screening regimen has been elusive.  Non-small cell lung cancer screening has developed increased momentum over the past 15 years with improvements in computed tomography (CT). However, despite a hypothesized reduction in disease-specific mortality with a CT-based screening program of high-risk patients, no study results published prior to 2009 succeeded in demonstrating this. The Early Lung Cancer Action Project (ELCAP) screened 31,567 patients who had a smoking history greater than 10 pack years. Four hundred eighty-four (484) cases of non-small cell lung cancer were detected, and 412 of these were stage I. Of these 375 were resected, of whom 302 were resected within 1 month after diagnosis. Of this last group, the actuarial 10-year survival was 92%. However, the cancer-specific mortality rate in the entire screened population was not improved in the ELCAP study. This may have represented lead-time bias in that early-stage cancers were merely found before they would have been detected without screening. Thus, for each tumor found by screening as compared to the same tumor not screened, survival seemed longer only because the identical tumor was found earlier. Also, over-diagnosis bias, the detection of tumors unlikely to ever produce adverse outcomes, may have contributed.

Other studies also noted that increased detection of small nodules in screening studies do not affect the disease-specific mortality of the screened population. Bach et al. examined CT-screened patient cohorts from the Mayo Clinic, the Moffitt Cancer Center, and Milan. They found higher numbers of early-stage small cancers (and, therefore, increased numbers of operations) in each cohort, but in each case improved disease-specific mortality was not noted. Furthermore, no reduction in advanced lung cancer cases was observed in the screened cohorts. However, as in the ELCAP study, this study contained no control group.

In 2002 the U.S. National Cancer Institute initiated a controlled trial, the National Lung Screening Trial, which randomized long-term, high-risk smokers and former smokers to either CT-based or chest radiograph-based screening. The trial closed in 2007 with initial results (2009) indicating modest advantages for overall mortality and for lung cancer specific mortality in a low-dose CT screening arm compared to PA chest radiography.  Outcomes of this study continue to appear.

question_text: A 53-year-old man presented with right shoulder pain radiating to his arm and fingers. The PA chest radiograph is shown. PET/CT imaging reveals significant FDG uptake within the lesion. No other PET activity is noted within the hilum, mediastinum, or extrathoracic sites. What is the procedure of choice to obtain a diagnosis?
critique:
This patient¬í's symptoms are typical for an apical lung cancer with involvement of the lower brachial plexus (Pancoast). Chest CT or MRI findings typically confirm invasion of the brachial plexus and the apicoposterior chest wall, with C8/T1 involvement causing shoulder and upper extremity pain radiating to the hand. A definitive tissue diagnosis is required to initiate therapy, but the peripheral location of these malignancies renders bronchoscopic techniques unreliable for biopsy. Transthoracic CT-guided needle biopsy is the most effective tool to secure a histological diagnosis. The diagnostic accuracy of CT-guided FNA and core needle biopsy of nodules greater than 1.5 cm exceeds 95%.

Cervical mediastinoscopy to assess nodal metastases is crucial to determine the surgical candidacy of these patients, but the diagnostic yield is low when PET/CT is negative. Thoracoscopic exploration is not optimal because it is invasive, requires a general anesthetic and recovery, and the tumor may be seeded into the pleural space. Supraclavicular node biopsy in the absence of palpable or image-demonstrated adenopathy is not indicated. Metastatic disease and atypical small cell lung cancer would mandate treatment different from standard Pancoast tumor protocols, so initial biopsy is mandatory.

Bimodality therapy consisting of preoperative external beam irradiation followed by resection was the standard of care for invasive apical cancers from 1961 through 2001. The favorable results seen in the Southwest Oncology Group (SWOG) Trial 9416 led to the current recommended treatment regimen of induction chemoradiotherapy for these patients. In this study, patients received two cycles of cisplatin and etoposide with concurrent external beam radiotherapy (45 Gy). Complete pathologic response was seen in 56% of resected specimens and five-year survival for these patients was 54%. Other trials have emphasized potential additional benefit from high-dose radiation therapy, and CT-guided radiation delivery may prove optimal as more experience is gained.

question_text: A 66-year old man with a 3.5 cm right upper lobe tumor is undergoing thoracoscopy for planned lobectomy. Which of the following is an absolute indication to convert to thoracotomy?
critique: The presence of resectable hilar lymph nodes, incomplete fissures, or resectable local invasion does not mandate conversion to thoracotomy. When the chest wall is involved, formal chest wall resection is indicated. VATS techniques may be used in a hybrid manner for hilar and mediastinal dissection, but determination of margins, transmural chest wall resection and extraction of the specimen is facilitated by an overlying incision. When a lung cancer involves the chest wall the principles of resection mandate en bloc removal with clear margins and a thorough mediastinal node dissection. The importance of mediastinal node dissection is apparent when the survival impact of N1 and N2 involvement in this patient group is appreciated.

critique: No prospective randomized trial has compared thoracoscopic (or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)) lobectomy with conventional open lobectomy for resectable non-small cell lung cancer. However, retrospective studies have identified at least equivalent survival between thoracoscopic lobectomy patients and historical controls on a stage-by-stage basis. For pathologic stage IA patients in each of these series, actuarial 5-year survival is approximately 70%. In addition, each of these series describes a significant number (5-10%) of patients who were pathologically N2 despite clinical staging of IA. This demonstrates that thorough mediastinal lymph node sampling/dissection was performed as part of each procedure. Two small studies demonstrated improved survival after thoracoscopic lobectomy and postulated that decreased inflammatory mediators may be responsible, but neither was controlled and neither group has presented long-term followup.

critique: Concurrent chemoradiation alone or neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by surgery are accepted treatment regimens for stage IIIA NSCLC. Historically it has been thought that radiation to definitive treatment doses of 60 Gy or higher prior to surgery resulted in unacceptably high complication rates, particularly with bronchial stump healing. However, recent data contradicts this and reopens questions about the limits and benefits of maximally aggressive preoperative preparation of patients for resection. The success of CT-guided radiation in early stage lung cancer provokes interest in its use in more advanced disease, but the spatial relationships of advanced primary tumors and nodal spread negate the strategy of extreme doses/small treatment numbers as a preoperative treatment option. The possible superiority of trimodality therapy versus chemoradiation alone for stage IIIA NSCLC awaits the results of the Intergroup 0139 study, which addresses this question.

title: lung cancer; oncogenesis; signaling pathway mutations; MAPK
question_text: Which of the following signaling pathways is most frequently mutated in primary lung adenocarcinoma?
critique:
PI3-K/protein kinase B (AKT) pathway is associated with radiation resistance mechanisms: intrinsic radiosensitivity, tumor cell proliferation, and hypoxia. The Wnt signaling transduction pathway plays an important role in both embryonic development and tumorigenesis through its target genes. Mutations in its components, including Œ≤-catenin, are responsible for the genesis of some human lung cancers. Mutation rates for these two gene pathways are less frequent than p53 or Ras.

The p53 gene encodes for a nuclear phosphoprotein involved in the regulation of cell proliferation. Alterations of either the gene or its protein product are one of the most common changes identified in human malignancies. In resected lung cancers, point mutations of the p53 gene have been found in all histologic types, including approximately 45% of resected non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and even more frequently in SCLC. However, alterations in the EGFR/Ras/MAPK signaling axis represent the most common mutations in NSCLC, with up to 2/3 of lung adenocarcinomas demonstrating mutations in the pathway. These mitogen- (or growth factor-) activated protein kinase aberrations, which require activation by growth factors such as EGF, are responsible for unregulated cancer cell growth.

critique: Historically, patients with completely resected (R0) N1 non-small cell lung cancer had only about a 50% 5-year disease-free survival. Improved outcomes have been sorely needed, and a clear benefit for postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy was demonstrated only recently. The International Adjuvant Lung Cancer Trial (IALT) results of 1867 randomized patients were reported in 2004, using 3-4 cycle cisplatin-based regimens that also included etoposide, vinorelbine, vinblastine or vindesine. Postop radiotherapy use varied among participating institutions. Additional high quality international and national trials have confirmed the benefits of additional postoperative treatment for patients with pathologic N1 disease. Improvements of 5-10% with cisplatin-based chemotherapy were achieved, and patients with Stage II versus Stage IB disease appeared to benefit most from postoperative treatment. While this improvement may be considered modest, it is the first demonstration of extended survival beyond what can be provided by surgery alone. Ongoing trials with alternate cytotoxic agents, growth factor targeting compounds, vaccine therapy, immune modulators, irradiation and novel insights from genomic/proteomic research may more effectively identify high-risk patients and better address the micrometastatic disease that is so frequently present before resection.

Based upon the PET/CT scan, this patient has clinical T1N2Mx stage IIIA non-small cell lung cancer. The enlarged, PET-avid right paratracheal lymph node suggests ipsilateral N2 disease. Optimal treatment of patients with pathologic N2 disease remains controversial. The overall 5-year survival is 10-25% for this subgroup of stage IIIA patients. N2 disease confers a higher risk of both local recurrence and development of distant metastatic disease vs. N1 or N0 disease.

Current treatment options include induction chemotherapy +/- radiation therapy followed by surgery, surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy +/- radiation therapy, or chemotherapy + radiation therapy without surgery. Long-term survival of patients with N2 disease is significantly better if complete resection is accomplished. Single station N2 disease identified at thoracotomy portends a better long term survival compared to patients with involved multi-station N2 nodes. Regarding induction therapy with chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy prior to surgery, patients who have sustained a complete pathologic response to induction therapy have improved survival compared to those with residual disease or disease progression.

Adjuvant chemotherapy after resection of NSCLC with N2 disease is beneficial. The absolute improvement in 5-year relapse free survival has ranged from 5%-11% in clinical trials. A meta-analysis by the Non-small Cell Lung Cancer Collaborative Group demonstrated an absolute improvement in 5-year survival with adjuvant therapy of 5% with platinum based regimens. Most historical data on adjuvant external beam radiation therapy (XRT) has failed to demonstrate any survival advantage. Adjuvant XRT has been shown to decrease locoregional recurrence in stage IIIA lung cancer, but without improvement in overall or relapse-free survival. More contemporary data regarding adjuvant XRT suggest a possible survival benefit in patients with N2 disease but not with N1 disease.

question_text: What is a minimum acceptable bronchial resection margin length for NSCLC?
critique:
Although a bronchial margin of 2 cm is typically recommended for lung resection in NSCLC, little evidence supports this distance. The best evidence is in the case of R0 versus R1 resections. Micro- or macroscopic disease at the bronchial resection margin has a worse recurrence and survival rates than an R0 or negative margin, independent of the distance involved.

A related topic is the minimum number of nodes in the pathologic examination required to accurately stage lung cancer. That number varies among published reports, but characterization of approximately 14 nodes or more appears necessary. If fewer nodes are reported, understaging is a risk. Curiously, this is the same number required for general colorectal cancer operations. The requirement that surgeons must remove or sample appropriate stations to achieve these numbers is obvious. Pathologists must take the time to dissect specimens and review individual nodes that are sent separately.

question_text: A 74-year-old woman underwent an uncomplicated intrapericardial left pneumonectomy for a non-small cell lung cancer that involved the pulmonary hilum (T3N0). Postoperatively the patient was noted to be hoarse, and aspiration of thin liquids was noted on a videofluoroscopic swallow study. Which of the following is the best initial management option for this patient?
critique:
The postoperative symptoms of hoarseness and aspiration suggest that the patient has a vocal cord paralysis. Removal of a malignant neoplasm of the lung or esophagus commonly requires dissection around a vagus nerve and/or its recurrent laryngeal branch. Vocal cord paralysis is a well recognized complication of thoracic surgery and can be a result of frank nerve removal because of tumor invasion or, more commonly, a neurapraxia secondary to manipulation during surgery. Patient tolerance of vocal cord paralysis is variable and depends on the ability of the affected vocal cord to move and the opposing vocal cord to cross the midline in compensation. Compensatory mechanisms tend to be less robust in older patients. Retrospective studies have shown that vocal cord paralysis is associated with significant postoperative morbidity. Inability to protect the glottic aperture from aspiration is especially dangerous in the pneumonectomy patient and early recognition and intervention for vocal cord paralysis is effective at minimizing complications.

The uncomplicated nature of this patient's operation suggests that the recurrent laryngeal nerve likely suffered neurapractic injury during left hilar dissection. Since this may require up to one year for full recovery, injection with a temporizing material such as gelfoam or collagen is the best option to quickly strengthen the voice and prevent aspiration. Vocal cord injection is relatively simple and can be done with a combination of topical, local and IV sedation. Continuing an oral diet in this patient poses a risk of aspiration pneumonia. Feeding tube nutrition and tracheostomy tube placement are not necessary. Unless there is documentation that the recurrent nerve was removed, cut or severely damaged (recovery not expected), then medialization that involves insertion of a permanent implant is not appropriate acute intervention.

question_text: A 54-year-old woman underwent right pneumonectomy for non small cell cancer. Twenty-six months later a solitary brain metastasis was identified and treated by gamma knife. She developed a productive cough and the chest radiograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
critique:
Postpneumonectomy bronchopleural fistula occurs with a frequency of 1.5 to 4.5 percent. This complication carries high mortality ranging from 29 to 79 percent, but prompt drainage is effective at controlling ongoing symptoms of infection and minimizing contamination of the opposite lung. Mediastinal fixation occurs within a few months after pneumonectomy, so shift and compromise of venous return are not likely to be problematic in this patient.

Whether definitive correction of this patient's fistula is prudent depends on the status of her cancer and general medical condition. All direct therapies to close the fistula will fail if there is cancer at the bronchial stump. While animal experiments have shown some success, endobronchial glues, sealants and plugs are ineffective strategies for this large space at this time. The added benefit of stent coverage is unclear if the space is effectively drained. Routine, first line pulmonary function testing includes forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1), and diffusing capacity (DLCO). In general, a predicted postoperative FEV1>40% and DLCO>40% is desired to avoid the high risk of postoperative respiratory insufficiency. Preoperative FEV1 and DLCO < 40% is considered high risk for pulmonary resection, although there are exceptions. Quantitative ventilation/perfusion scans may help identify high risk patients that could tolerate lung resection even with such a low FEV1 and DLCO.

Anemia causes an artifactually low measured DLCO value. When interpreting pulmonary function tests or risk assessment, the "adjusted" DLCO (corrected for anemia) should be considered instead of the measured value. A patient with predominant upper lobe emphysema may actually benefit from resection. Both CT scans and ventilation/perfusion images help to identify patients with heterogeneous emphysema that predominantly involves an upper lobe. Resecting a tumor in a poorly functional upper lobe may be feasible in such patients.

Cardiopulmonary exercise tests measure maximum oxygen consumption (VO2max). This value is an adjunct to standard PFTs, particularly in patients with marginal function or when dyspnea seems to be out of proportion to standard measured PFTs. VO2max > 15 ml/(kg*min) generally indicates normal risk, although a threshold of 20 is preferred by some surgeons. VO2max < 10 is generally considered prohibitive for resection. VO2max = 10-15 ml/kg/min is considered high risk, although not necessarily prohibitive.

If VO2max testing is not available, a basic exercise testing such as the 6 minute walk test can be performed in the office. A six minute walk distance > 1000 meters corresponds to a VO2max > 20 ml/(kg*min). Achieving a distance < 250 meters generally corresponds to VO2max < 15. Another meaningful exercise test is a simple stair climbing challenge. While there may be variability in the speed of climbing, step height and number of steps, an inability to walk one flight of stairs generally corresponds to a VO2max < 10 ml/(kg*min).

Using absolute numbers such as FEV1 greater than 1.5 L has the potential to bias against smaller patients and women, so spirometry and DLCO should be viewed as complementary tests. In formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), several measured parameters are measured and correlated, including exercise EKG, heart rate, response to exercise, minute ventilation, and oxygen uptake per minute. However, patients with a VO2max less than 10 ml/(kg*min) have a very high risk of postoperative complications. Desaturation during exercise testing has been shown to be associated with an increased risk for postoperative complications. Greater than a 4% desaturation indicates an increased risk for perioperative complications.

If CPET is unavailable, other types of exercise testing may be performed. Stair climbing has historically been used, although it is not performed in a standardized manner. Other surrogate tests are the shuttle walk and the 6-minute walk test, but the correlation of these to VO2max is poor.

Although QOL is difficult to measure and although multiple different instruments have been used across studies, subjective quality-of-life studies reproducibly demonstrate less pain in the short-term (within 72 hours) after thoracoscopic lobectomy. Other metrics are somewhat controversial, but several studies have objectively addressed pulmonary function after lobectomy and found significantly superior short-term outcomes in the thoracoscopy group in FEV1 within 36 hours and oxygenation at 15 hours. Some advantages may persist, as one study demonstrated improved vital capacity for up to 6 months in thoracoscopic lobectomy patients. Other reports, however, found pain assessment at three weeks, spirometry after two weeks and 6-minute walk results at two weeks to be similar between patients after conventional thoracotomy and thoracoscopy. While these data are encouraging, few data exist regarding long-term QOL in thoracoscopic lobectomy patients. Several reports suggest no long-term differences, but the literature is growing and enthusiasm for minimally invasive resection for early stage lung cancer is increasing. Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) are abnormal communications between pulmonary arteries and veins that bypass the alveoli. They become symptomatic as a consequence of right-to-left shunting with single or multiple draining arteries and veins. Pulmonary AVMs may be single or multiple. Systemic desaturation can be demonstrated in most patients with significant shunts, but potential hemoptysis and major neurologic complications mandate aggressive treatment. Approximately 70% of all PAVMs occur in association with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) and more than 20% of patients with HHT develop pulmonary arteriovenous malformations. Mucosal and epidermal AVMs (telangiectasias), such as those seen in the patient's photo, are typical of this autosomal dominant syndrome.

The natural history of PAVMs is gradual enlargement, and diagnosis is often made with contrast CT. Surgical resection was applied to most patients in the past, but pulmonary angiography with embolization has become the usual initial treatment. The reported overall success rate for embolotherapy is 83%. After initial treatment with balloon occlusion or coil embolization the recanalization rate is approximately 8%. When applied again for failure, lasting occlusion is achieved in only 25%. Embolotherapy complications include device migration or systemic embolization, transient ischemic attack (TIA), stroke, cerebral abscess, and angina. Resection remains effective therapy for all PAVMs and is optimal treatment for large lesions and embolotherapy failures.

Pulmonary CT angiography has supplanted contrast angiography as the diagnostic imaging gold standard in the workup of pulmonary embolism. Quick data acquisition is an advantage, and subtle findings can characterize central vascular flow dynamics and right heart function as well. In dire situations contrast reflux or pooling into the azygos vein and IVC can be related to cardiogenic shock. In more normal circumstances it can occur from an infusion rate that exceeds 5 mL/second (3-4 mL/second is routine). However, such reflux may not be imaged if normal forward flow is maintained. The severity or conspicuity of the reflux may also coincide closely with ventricular and atrial systole and less so with diastole. Tricuspid regurgitation is closely associated with reflux into the IVC, especially during ventricular systole, which transmits the elevated pressures and retrograde flow into the IVC and hepatic veins. Cardiac changes with dilation of the right heart chambers may include myocardial hypertrophy (chronic), straightening or left shifting of the interventricular septum or dilation of the coronary sinus. Etiologies of elevated right heart pressures include right heart failure, tricuspid valve disease, increased right ventricular mass, pericardial constriction, pulmonary valve stenosis, and pulmonary hypertension (acute and chronic).

With contrast reflux into the supradiaphragmatic IVC only, as in additional Figure 1, mild to moderate increases in right heart pressures are likely present. Contrast reflux extending into the infradiaphragmatic IVC or hepatic veins (additional Figures 2 and 3) suggests moderate-to-severe elevation of pressures (> 40 mmHg mean). Straightening of the interventricular septum (see the additional Figure) or bowing of the septum into the left ventricle indicates a systolic pressure greater than 60 mmHg. In the additional Figure there is pulmonary arterial mosaic perfusion and right ventricular myocardial hypertrophy (wall thickness 4 mm or greater), each of which is associated with long-standing outflow pressure elevation. The images presented in the question show hepatic vein reflux, RV hypertrophy and septal bowing, each of which is consistent with severe pulmonary hypertension. Without further testing the flow void in the left PA must be assumed to be a mosaic flow artifact rather than a pulmonary embolus. Chronic or acute-on-chronic PE, however, may be a cause of this patient's pulmonary hypertension, which was worsened by the lung resection.

Silicosis and fungal or mycobacterial infections may incite lymphadenitis, which may secondarily calcify and erode into an airway or other mediastinal structures. Histoplasma capsulatum is the most common pathogen in the United States. Prophylactic removal of calcified peribronchial and mediastinal nodes is not indicated. Symptomatic broncholithiasis (cough, hemoptysis, and dyspnea) is found about equally in men and women. Traditional teaching is that broncholiths must not be manipulated for fear of massive hemorrhage. Failed extraction and early and late complications, including recurrent broncholithiasis, were frequent in the selected patients who underwent bronchoscopic procedures. Broncholithectomy via thoracotomy was the alternative, with extraction success in nearly all patients, minimal mortality, acceptably low perioperative complications and no recurrent broncholithiasis. Endobronchial stents and additional instrumentation have now challenged this traditional dogma when elective care is possible. Broncholiths have been described as either fixed or mobile, characteristics that may be determined by rigid bronchoscopy. When mobility is clearly demonstrated, and in the absence of massive hemoptysis, a Nd-YAG laser may be useful to control inflammatory bleeding around the erosion site, and the holmium laser may assist fragmentation of a broncholith for forceps extraction. Endobronchial balloons may be useful for local tamponade and fragment clearance.

The CT image shows paratracheal hemothorax or a mediastinal hematoma, which suggest vascular erosion. Broncholiths eroding into the proximal intermediate bronchus are evident, but endobronchial interventions are not reasonable treatment choices for this patient. Massive hemoptysis has already occurred, and together with the CT appearance it is clear that a vascular complication is also present. Whether related to a bronchial artery or pulmonary artery, the scope of the underlying trouble cannot be addressed by bronchoscopic methods. The peribronchial node erosions seen at bronchoscopy seem unlikely to be responsible for the witnessed bleeding, so a distal bronchial or parenchymal source is suspected. Arteriographic embolization is virtually never successful definitive therapy because of the complex inflammation and potential dual sources of bleeding. Incomplete immediate bleeding control, secondary complications and frequent recurrent bleeding are common. However, preoperative embolization may be considered to minimize operative blood loss. Thoracotomy is indicated for this patient. Decortication followed by a parenchymal sparing operation with extraction and curettage of the calcified nodes, airway repair and viable tissue interposition/reinforcement is the goal. An intercostal muscle flap may be a useful adjunct. If repair is not possible, then anatomic resection is the best option. Tissue cultures must be taken, which will guide long-term antibiotic treatment for the underlying pathogens.

The two types of bronchopulmonary sequestrations account for 0.15% to 6.4% of all congenital lung malformations. These anomalies have no tracheobronchial connections, the blood supply is systemic, and most have pulmonary venous drainage. Three quarters of these anomalies are intralobar sequestrations, which are abnormal lung tissue along or within normal lung that is invested by normal pleura. Extralobar sequestrations (25%) have a separate pleural investment. Sequestrations are most commonly located in a lung base with a 2:1 predominance on the left side. The blood supply often arises from the descending thoracic aorta but multiple arteries may be present. Uncommonly, some or all of the blood supply originates below the diaphragm and ascends into the lung via the inferior pulmonary ligament.

Intralobar sequestrations are typically symptomatic at diagnosis, with recurrent pulmonary infections, pain, chronic cough, hemoptysis and/or fever in teenagers or young adults. Diagnostic delay is common. They are usually not associated with other congenital anomalies. However, the venous drainage is usually systemic through the azygos and hemiazygos systems. Extralobar sequestrations also have aortic blood supplies, but half are associated with other congenital anomalies (cardiac, diaphragm, lung) and 80% occur in males.

Extralobar sequestrations may present in the first few months of life from compression of normal lung parenchyma, and about half are diagnosed before one year of age. Approximately 10% of extralobar sequestrations communicate with the esophagus or stomach. This should be evaluated preoperatively with an upper gastrointestinal study.

Resection is the recommended treatment for both types of sequestration. Resection of only the sequestrum can be done for extralobar lesions, but lobectomy is usually necessary for intralobar sequestrations. An important principal of management is adequate preoperative imaging to define anatomy and blood supply to facilitate early identification and control of the arterial blood supply at surgery. Inadvertent division of a systemic collateral artery with retraction of the vessel into the mediastinum or abdomen can be a lethal event. Otherwise, postoperative complications are rare and long-term outcomes are excellent.

Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (CCAM) results from segmental bronchial atresia. Lung distal to the atretic segment is dysplastic, and this development is almost always unilateral and. Type I CCAM is most common and is characterized by large cysts within a single lobe. Type II represents a collection of multiple small cysts and Type III is a more solid mass of adenomatoid hyperplasia and microcysts. CCAM may be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasound. This curious malformation also may spontaneously regress after birth, and several anomalies are associated, including renal agenesis, jejunal atresia, diaphragmatic hernia, hydrocephalus, cardiac malformations (truncus, tetralogy), and skeletal anomalies.

Diagnosis of CCAM can often be made by prenatal ultrasound, and the differential diagnosis includes diaphragmatic hernia, mediastinal cysts (bronchogenic, enteric, pericardial), neuroblastoma, and bronchopulmonary sequestration. The cysts grow most rapidly between 20-25 weeks gestation. Surveillance is warranted because polyhydramnios or fetal hydrops can develop as a result of esophageal or cardiac compression by the mass. Fetal surgery for these lesions is feasible, with aspiration of Type I lesions and resection of Type II.

If not noted on prenatal screening, then affected patients often present in early infancy with cough and recurrent infections. Chest radiographs may show single or multiple cysts or a solid mass. Initial treatment options include observation in young asymptomatic infants. If spontaneous resolution does not occur then resection should be undertaken regardless of symptom status because of the potential for malignancy. CCAMS seem to have a potential for malignant transformation into or association with bronchoalveolar carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, pulmonary blastoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma. Pulmonary lobectomy is the most common procedure, but caution is advised -- as with sequestrations, a systemic arterial supply is found in some CCAMs. Surgical outcomes are excellent.

The case describes a patient with primary coccidioidomycosis (valley fever, San Joaquin Valley fever). Coccidioides immitus is a fungus found in the soil endemic to the southwestern United States. Spores are inhaled and often cause no symptoms with primary infection. In symptomatic cases, patients present with nonspecific flu-like symptoms of fever, chills, cough, pleuritic chest pain and malaise. Occasionally, erythema multiforme or erythema nodosum can be seen, particularly in women. This woman's chest film shows a left upper lobe nodule. Severe pulmonary complications are unusual but may include pneumonia, lung nodules, fibrocavitary disease, empyema and ARDS. Progressive infection is more common in pregnant women and immunocompromised patients.

The diagnosis can be made by histological analysis of tissue, culture, or serologic testing. The fungal DNA can be amplified or hybridized with fungal RNA for specific identification. Gross histology typically reveals mature fungal spherules with endospore formation. Cryptococcosis occurs predominantly in immunosuppressed patients and is typically caused by the organism Cryptococcus neoformans, an encapsulated yeast. The major sources in the environment include soil contaminated with pigeon droppings or eucalyptus trees. Infection begins following inhalation of the yeast. The most common sites of involvement are the lungs and the central nervous system. Pulmonary symptoms consist of fever, cough, and dyspnea which may progress to hypoxemia and respiratory failure. Imaging shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates often worse in the lower lobes, as in this case. The diagnosis is made by positive culture from sputum or biopsy specimen or by special staining on histopathology (India ink or mucin stain).

Amphotericin B is the most appropriate therapy for severe infections, and it may be possible to transition to fluconazole if clinical improvement is rapid. Several recent reports suggest that amphotericin B plus flucytosine may be optimal acute therapy, particularly for meningitis. Parameters of HIV infection status and "fungal burden" can each be quantified, and they influence treatment recommendations and drug dosages. The primary role of surgery is to assist in diagnosis by lung biopsy of diffuse infiltrative lesions or excision of a solitary pulmonary nodule.

critique:
Endemic areas for paragonimiasis include Africa, Central and South America, and Asia. Several species are responsible for human infection by this hermaphroditic fluke. Transmission is through raw or undercooked seafood, and the life cycle involves an intermediate snail. Ingested larvae enter the lungs, and manifestations can include pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and eosinophilia. Further reproduction of the worms can lead to infiltrates and hemoptysis with eggs recoverable in the sputum. Untreated pulmonary infection leads to pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, and persistent pleural effusion. Imaging findings may be confused with tuberculosis.

Amebiasis, which is infection by Entamoeba histolytica, follows ingestion of mature cysts in fecally contaminated food, water, or by hand transfer. Cysts rupture in the small intestine and the released trophozoites continue movement to the large intestine and multiply. Invasion of mucosa leads to liver, brain and lung infections (pleuropulmonary abscess). Intestinal manifestations of infection dominate the spectrum of symptoms, but secondary spread leads to predicted end-organ signs and symptoms.

Schistosomiasis (bilharziosis or snail fever) is, arguably, the second most socioeconomically devastating disease after malaria. The lungs are an intermediate stop in the life cycle of human schistosome infection, which begins with skin penetration by a larval form. The organism burrows into a post-capillary venule and then travels to the lungs. After additional 8-10 days of maturation it migrates to the liver sinusoids. The only unique pulmonary symptom is cough, although inflammation and late pulmonary hypertension have been reported.

Most human hydatid disease of the lung is caused by larvae of the dog tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. Humans are accidental, intermediate hosts and acquire the organism by ingestion of eggs present on dog fir or the local environment. Eggs hatch in the small intestine, enter the portal circulation and then are systemically distributed. In the lungs the immature organism lodges and grows to form a fluid-filled cyst. The reproductive potential within the cyst is prodigious. These are commonly solitary, well circumscribed, polycyclic, unruptured, at the lung bases, and involve posterior segments. Most patients are asymptomatic. The cyst wall is minimally antigenic and the organism produces "anticomplement factor" that may dampen the human immune response. Growth of cysts can be impressive (up to 20 cm) and local intrathoracic compressive effects may cause symptoms of airway or esophageal obstruction. A cyst can rupture spontaneously, from trauma or from secondary infection. Rupture into the airway leads to expectoration of fluid containing scolices, and intrapleural rupture leads to dissemination of the parasite within the pleural cavity. Release of antigenic material results in fever and an acute hypersensitivity response (hives, wheezing, possible anaphylaxis).

Surgery is indicated in most cases of pulmonary cystic echinococcosis as operative mortality is low (1-2%), morbidity rates are acceptable and the recurrence rate is low (1-3%). Resection is the treatment of choice since the parasite can be completely removed and the patient cured. The surgical options for lung cysts include lobectomy, wedge resection, pericystectomy, intact endocystectomy and capitonnage (drainage, debridement and cyst closure). The surgeon must guard against intraoperative dissemination by delivering the intact cyst or by initial cyst aspiration and injection of hypertonic saline, povidone-iodine, formalin, ethanol or hydrogen peroxide. If possible, preoperative preparation with albendazole is ideal.

This man has incompletely treated pneumonia with chronic empyema. Initial septic shock resolved with appropriate treatment, but imaging and diagnostic tests indicate that the next step should be to proceed with complete drainage of the empyema and decortication of the left lung. Further nonoperative management will be futile, as medical care has reached maximum benefit. The CT of another patient (see added figure) shows a multiloculated collection with thickened pleura and residual gas bubbles from thoracenteses for culture. The operative approach should not limit the effectiveness of the operation, and an open thoracotomy should be used if needed to achieve complete expansion of the lung. Simply draining the empyema without decortication will result in persistent local sepsis and a poor clinical outcome.

Current principles of empyema management were defined in the work of the "Empyema Commission" of the United States Army during World War I (1918). When treatment is delayed beyond 1-2 weeks from the initial infection, typical best care has been open thoracotomy with excision/debridement of the empyema space, complete decortication of the lung, and drainage of the chest. Such operations are tedious, but it is now possible to achieve similar technical endpoints with minimally invasive methods with equal operative times. Some authors have found VATS for formal decortication and drainage to offer benefits over thoracotomy with respect to time to chest tube removal and hospital stay.

Streptokinase and other lytic agents have generated cyclical interest for nonoperative, "medical" management of early empyema. The First Multicenter Intrapleural Sepsis Trial (MIST1) was a contemporary double-blind trial in the U.K. that found no benefit to streptokinase (twice daily for 3 days) in terms of mortality, rate of surgery, radiographic outcomes, or length of the hospital stay between streptokinase and placebo. Serious adverse events (chest pain, fever, or allergic reactions) were more common with streptokinase. Streptokinase is no longer available in the United States, but using tissue plasmin activator (tPA) and deoxyribonuclease (DNAse) has proponents. When applied to empyema of longer duration (late fibropurulent or organizing) the efficacy of nonoperative intrapleural treatment is nil.

critique:
Diffuse interstitial lung disease is a heterogenous group of pathologies that includes over 200 diseases. Thoracic surgeons are often asked to perform a lung biopsy to achieve a diagnosis for optimal treatment of these diseases. The biopsy, however, is diagnostic and not therapeutic. Delays in diagnosis are frequent, and many patients are critically ill (requiring oxygen or mechanical ventilation) by the time a surgical biopsy is requested. Three questions are important to ask:

1. Is the biopsy necessary to make a diagnosis?
2. Will knowing histologic details change therapy?
3. Will biopsy-driven therapy change the outcome?

Flexible bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy has a low morbidity rate (about 3%) and can often be performed as an ambulatory procedure, making it an attractive first procedure to obtain a lung biopsy. The success rate of this procedure varies widely, but 25 to 60% has been reported. In immunocompetent patients with interstitial lung disease, an adequate lung biopsy has been found to change therapy between 50% and 80% of the time. 'The diagnostic yield is low in patients with truly homogeneous, diffuse involvement; it is much better when one or a few areas of the lung are more focally involved. Because of the complex, often advanced lung pathologies in these patients, perioperative mortality is quite significant. For non-ventilated hospitalized patients it is about 30% and for an ambulatory patient 15%. Ventilated immunocompetent patients are critically ill, and the diagnostic yield of the biopsy must be weighed against a mortality rate of nearly 60%. Response rates and survival are each substantially worse in patients with respiratory failure. More than half of patients who have an "emergency" biopsy die, and the results of the biopsy rarely suggest any change other than immunosuppression.

The superiority of a thoracoscopic biopsy versus a mini-thoracotomy for lung biopsy is still debated. One study by Miller, et al compared the two in a prospective randomized fashion and found no difference in diagnostic yield, operative time, hospital length of stay, complications, pain scores or post-operative spirometry. If single lung ventilation can be done and tolerated, thoracoscopy affords better ipsilateral lung visualization and biopsy access than a mini-thoracotomy. An expeditious thoracotomy without lung isolation is safer for patients with respiratory failure, but the limited impact of a tissue diagnosis and the associated mortality in this group of patients argue against doing the biopsy.

question_text: A 59-year-old man underwent an uneventful right upper lobectomy for early stage lung cancer. Four days later he is febrile to 38.9oC and tachycardic to 120 bpm. Physical exam reveals no breath sounds on the operated side. His chest radiograph is shown. The best next step in management is
critique:
Torsion of the lung about its bronchovascular pedicle is a rare complication following thoracotomy, with a reported incidence of 0.089%. Although right middle lobe torsion is legendary, any remaining lobe, bi-lobe, or lung can become torsed. Predisposing factors to lobar torsion include division of the inferior pulmonary ligament, failure to re-expand the lung (collapsed lung parenchyma at the completion of the case), residual pleural effusion or pneumothorax, and a remaining "complete" fissure.

Lung torsion usually leads to loss of the involved lobe(s) due to ischemia, and recognizing lobar torsion requires a high degree of suspicion. Fever, tachycardia, and loss of breath sounds on the involved side are the most common findings. The chest radiograph can show opacification of the involved lobe or lobes, which may occupy an unusual position. The chest film in this case shows an atelectatic right middle lobe following upper lobectomy, due to twisting and occlusion of the middle lobe bronchus. Inversion of the pulmonary vasculature may be suspected if pulmonary vasculature markings extend laterally from the hilum and then sweep superiorly (as opposed to inferiorly). Another subtle hint may be a change in the angle of displacement of the hilum in a direction inconsistent with the lobe that appears atelectatic (e.g., right middle lobe collapse with an elevated right hilum.

The differential diagnosis for some of the signs and symptoms of torsion includes pneumonia, mucus plugging, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and pleural effusion. On bronchoscopy, the torsed airway will be narrowed with a "fish mouth" appearance. It may be possible to push through this stenosis, finding copious secretions trapped behind. Lobar torsion is a surgical emergency with a goal of untwisting the involved lung. This can be done thoracoscopically or with a thoracotomy. Once untwisted and inflated, the involved lung should be assessed for viability.

Lobar torsion is prevented by ensuring the remaining lobes inflate completely and are correctly oriented in the chest at the end of the case. If the remaining hilar bronchovascular pedicle is narrow, then twisting can be prevented by anchoring the lung tissue at two points (the hilum and somewhere else), thus creating a line of fixation. For example, after right upper lobectomy the lateral edge of the middle lobe can be sutured or stapled to the lower lobe.

The incidence of regional or mediastinal lymph node metastases has only rarely been reported in pulmonary metastasectomy series. The International Registry of Lung Metastases claimed a 5% incidence among 5206 patients. However, only 4.6% of the patients in the registry had lymph nodes sampled or removed at the time of metastasectomy. A Mayo Clinic series found a 28.6% incidence of metastatic lymph nodes when complete lymph node dissections were done. As expected, this was an indicator of poor prognosis. Three-year survival for patients with involved lymph nodes was 38% vs. 69% for patients with negative nodes (p<0.001). No matter which operative approach is chosen for pulmonary metastasectomy, mediastinal lymph node sampling or dissection should be considered for malignancies metastatic to the lungs.

critique:
This patient's clinical scenerio is consistent with post-pneumonectomy bronchopleural fistula. Watery sputum production with fever and malaise plus an air fluid level in the post-pneumonectomy space are classical signs of this condition. The sputum cytology may show acute inflammatory cells, but inflammatory findings are not diagnostic. Additional imaging with chest radiographs, CT studies or laminograms (now obsolete) may also suggest a bronchopleural fistula, but none of these studies has enough resolution for definitive diagnosis. Right pleural fluid sampling will be consistent with empyema but will not prove whether a bronchopleural fistula is present or not.

Bronchoscopy is the most definitive test to establish the diagnosis of post-pneumonectomy bronchopleural fistula. It will also show the size of the opening, length of the bronchial stump and characteristics of the tissue in the bronchial stump (including tumor or necrotic tissue). Even small openings can be identified by watching for bubbles at the stump during respiration. The residual pneumothorax left after pneumonectomy may not resolve completely in all patients after one month, but only a small apical cap is expected. The residual air in the chest radiograph is suspicious, and bronchoscopy should be performed in all patients suspected of having a bronchopleural fistula after pneumonectomy.

Postpneumonectomy syndrome is due to excessive mediastinal shift after pneumonectomy, which causes compression of the remaining bronchus and consequent symptoms. It is rare, but most common after right pneumonectomy. Exaggerated displacement of the heart and counterclockwise rotation of the great vessels and trachea may develop, and stretching and narrowing of the left main stem bronchus between aorta and pulmonary artery can result. Diagnosis is typically made many years after pneumonectomy.

Medical management is not effective for this mechanical obstruction. Endobronchial stenting and instilling air in the post-pneumonectomy space have been tried with poor results. Lung transplantation for this condition is not indicated since it can be corrected. Reoperation to reposition the mediastinum can be successful, but complete dissection of mediastinum and pericardium is required to place a right intrathoracic tissue expander or breast prosthesis in the side of previous resection. The pericardium is also fixed to the sternum to achieve the highest success rate. This operation is considered the treatment of choice for good risk patients.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is the most common causative agent in the pathogenesis of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), and elevated EBV circulating DNA is regarded as a marker for PTLD in solid organ (including lung) transplant recipients. An EBV negative recipient who receives a donor organ from a EBV positive donor is at highest risk for developing PTLD, and these malignancies often develop within the first year after transplantation. "Standard" serologic antibody testing seems not to keep pace with the clinical aspects of EBV infection and response in these patients, likely because of the modulated immunosuppression status. Seroconversion does not occur in all mismatched recipients, but almost all cases of PTLD are associated with seroconversion. Lung transplant recipients with a high degree of HLA matching when D/R EBV was mismatched had an elevated risk of PTLD. The use of cytolytic induction therapy at the time of transplant has been associated with higher rates of PTLD. Agents chosen for immunosuppression, identified allograft rejection, and infection each influence survival.

Most PTLD are of B lymphocyte origin. Anti B-cell monoclonal antibody therapy (rituximab) has proven most helpful to treat PTLD, but mortality from this complication remains high. FDG-PET scanning is a helpful tool to stage and to gauge response of malignant lymphoma. CMV mismatch status between donor and recipient and prior episodes of acute rejection are not associated with an increased risk of developing PTLD.

Following a single lung transplant pulmonary venous obstruction is responsible for serious morbidity and potential death. Pulmonary venous anastomotic problems are most often identified early after lung transplantation. This vascular complication has been identified much more frequently than arterial problems. Following lung transplantation pulmonary venous obstruction should be suspected if pulmonary edema appears early. Frothy, blood-stained endotracheal tube secretions, refractory hemodynamic instability, and measured wedge pressures that are different on opposite sides (high on the transplanted side) strongly suggest venous obstruction. A chest radiograph or CT scan showing parenchymal consolidation suggests this diagnosis, and either MRI or quantitative ventilation/perfusion scanning may be suggestive but are not diagnostic.

Obstruction may be caused by stenosis of the pulmonary venous anastomosis or partial thrombosis. Both anatomic and functional (flow) information is gained by transesophageal echocardiography with color flow Doppler, a superior test to detect stenosis of the pulmonary veins. A TEE-identified diameter of 0.25 cm or less indicates significant stenosis and is associated with a poor outcome if not treated. This complication can only be managed by surgical revision and refashioning the atrial anastomosis.

Several recipient-specific factors are used to prioritize donor lungs for transplantation. The United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) determines these factors and their weighting to assign a Lung Allocation Score (LAS) to each listed recipient (see figure). Neither dependence on mechanical ventilation nor previous thoracic surgery (or pleurodesis) is a specific contraindication to lung transplantation. Adhesions and anatomic distortion from prior thoracic surgery increase the technical complexity of the transplant procedure and introduce higher risks of postoperative bleeding and phrenic nerve injury. Additional time may also be needed to explant the native lungs. Pulmonary hypertension is a common finding in patients with restrictive lung diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. In 2005, the ISHLT Registry report indicated that IPF was the second most common indication for single-lung transplantation and the third most common indication for bilateral lung transplantation. In patients with primary pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular function improves immediately after transplantation.

Age greater than 65 is not a uniform contraindication to lung transplantation. In the ISHLT Registry report, age greater than 70 is an independent predictor of poor outcome. However, several reports from single centers have shown that selected patients older than 60 have acceptable outcomes. High-dose corticosteroid therapy (i.e., more than 20 mg/day of prednisone) is an absolute contraindication to lung transplantation. Such high doses of corticosteroids have a well-documented negative effect on bronchial healing and induce susceptibility to postoperative infection. If a patient still requires mechanical ventilation at the time of diagnosis, then the complication should be palliated until the patient is weaned. Transmediastinal gunshot injuries present difficult diagnostic and treatment challenges. The velocity and caliber of the missile determine the potential tissue damage, and secondary fragments of bullet and bone may compound the trauma. Patients presenting with hemodynamic instability due to cardiac or great vessel injury require rapid decisions and immediate, heroic operative intervention. Unfortunately, supportive maneuvers are limited, the spectrum of injury is often massive, reconstructive options may be unsatisfactory, and mortality is high.

Patients who present with stable hemodynamics pose a diagnostic dilemma, and although available time may be limited, a rational approach with CT angiography has been shown to be most helpful. Fortunately, after a gunshot wound occult serious injuries are uncommon. Significant cardiovascular injury is less likely when vital signs are relatively stable, but injuries to the trachea, bronchus, and esophagus must be ruled out. Intubation and mechanical ventilation is appropriate for clinical signs of respiratory distress, but positive pressure support should be applied with caution if hilar injury is suspected. Positive pressure ventilation and PEEP enhance the chance of air embolism in this setting.

While invasive studies (endoscopy and angiography) were once standard methods of diagnosing hollow viscous injuries, non-invasive CT imaging is the initial examination of choice for stable patients. CT is rapidly done and it is extremely sensitive for detecting abnormal air and fluid collections that reveal the path of transthoracic projectiles. If the trajectory of the penetrating injury across the mediastinum does not involve the trachea, bronchus or esophagus, then no additional studies are required and observation and supportive care are warranted. If the missile trajectory is central, however, then further evaluation with endoscopy and/or angiography is mandatory.

critique:
This patient has the features of Goodpasture's syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease), also described as "lung purpura with nephritis." Goodpasture was a Boston pathologist investigating the 1918 influenza pandemic. In one autopsy the lung showed extensive bilateral hemorrhage, necrotizing angiitis of the systemic vessels and glomerulonephritis. Patients are typically young men and present with hemoptysis, dyspnea, and acute renal disease.

Goodpasture's disease has now become synonymous with the variant of pulmonary hemorrhage associated with circulating antiglomerular basement membrane antibodies. In this disease antibodies are visualized in the kidney (and less well in the lung) by immunofluorescence as linear staining of the basement membrane (see the figure). These antibodies are a primary differentiation of Goodpasture's from Wegener's granulomatosis. Histologically, the alveoli are filled with red blood cells and there is suggestive evidence of "alveolitis" in the form of neutrophils in and around alveolar capillaries. As in Wegener's granulomatosis, the renal symptoms are more important than the pulmonary symptoms for the outcome.

The clinical assessment is comprehensive and the diagnostic information collected is adequate for diagnosis, although stains for anti-GBM antibodies must be done. The treatment program is plasmapheresis combined with prednisone and cyclophosphamide. Plasmapheresis is beneficial in the acute phase of this disease because it removes circulating antibodies, while these drugs decrease inflammation and minimize new antibody formation. Hemodialysis palliates the renal dysfunction until recovery.

Two definitions have been applied to massive hemoptysis in patients with airway bleeding. One is based on the volume of blood expectorated and the other on the clinical effect. The generally accepted volume threshold is greater than 600 cc of blood in a 24-hour period. The mortality associated with medical management in such patients is 12-50%. If bleeding exceeds 1600 cc in 16 hours, the mortality increases to 75%. Although the single most important risk factor is the rate of bleeding, several other characteristics contribute to mortality, including severe underlying cardiopulmonary disease, the underlying mechanism of hemorrhage, coagulation disorders, decreased or impaired cough, oversedation or altered mental status, generalized malaise, and fatigue. This risk of death should dictate management, as whether there is an opportunity to stabilize and proceed with angiographic embolization, or if immediate operative intervention should be pursued.

If bleeding is brisk enough that the airway must be controlled, options include intubation with a double lumen endotracheal tube or a size 8 single lumen tube for bronchoscopic evacuation of blood and clots. The patient should be positioned with the bleeding side down to prevent drowning. The primary role of flexible bronchoscopy in this setting is to maintain ventilation, to lateralize the source of bleeding and to direct endobronchial blockade. The utility of rigid bronchoscopy in massive hemoptysis should not be overlooked, as rapid clearing of blood and clots is far superior to flexible instrument potential. Anatomically there are three major sources of bleeding: bronchial arteries, bronchial veins and pulmonary arteries. The bronchial arteries are the major source of bleeding in 90% of cases and the pulmonary artery in 5-10%. Therefore, arteriography and embolization can play important roles in treating active and recurrent bleeding.

critique:
Air leaks following pulmonary resection are common and are most often due to alveolar-pleural air leaks rather than broncho-pleural leaks. Although it is unusual for air leaks to persist more than 5-7 days, those leaks that extend beyond seven days are considered prolonged and are responsible for increased morbidity and resource utilization. The majority of prolonged air leaks will seal with watchful waiting. In a few cases extra measures will be required to seal leaks and to facilitate patient recovery. Since most prolonged air leaks will seal without aggressive interventions, a period of a several days to a few weeks of observation is appropriate. This observation period does not necessarily have to be done during an inpatient hospital stay. Several authors suggest that outpatient observation with a Heimlich valve attached to the chest tube is both safe and cost effective.

In the unusual situation where a prolonged air leak does not seal after a 2-3 week observation period, more aggressive measures are indicated. Pleurodesis with either a chemical sclerosing agent or with autologous blood is often effective. Hypertonic glucose solution (D50/W) is not an effective sclerosing agent, but chemotherapeutic agents like bleomycin may help seal prolonged air leaks associated with pulmonary malignancy. If sclerosing agents fail, then reoperation (either open or VATS) is indicated. In a patient who is hemodynamically unstable with a large persistent leak an unusual intervention such as differential ventilation with a double lumen endotracheal tube (via two ventilators) may be necessary.

critique:
Lymphangiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare, benign, but often ultimately debilitating condition that most commonly affects women of childbearing age. An obstructive pattern of disease develops with increase in lung size and marked decrease in lung compliance. At the microscopic level it is characterized by smooth muscle proliferation in bronchioles and venules. The underlying cause of the disease is not clear, although it has been proposed that it may be a forme fruste of tuberous sclerosis. Bronchiolar obstruction leads to air trapping. Proliferation of venous smooth muscle causes venous obstruction, pulmonary hemorrhage, and hemosiderosis. Lymphatic obstruction causes generalized enlargement of regional lymph nodes and chylous accumulations in the pleural space. The illustrations portray macroscopic characteristics of ovoid, fleshy, salmon-colored hemorrhagic blebs. These typically measure over one centimeter in diameter and are spread throughout the lungs, but are most characteristic at the bases. Complications include pneumothorax, chylothorax, and hemoptysis. Diagnosis is made by biopsy.

Lymphangiomyomatosis is a progressive disease causing honeycombing and loss of lung parenchyma. It is not associated with malignancy. The tissue often stains strongly for estrogen and progesterone receptors, and some cases respond to antiestrogens or oophorectomy. The mainstay of management is conservative anatomic resection, although this often proves difficult due to the progressive and diffuse nature of the disease process. For patients with end-stage LAM, single or double lung transplantation has been successful.

critique:
Blunt trauma to the airway occurs in 1-3% of patients, whereas 5-8% of neck injuries present with concomitant penetrating airway injury. Penetrating injuries to the airway are often due to projectiles or stab wounds and occur more commonly in the cervical trachea. Blunt injury to the airway can occur from direct chest trauma, sudden hyperextension, strangulation and caustic injury. There are three prevailing theories for mechanism of blunt injury. Crush injury to the chest causes a decrease in AP diameter and an increase the transverse diameter thus exerting lateral force and splaying the carina. A second theory focuses on high airway pressure elicited from airway compression against a closed glottis. The part of the airway with the largest radial diameter, and the greatest wall tension per Laplace's law, is the carina. A third theory involves deceleration injury and shearing of the bronchus from points of relative fixation (near cricoid and carina).

In a review of 183 blunt tracheobronchial injuries over 20 years (1970-1990) 74% were transverse rupture, 18% longitudinal tears, and 8% were complex. Complex airway injuries, although rare, may require cardiopulmonary bypass to address associated pulmonary artery or other local injuries. Reports on tracheobronchial trauma consistently find that most injuries occur within 2.5 cm of the carina, and distal trachea and proximal right mainstem injuries are most common. Selected small lacerations can be managed conservatively but larger tears and disruptions need operative closure by right thoracotomy. The most common indicator of airway injury is pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum. Diagnosis should be confirmed with bronchoscopy. Delayed diagnosis is common. Fortunately, the results of late repair are quite good.

critique: There are many reasons why obese patients are more susceptible to gastroesophageal reflux than normal weight individuals. critique:
Achalasia is due to abnormalities in Auerbach's plexus within the esophageal wall, although the etiology is unknown. Characteristically, the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax and peristalsis is absent. The treatment for achalasia is aimed at reducing the high pressure gradient across the lower esophageal sphincter, which then allows the esophagus to empty into the stomach by gravity. Pneumatic dilation is one of the best initial treatments for achalasia and it is probably the most cost-effective first option. However, the long-term results are inconsistent. Surgical esophagomyotomy as initially described by Ernest Heller (1913) is definitive treatment for achalasia. Excellent long-term results should be expected whether this is performed from the abdomen or through the chest. A fundoplication is frequently added to help control gastroesophageal reflux.

A properly performed myotomy will reduce the pressure gradient, but the esophagus remains aperistaltic and must empty by gravity. Thus, patients with an end-stage or sigmoid esophagus (as seen in the barium swallow) should be offered esophagectomy. This recommendation was once controversial, but improved operative techniques and patient management following esophagectomy result in low morbidity in experienced centers. Lesser operations or procedures for sigmoid esophagus are marginally palliative, and the average age of patients in surgical series is typically 50-55 years. If comorbidities are limited, most achalasia patients have long life expectancies, and swallowing and even reflux complaints will be improved following esophagectomy.

critique:
The blood supply of the esophagus derives from multiple small segmental vessels. These are typically less than 1 mm in diameter and pass for a number of centimeters from their origin before branching at or in the esophageal wall. The cervical esophagus is supplied by branches from the superior and inferior thyroid arteries and, on occasion, by direct branches of the subclavian artery. The thoracic esophagus receives its blood supply from tracheal and bronchial arteries. Although up to two esophageal branches arising directly from the aorta have been reported, in a third of autopsies no esophageal branches are found. Intercostal arteries by themselves, and sometimes through bronchial and tracheal arterial branches, may also supply the thoracic esophagus. The abdominal esophagus receives its blood supply along with the proximal stomach, from the left gastric and splenic arteries.

When arteries reach the esophagus, their orientation is horizontal to the axis of the esophagus in the upper esophagus and vertical in the lower. In the thoracic esophagus, these arteries branch in the periesophageal tissue before entering the esophageal wall. Elegant corrosion casts of the esophageal blood supply demonstrate the dense vascular network within the mucosa and submucosa, which is the terminus of these arteries. This unique esophageal blood supply allows extensive esophageal mobilization, esophageal devascularization for varices without necrosis, and transhiatal (blunt) esophagectomy without exsanguination.
