The patient described has an early esophageal stricture from a second degree lye injury to the esophagus. Acute caustic injury to the esophagus is described in three stages: (1) the initial injury (the first week); (2) the latent phase (1-4 weeks); and (3) the chronic phase (after 4 weeks). The phases are defined by pathologic response to the initial ingestion. The first phase represents acute injury, the second phase represents the beginning of remodeling and healing, and the third phase is long-term healing with or without fibrotic change.

The management of caustic ingestion requires sound judgment and experience. If perforation is not present on presentation and does not develop during the recovery phase, then the treatment is supportive. This may include fluid resuscitation, broad spectrum antibiotics and maintenance of nutritional status. Unfortunately, history and physical examination alone do not predict esophageal injury severity. Severe injury can occur in the absence of significant pharyngeal burns, and complete examination of the esophagus is required. When the ingestion is minor or questionable and there are no symptoms, the patient should be observed and flexible upper endoscopy carried out at 24-48 hours. Immediate endoscopy may underestimate the extent of damage. In symptomatic patients or those with suspected large ingestions of strong caustic agents, immediate esophagoscopy should be performed. The endoscopic grading of esophageal injury is shown in the second table. Patients with grade I and IIA injuries are treated with 48 hrs of NPO, intravenous hydration and observation. Their diet is then advanced as tolerated. Patients with grade IIB and III findings are treated with intravenous hydration, antibiotics, close observation and nutritional support. Corticosteroids do not shorten the acute course or lessen stricture rates and should be avoided. Patients with acute perforation, a rigid abdomen, chest wall crepitus, cardiovascular shock, sepsis, profound acidosis or disseminated intravascular coagulation require emergency surgical exploration.

The patient in this question has developed the most common complication of endoscopic grade II caustic esophageal injury -- a stricture. Stricture formation peaks between 4 and 6 weeks following injury. Gentle, repeated dilation over a guide wire under fluoroscopy with a Savory dilator is the best initial management strategy. Blind bougie dilation with a Maloney dilator is contraindicated initially. Dilation should not be done in the first weeks following injury because of perforation concerns. In children, a common practice has been to leave a string between the nose and a gastrostomy to avoid complete esophageal obliteration during the healing phase and to facilitate later retrograde dilation of the esophagus. Esophagectomy, substernal bypass and esophageal diversion may play a role in the emergent management of a patient who presents with a caustic perforation. However, radical operation is not the best initial management of a patient who presents with an early stricture. Symptomatic strictures can also occur late (years) following a caustic injury. The mechanism of late stricture is unclear, but it may be associated with an acquired motility disorder and secondary reflux. Following caustic ingestion, all patients must have long-term endoscopic surveillance because of the lifelong risk of developing esophageal carcinoma.

critique:
Iatrogenic injury to the esophagus is the most frequent cause of esophageal perforation and accounts for 60% of all cases. Spontaneous perforations make up 15% of cases. Other less common causes of injury include foreign body ingestion, trauma, operative injury and tumor. Esophagoscopy, transesophageal echocardiography, sclerotherapy, variceal ligation, pneumatic dilation, bougienage, and thermal ablation devices cause occasional perforation injuries. Curiously, almost all reported TEE perforations involve octogenarian women. The risk of esophageal perforation during flexible esophagoscopy is low (0.03%) compared to 0.11% during rigid esophagoscopy. Simultaneous dilation during endoscopy increases the risk of perforation. Endoscopic sclerotherapy for esophageal varices leads to perforation in up to 6% of cases, as the sclerosing agents induce a transmural necro-inflammatory injury in the esophageal wall. Esophageal perforation can also occur during endoscopic variceal ligation if mucosa is caught and torn between the overtube and the endoscope. The risk of perforation during pneumatic dilation for achalasia is 1-5%, and high inflation pressure and previous pneumatic dilation increase this risk.

In a normal esophagus, the location at greatest risk of instrumental injury is Killian's triangle, which is formed by the paired inferior constrictor pharyngeus and the cricopharyngeus muscles. At this location, the posterior esophageal mucosa is unprotected by muscularis, and is separated from the retroesophageal space by buccopharyngeal fascia only. Cervical osteophytic spurs, kyphosis of the spine, or hyperextension of the neck during a procedure further increases the risk of perforation in this area during endoluminal procedures. This patient suffered a cervical esophageal perforation during the passage of the transesophageal echo probe. The leak is seen at the upper margin of the clavicle on the contrast swallow. Instrumental perforations are also more probable at sites of anatomic esophageal narrowing such as the aortic arch and left main stem bronchus.

Treatment objectives for esophageal perforation include prevention of further contamination, control of mediastinitis, and maintenance of nutritional status during the recovery period. The conservative management of esophageal perforation is operation. Nonoperative management is appropriate in highly selected patients but surgical judgment and experience is required. The patient described has tachycardia and the mediastinal collection is large, which excludes her from a non-operative management strategy. Cervical esophageal perforations down to the level of the carina are often best managed by drainage via a cervical incision. The neck incision can either be left open and packed or closed over a large drain. Unlike intrathoracic perforations, cervical esophageal perforations do not require mucosal reapproximation for a successful outcome. Drainage, perioperative antibiotics, avoiding oral intake and providing alternative nutritional support almost always results in healing. Diversion and T-tube placement are not required for a simple instrumental perforation. Stenting plays no role in high cervical esophageal perforations. A right thoracotomy for primary repair would be appropriate for a mid-thoracic perforation, and left thoracotomy would be favored for a low intrathoracic perforation.

critique:
High resolution manometry (HRM) uses a catheter with dozens of pressure sensors along its length from the pharynx to the proximal stomach. HRM allows generation of a spaciotemporal plot, where segments of the peristaltic wavefront can be separately analyzed. Esophageal body parameters to assess include antegrade esophageal peristalsis, contraction amplitude, and contraction duration. Direct comparison with traditional manometry shows that HRM is more accurate at predicting abnormal barium bolus transport, especially with mild-to-moderate esophageal dysmotility. Lower esophageal sphincter (LES) resting pressure, length, and completeness of LES relaxation are measured. Notably, HRM allows more accurate measurement of LES relaxation than traditional manometry by compensating for the LES movement during swallows.

The HRM tracing of a normal esophagus (see first critique graphic) is divided into anatomic segments from pharynx to stomach. The pharynx is from 16-18 cm, and pharyngeal contraction occurs as the upper esophageal sphincter (UES, 18-20 cm) relaxes after a 5 cc swallow from 50 to 0 mmHg. Striated muscle contraction wave begins as the UES recovers, and advances from 21-24 cm, where a transition zone (24-26 cm) of lower pressure occurs. Smooth muscle peristaltic contraction wave extends from 26-44 cm, is antegrade (3 cm/sec [normal < 8]), and normal in amplitude (50-75 mmHg [normal < 180]), duration, and intrabolus pressure. LES extends from 44-47 cm, relaxes just after a swallow occurs from 15 mmHg to near 0, and then overshoots to 30 mmHg.

The HRM tracing shown in the question is classic for achalasia. The UES relaxes with swallowing. There is perisatalsis in the proximal (striated muscle) esophagus, but after the transition point the esophageal body is aperistaltic with an isobaric tertiary contraction in the esophageal body. The LES is normotensive but nonrelaxing. The additional critique graphic shows typical findings of scleroderma, with preserved striated muscle contraction in proximal esophagus, absent smooth muscle contraction in the distal esophagus, and a hypotensive LES (resting pressure < 5 mmHg), while the UES functions normally. A "nutcracker" esophagus tracing features normal UES relaxation on swallowing. There is normal esophageal peristalsis, but esophageal contraction amplitude is > 200 mmHg (normal < 180) in the distal half of the esophagus. The LES is normotensive and relaxes.

Other causes of pseudoachalsia include prior surgery in this region, lymphoma, or malignancies in the upper abdomen that may infiltrate the distal esophagus or its surrounding neural plexuses.

Further testing is important to differentiate these two entities. The gold standard for distinguishing these two conditions is esophago-gastroduodenoscopy with biopsy. Rarely, a tumor responsible for pseudoachalasia will not be seen on endoscopy. This is usually because the tumor is in the muscular wall of the esophagus without penetration into the lumen. Such findings are most characteristic of metastatic tumors, and the true details of involvement may be best assessed with endoesophageal ultrasound. Rarely the diagnosis can remain elusive, in which case surgical exploration offers a chance for repair of achalasia or for optimal treatment or palliation of underlying malignancy.

critique:
A large squamous cell carcinoma of the upper thoracic esophagus that may involve all layers of the thoracic esophageal wall should be handled with an operation that provides direct, wide thoracic exposure and allows for the highest possible anastomosis to achieve an optimal margin. The surgeon must be suspicious of airway involvement for a tumor of this type and location, and bronchoscopy is a requisite preliminary evaluation at the time of surgery. Airway invasion is a contraindication to resection. The esophagus and trachea share a common blood supply, and combined esophagectomy and tracheal resection is a highly morbid procedure. A neoadjuvant strategy can be considered, and if response is substantial then resection can be reconsidered.

Regarding this case, an Ivor-Lewis approach is not optimal because the anastomosis must be in the thorax. An adequate proximal margin likely cannot be achieved because of the high position of the tumor. A left thoracoabdominal incision offers even less access to the upper esophagus, and this approach is inadequate for the described lesion. Although a transhiatal approach removes the entire thoracic esophagus, a blind dissection is not safe for this tumor. For a large cancer with possible full thickness involvement near the azygos vein and adjacent to the trachea, a technique that does not allow direct visualization allows poor nodal assessment and is unreliable or dangerous regarding the radial margin. Although experience is increasing, a minimally invasive approach in a patient with possible airway invasion poses similar concerns. question_text: A healthy 36-year-old patient presented with a history of several months of mild facial swelling. A chest CT slice is shown. There were no other abnormal CT findings. The most appropriate management is
critique:
The CT demonstrates extensive calcification of the visceral mediastinum and secondary near-total SVC occlusion. There also has been formation of venous collaterals in the chest wall soft tissues. Lymphomas are rarely isolated to the visceral mediastinum and they rarely demonstrate extensive calcification. This diagnosis is possible but unlikely. Mediastinoscopy in this case does present a risk of bleeding due to dense contiguous fibrosis involving the innominate artery and SVC as well as the presence of large collateral venous channels. Histoplasma capsulatum is the most prevalent endemic mycosis in North America. Infection with the organism most commonly manifests as a benign self-limited respiratory illness, and many adults living in endemic areas have serologic and/or radiographic evidence of previous infection. The most common sequelae of histoplasmosis are asymptomatic pulmonary calcifications and/or calcified mediastinal and peribronchial lymph nodes. No active intervention is warranted for these findings. Occasionally, fibrosing mediastinitis will develop, initially characterized by abnormal proliferation of collagen and fibrous tissue followed by calcification within the visceral mediastinum. Organs such as the SVC, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, airways, and esophagus can be involved. The compressibility and location of the SVC account for its common involvement with this process. SVC stenosis secondary to fibrosing mediastinitis occurs slowly over time, allowing venous collaterals to develop. The symptoms of SVC obstruction in this benign process tend to be insidious compared to neoplastic SVC occlusion.

Mediastinal debridement and SVC reconstruction can be a formable surgical procedure and should be reserved for patients with severe or critical symptoms such as moderate to severe facial swelling, oropharyngeal swelling, or neurologic symptoms of cerebral venous congestion. Although benefit has been reported in selected patients, it is unlikely that percutaneous dilatation and/or stent placement would be helpful in this case due to the dense surrounding fibrosis and calcification. Other less common agents reported to cause mediastinal fibrosis include blastomyces, mycobacterium, aspergillus, mucor, and cryptococcus. Serologic and skin testing to identify an infectious agent and further observation is the appropriate recommendation for this patient.

A CT slice is shown, and serum tumor markers reveal a mildly elevated human chorionic gonadotropin and normal alpha fetoprotein. Pathology obtained by CT-guided core needle is also shown. critique:
An anterior mediastinal mass in a young adult male should prompt measurement of serum tumor markers. Any alpha fetoprotein (Œ±FP) and/or beta human chorionic gonadotropin (Œ≤-hCG) elevation over 100 mIU/mL is diagnostic for a primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell cancer. This situation is treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by surgery regardless of biopsy findings. Mildly elevated or normal Œ≤-hCG levels are consistent with primary mediastinal seminomatous germ cell cancers. However, pathologic confirmation by CT-guided core needle or surgical biopsy is necessary to establish this diagnosis and to rule out lymphoma or invasive thymic neoplasms. A slowly growing, large, and relatively homogenous mass with occasional areas of central necrosis on CT scan is most consistent with a primary mediastinal seminomatous germ cell cancer. The homogeneity of CT findings corresponds well to the typical pathologic findings of monotonous sheets of round to polygonal cells with septae containing lymphocytes. Eighty percent of seminomatous germ cell cancers stain positive for placental alkaline phosphatase, which is also diagnostic.

Radiation therapy has historically been the treatment of choice for primary mediastinal seminomatous germ cell cancer, but irradiation does not control systemic metastases. Another concern about these relatively young patients is the long-term morbidity associated with mediastinal irradiation. Cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy regimens are now considered the first-line treatment of choice for mediastinal seminoma. Cisplatin-based chemotherapy alone has up to a 100% response rate and an 85% 5-year survival even in the presence of metastatic disease. Follow-up surveillance is by imaging only. If a residual mass has local growth during follow-up then surgical removal should be considered for both diagnosis and therapy.

title: mediastinum; germ cell tumor; treatment after chemotherapy; role of surgery
question_text: A patient was treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy for a primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell cancer. Alpha fetoprotein levels were elevated at presentation but are now normal. CT scan demonstrates reduction in the size of the mediastinal mass from 12 cm to 6 cm. The most appropriate next management step is
critique:
Following cisplatin-based chemotherapy for a primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumor, there is typically a reduction in tumor dimensions and decrease in serum tumor marker levels. However, a residual mass is invariably present and complete tumor necrosis occurs in only a distinct minority of cases. Therefore, teratoma, persistent nonseminomatous germ cell cancer, and/or degenerative non-germ cell cancer is pathologically present in most residual masses. Each of these pathologic categories is poorly responsive to radiation therapy and further chemotherapy. Surgery is indicated to remove these residual masses. Unfortunately, teratoma does not demonstrate PET avidity similar to complete necrosis. Although considered benign, teratoma in primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumors has a high propensity to degenerate into frank malignancy. PET additionally lacks sensitivity to identify microscopic foci of persistent nonseminomatous germ cell cancer or degenerative non-germ cell cancer.

Optimally, serum tumor marker levels normalize and surgery is planned after adequate functional and hematologic recovery, which usually occurs 4-6 weeks following completion of chemotherapy. Historically, primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumor patients with persistently elevated serum tumor marker levels after chemotherapy were treated with second-line cisplatin-based chemotherapy prior to considering surgery. However, in contrast to the 50% salvage rate of second-line cisplatin-based chemotherapy for nonseminomatous germ cell tumors arising in the testes, the response rate for primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumors is very poor. Given this poor response of second-line chemotherapy, the imperfect correlation of elevated postchemotherapy serum tumor marker levels to pathologic findings, and the ability for surgery to salvage patients with residual malignancy, resection of residual disease after first-line cisplatin chemotherapy is desirable regardless of serum tumor marker levels.

Conversely, normalization of serum tumor markers following chemotherapy is not a good predictor of benign pathology. Up to one-third of such patients have persistent nonseminomatous germ cell cancer, and/or degenerative non-germ cell cancer when residual mass is resected. Surgery, therefore, needs to be complete even in the face of normal serum markers. Such resections are technically demanding as preoperative chemotherapy renders surrounding mediastinal tissues fibrotic and normal anatomic planes are obscured. Cisplatin-based chemotherapy for germ cell cancers usually results in extensive tumor necrosis which is more marked around the periphery. With support from frozen section analysis this finding usually allows a complete resection. Lung, great veins, phrenic nerves, and occasionally cardiac chambers are critical structures which can abut, but if not directly involved with the residual mass, they can be preserved. Any nonessential tissue directly involved with the residual mass should be removed en bloc, however. Complete tumor necrosis in the residual mass correlates with excellent long-term survival, while an incremental decrease in survival is associated with findings of teratoma and persistent germ cell cancer and/or degenerative non-germ cell cancer.

critique:
The initial diagnosis of myasthenia gravis is primarily clinical via a full neurologic examination. The differential diagnosis includes brainstem and motor cranial nerve pathology, Kearns-Sayre syndrome with ophthalmopathy, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, generalized fatigue, and several neuromuscular diseases. Edrophonium chloride (Tensilon) is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with rapid onset (30 to 45 seconds) and short duration of action (5 to 10 minutes). This agent prolongs the presence of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction and results in an immediate increase in muscle strength in many of the affected muscles of myasthenic patients. The test (10 mg IV) has a sensitivity of 80-90%, but it there are false-negative and false-positive results and the test can exacerbate severe asthma and cardiac disease. Availability of the drug has been somewhat irregular.

The ice pack test can be used in patients with ptosis, particularly those in whom the Tensilon (edrophonium) test is considered too risky. Neuromuscular transmission improves at lower muscle temperatures, and myasthenic ptosis improves after an ice pack is placed on the closed lid for two minutes. Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) is a practical, and the most frequently used electrodiagnostic test for MG. Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) is more technically demanding than RNS and is less widely available, but it is the most sensitive diagnostic test for myasthenia gravis whether generalized or ocular (see table). Each of the tests above is useful in the functional diagnosis of myasthenia gravis, but demonstration of acetylcholine receptor binding antibodies (found in 88-94% of patients with generalized disease) confirms the diagnosis. In select patients, assays for blocking and modulating antibodies, including muscle specific receptor tyrosine kinase (MuSK), may also be helpful.

Preoperative preparation of patients with myasthenia gravis prior to thymectomy can minimize postoperative complications including respiratory failure. Normal preoperative vital capacity does not rule respiratory muscle weakness. Patients with a history of myasthenic crisis, preoperative bulbar symptoms, or a preoperative serum level of anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody > 100 nmol/L are at increased risk of postoperative myasthenic crisis. These patients require meticulous management and usually undergo plasmapheresis. A typical treatment protocol involves removal of 2-3 L of plasma three times per week for 5-6 treatments. This is usually well tolerated, but fibrinogen levels must be monitored and replacement may be required. The symptomatic improvement lasts for up to three months, and these treatments are not cumulative.

Optimizing a patient's medical regimen prior to thymectomy is an important goal, and this may include a steroid wean. However, steroid dose changes should be made cautiously and glucocorticoids should not be weaned at the expense of control of myasthenic symptoms. "Stress dosing" of steroids may be appropriate starting at the time of operation, but early increases are not necessary. Immunomodulatory drugs such as cyclosporine, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, and mycophenolate mofetil are often used for refractory patient symptoms or to facilitate steroid weaning. Azathioprine improves weakness in most patients, but benefit may not be apparent for 4-8 months. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) may also be used for preoperative preparation, and additional options for treatment include other cholinesterase inhibitors, including neostigmine bromide, which, unlike pyridostigmine (Mestinon), does require occasional bromide level checks. critique:
The most common indication for thymectomy is myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disorder caused by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies that reduce the number of available acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular end plate. Clinically, this results in muscle weakness and muscle fatigability. During a myasthenic crisis the weakness is so profound that the patient cannot support speech, swallowing or respiratory functions. Thymectomy is not a treatment for acute myasthenic crisis and should not be considered during a crisis. The treatment of myasthenic crisis is medical and can include immunosuppressants, immunoglobulin therapy and plasmapheresis.

The exact role the thymus plays in this disease remains poorly understood. However, observations made over 50 years ago suggest that surgical thymectomy can induce remission of myasthenia gravis in some patients. Unfortunately, precise preoperative selection criteria for patients likely to achieve remission have not been defined. The extent of operation required, either radical or simple thymectomy has not been established. critique:
Thymic tumors comprise 40% of anterior mediastinal masses in adults. The mean age at presentation is between 40 and 60 years and there is no sex predominance. Half are encapsulated at presentation. In the WHO histologic classification criteria (see below) the letters represent the morphology of the cells and the numbers represent the epithelial/lymphocyte ratio and degree of atypia. Thymic carcinomas comprise types B3 and C (tumors with true malignant cytological characteristics). Although SUVmax has been found to predict pathology to some extent, it has not been shown to be a prognostic indicator for survival in thymic carcinoma patients. When surgical removal is anticipated to be difficult, biopsy is warranted to confirm the diagnosis and to rule out lymphoma. Incomplete resection is associated with poor survival rates. The size of the tumor is not as important as involvement of structures that can be resected. Occasionally, complete removal may require pneumonectomy or superior vena caval resection and reconstruction.

Thymoma:   World Health Organization (WHO) Histologic Classification
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A        A tumor composed of a population of neoplastic thymic epithelial cells having spindle/oval shape, lacking nuclear atypia, and accompanied by few or no non-neoplastic lymphocytes. 
AB     A tumor in which foci having the features of type A thymoma are admixed with foci rich in lymphocytes. 
B1     A tumor that resembles the normal functional thymus in that it combines large expanses having an appearance practically indistinguishable from normal thymic cortex with areas resembling thymic medulla. 
B2     A tumor in which the neoplastic epithelial component appears as scattered plump cells with vesicular nuclei and distinct nucleoli among a heavy population of lymphocytes. Perivascular spaces are common and sometimes very prominent. A perivascular arrangement of tumor cells resulting in a palisading effect may be seen. 
B3     A type of thymoma predominantly composed of epithelial cells having a round or polygonal shape and exhibiting no or mild atypia. They are admixed with a minor component of lymphocytes, resulting in a sheetlike growth of the neoplastic epithelial cells. 
C       A thymic tumor exhibiting clear-cut cytologic atypia and a set of cytoarchitectural features no longer specific to the thymus, but rather analogous to those seen in carcinomas of other organs. Type C thymomas lack immature lymphocytes; whatever lymphocytes may be present are mature and usually admixed with plasma cells.

Excision of these lesions resolves uncertainty about their nature and the operative risks are minimal. Aspiration and sclerosis of these lesions has been reported, but the outcomes are inconsistent and recurrence is common.

critique: The radiograph shows a neonate with a left foramen of Bochdalek hernia. Foramen of Bochdalek hernia is being recognized with increasing frequency and it is the most common cause of pulmonary atresia. Associated anomalies are noted in over 50% of children with Bochdaleck hernias, and these can involve multiple systems (ie, cardiac, renal, neurologic, GI). The lung on the ipsilateral side does not develop because there is no space for it to grow. If mediastinal shift occurs, as suggested by the endotracheal tube position on the chest radiograph, the contralateral lung also may not develop normally and studies of surviving children have demonstrated 8%-20% reduced function on the contralateral side. At birth these children often have early respiratory distress that may worsen with assisted face mask breathing because of distention of the intestinal tract. Thus, early intubation is indicated. Since diagnosis can be made in utero by sonography (particularly in mothers with polyhydramnios), preparations for operation can be made prior to birth.

Problems that arise after uneventful operations can be frustrating, yet a thoughtful approach to diagnosis and prompt management can be life saving. Emergent cardiac catheterization in a postoperative patient with new onset ventricular arrhythmias may be indicated, but several factors make coronary disease unlikely in this case. No native occlusive lesions were identified at preoperative catheterization. With the aorta open, return of retrograde cardioplegia from both coronary ostia would have been visualized. This problem can occur despite aggressive de-airing and the use of transesophageal echo. In a supine patient the right coronary ostium is superior in the ascending aorta and is, therefore, the most common site of coronary air embolism. Air embolism into the carotid circulation can cause early postoperative seizures. Ambient air (80% nitrogen) is absorbed into solution much more slowly than pure oxygen or CO2. For this reason insufflation of the pericardial well during operation with CO2 is routinely practiced by many surgeons.

Anticonvulsant medications are indicated and obtaining a CT scan emergently is reasonable for a stable patient, but a neurosurgical problem such as an acute bleed is unlikely in this situation. Hyperbaric oxygen is an appropriate treatment to help clear nitrogen-rich gas bubbles, but chambers are seldom available and postoperative cardiac patients are not easily transported or cared for in such microenvironments. Fortunately, most air embolism complications are self-limited problems and injury can be minimized by employing brute force (increasing cardiac output and systemic pressure) to purge the obstructing gas bubbles. Induced moderate hypothermia will minimize the metabolic demands of the heart and brain until the problem is resolved.

question_text: A 45-year-old man was referred for surgical evaluation after a 4.6 cm ascending aortic aneurysm was found. Cardiac catheterization demonstrated no significant coronary artery disease. He has a murmur heard best in the right second interspace and echo showed a bicuspid aortic valve with a valve area of 0.9 cm2. critique:
A bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is a recognized risk factor for the development aneurysms of the ascending aorta and subsequent complications such as dissection or rupture. BAV disease seems to follow an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with incomplete penetrance. A number of histologic abnormalities have been identified in association with BAV including decreased fibrillin 1 concentration, increased metalloproteinase 2 activity, elastin fragmentation and smooth muscle cell reorientation. Distances between elastic lamellae are greater than in patients with tricuspid aortic valves. Subsequently, these patients also have higher rates of dilation of the ascending aorta on long-term echo surveillance than do patients with tricuspid valves.

A patient with a BAV and ascending aortic diameter greater than 45 mm is at increased risk of late aortic dissection and sudden death compared to patients with smaller aortic diameters. Reconstruction of the entire aortic root and ascending aorta with a composite graft should be considered if the aortic root is also dilated. The increased complexity and operative risk of a Bentall procedure mitigate against its routine use in patients without coexistent root dilatation. Replacement of the ascending aorta with a tube graft in addition to valve replacement or repair is an appropriate procedure in the absence of root enlargement. Reduction aortoplasty with external wrapping of the ascending aorta has been reported to have acceptable mid-term results, but long-term follow-up suggests an increased incidence of progressive dilatation in comparison to tube graft replacement of the ascending aorta.

question_text: One week ago a 40-year-old man patient on chronic hemodialysis underwent AVR with a mechanical valve for calcific aortic stenosis. Preoperative ventricular function was normal. A routine followup transthoracic echo identified a paravalvular leak in the non-coronary sinus with a vena contracta of 0.6 cm. Discharge plans are complete and the patient is asymptomatic. Blood cultures are negative, there is no evidence of hemolysis and the ejection fraction is 45%. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
critique:
Paravalvular leak occurs in approximately 1-3.4% of patients after aortic valve replacement. Factors implicated in the development of periprosthetic leaks include inadequate debridement of annular calcium, endocarditis, using non-pledgeted annular sutures, and anatomic weakness in the area of the non-coronary sinus. Indications for intervention include regurgitation worse than "mild," worsening ventricular function, hemolysis, and endocarditis. "Vena contracta" refers to the point in a fluid stream through an orifice where the diameter of the stream is the least. In the case of a paravalvular leak the abnormal fluid stream can be imaged and measured by echo techniques. The maximum contraction is usually identified slightly downstream from the orifice. A regurgitant jet vena contracta of 0.6 cm indicates moderate to severe regurgitation, which is consistent with this patient's postoperative ejection fraction deterioration.

Percutaneous closure of prosthetic paravalvular leaks is an appealing alternative to reoperation, but embolization, hemolysis and lack of successful complete closure have plagued such attempts. The devices used in reported cases have been designed for other purposes to resolve lesions such as muscular VSD, ASD, and PDA. Reoperation is the conservative and only reliable approach to resolve the complication described. The simplest repair technique, when anatomically feasible, is to close the defect with one or more transmural pledgeted sutures that incorporate the sewing ring and the aortic wall. In the noncoronary sinus sutures can be placed from outside-to-inside and up through the sewing ring at the level of the annulus. Leaks in other paravalvular locations can be more difficult to resolve, but further dissection and alternate exposures may allow similar transmural suture repair in the left and right coronary sinuses. Prosthetic valve re-replacement may be required, but this is associated with reduced postoperative survival.

It was hypothesized that the secondary hyperparathyroidism associated with end-stage renal disease and the resulting increased serum calcium and phosphate levels could potentially lead to accelerated calcification of a bioprosthetic valve. Supportive evidence for this theory, however, has been challenged.

Despite incremental improvements in the management of end-stage renal disease, dialysis dependency carries a 25% annual mortality rate. For patients 55 to 64-years-old, the 3 and 5-year survival rates from time of initiation of dialysis are approximately 52% and 33% respectively. Several studies have also identified an increased risk of bleeding and stroke in dialysis patients with mechanical prosthesis and conclude that use of a bioprosthesis did not adversely affect survival or increase the rate of reoperation. Use of non-stented tissue prostheses may be indicated in specific situations, but they generally do not offer significant benefit in this population and are technically more challenging to implant, requiring longer bypass and ischemia times than stented prostheses.

critique:
This patient's dampened radial arterial pressure should be verified, but this finding along with the noted local aortic abnormality strongly suggests an iatrogenic aortic dissection with innominate artery involvement. Further dissection and malperfusion are likely. Intraoperative iatrogenic ascending aortic dissection is a catastrophic problem, and creative or unconventional approaches usually result in poor outcomes. Definitive repair should follow a plan similar to the repair of a primary aortic dissection.

Simple removal of the aortic cannula with or without local repair or other maneuvers, while tempting, may result in uncontrolled bleeding. Access to the axillary artery may be desirable but it is time consuming and can be difficult, hence femoral cannulation should be the first step. Cardiopulmonary bypass should be initiated with systemic cooling. Although the tear typically involves the cannulation site, involvement of the arch and head vessels should be anticipated and the interior of the aortic arch should be explored under hypothermic circulatory arrest. Usually replacement of the ascending aorta is all that is required. Once this is completed in a standard fashion the remainder of the planned operation can be performed. If execution of this modified sequence is prompt, then results similar to other types of aortic dissection repair can be expected.

If an aortic dissection is identified following recent surgery, management should proceed swiftly and the evaluation should be complete. If this complication follows CABG, then replacement of vein grafts should be anticipated. Under such elective or urgent reoperative conditions, axillary cannulation may be an excellent strategy. Once postoperative dissection is identified, reoperation should not be delayed, as the clinical course cannot be predicted and there are ongoing risks of rupture or systemic malperfusion complications.

He has never had a stroke or TIA, he lives independently and remains active. Non-specific EKG changes and criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy were present on EKG. critique:
Identification of moderate aortic stenosis at the time of myocardial revascularization presents a clinical dilemma. Concomitant valve replacement poses and increased operative risk, but the stenosis may progress and require a reoperation later, when risks are even higher. Aortic stenosis is a progressive disease process with a long latent period in which patients may be asymptomatic. Once symptoms do develop, the risks progress exponentially to death unless the obstruction is removed by valve replacement. The natural history of asymptomatic carotid stenosis is relatively benign, and surveillance plus antiplatelet drugs are recommended for nearly all such patients. Combined carotid endarterectomy and CABG may be appropriate for selected patients with high-grade carotid lesions.

Recent studies offer some insights into which patients can be expected to have accelerated progression of aortic stenosis. Valve obstruction correlates with valvular calcification. Therefore, valves with moderate stenosis and heavy calcification of the annulus and leaflets tend to worsen and cause symptoms sooner than valves with minimal calcification. Additionally, the starting valve area is related to the interval time to symptom development. Studies of aortic stenosis have shown an annual decrease in aortic valve area of approximately 0.12 cm2 per year and an increase in mean gradient of 5-10 mmHg per year. Some authors suggest that this progression is more rapid in elderly patients. Regarding the described patient, the calcification and moderate gradient indicate that failure to replace the aortic valve at this time puts him at high risk for a required second operation within a few years. The potential role of transcatheter valve insertion in this setting remains to be defined.

She developed unstable angina and a cath revealed a 90% left main stenosis and occlusions of the native right coronary and the OM and PDA grafts. There was a 90% stenosis of the saphenous vein graft to the LAD. At reoperation, a LIMA was placed to the LAD and the old saphenous vein graft was ligated. New saphenous vein grafts were placed to the obtuse marginal and PDA. The patient cannot be weaned from bypass because of left heart failure and anterior akinesis. TEE shows no valve pathology, and ultrasonic flow measurements of the LAD, OM and PDA grafts are 26, 50, and 35 mL/min respectively. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to take?
critique:
Reoperative bypass surgery is becoming less common with increased application of percutaneous revascularization. Before IMA advantages were generally accepted, LAD revascularization was routinely done with a saphenous vein graft. If reoperation is necessary, use of the LIMA would appear to be an attractive option. However, its use in this context can result in marginal LAD perfusion prior to full maturation of the arterial graft. When a saphenous vein graft was previously placed to the LAD acceptable reoperative strategies include either replacing the old graft with a new saphenous vein graft (removing or ligating the old graft), or placing a LIMA to the LAD and leaving the old graft intact.

This woman's old patent LAD vein graft was ligated, so the LIMA inflow is now the sole source of anterior wall perfusion. Noninvasive determination of LIMA flow is reliable, and if no technical error was made then going back on bypass to redo the LIMA-LAD anastomosis will not resolve the ongoing ischemia, which is the underlying problem in the described scenario. The measured flows are reasonable values for fresh grafts of the types specified. Augmenting anterior wall flow is the appropriate immediate response. Placing an intra-aortic balloon pump and adding inotropic support may temporize the situation, but the underlying cause remains untreated. LVAD placement fails to address the pathophysiology and is premature. If another graft fails to resolve the problem, then embolized debris from old graft manipulation and/or other etiologies must be considered, and extraordinary circulatory support may be justified.

Most authorities recommend repair of the mitral or tricuspid valve in any patient with severe regurgitation of either valve. The American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guidelines recommend repair for severe ischemic mitral regurgitation or severe tricuspid regurgitation at the time of concomitant coronary bypass or other surgery. Severe pulmonary hypertension and poor left ventricular function are each associated with persistent or progressive postoperative tricuspid regurgitation (even after repair), so many surgeons advocate an aggressive strategy to correct even lesser degrees of tricuspid regurgitation.

The severity of ischemic mitral regurgitation or functional tricuspid regurgitation is highly dependent on preload, afterload and ventricular function. Fasting and sedation under general anesthesia may result in substantial down-grading of mitral or tricuspid regurgitation when assessed in the operating room. The preoperative echo assessment under normal loading conditions offers the most accurate assessment of atrio-ventricular valve regurgitation. An aggressive plan for CABG plus mital and tricuspid repairs is correct. Excellent results have been reported for repair of ischemic mitral valve regurgitation with flexible, rigid and semi-rigid rings. The best mid-term results of survival and freedom form recurrent ischemic mitral regurgitation have been reported with semi-rigid annuloplasty rings. The atrio-ventricular node and penetrating bundle of His are close to the septal leaflet base and the commissure between the septal and anterior leaflets. The anatomy of the valve and the triangle of Koch are seen in the second figure (forceps tips are in the coronary sinus). The apex of this triangle corresponds to the area of most concern for injury from suture placement.

Angina, syncope, arrhythmias and thromboembolism are seen in a small percentage of patients. True aneurysms form following infarction from scar formation and thinning of the myocardium. False aneurysms develop after extensive full-thickness infarction and survival depends on local pericardial adhesion and clot containing the free-wall rupture. True and false aneurysms differ in four ways: (1) false aneurysms do not contain myocardial cells; (2) false aneurysms are more likely to form posteriorly; (3) false aneurysms have a narrow neck; and (4) false aneurysms have a greater propensity to rupture.

Distinguishing between the two general types of ventricular aneurysms is critical, as treatment recommendations differ substantially. While a true ventricular aneurysm is treated conservatively unless symptoms or complications develop, the prognosis for false aneurysms is much worse. False aneurysms less than 2 to 3 months old, as in this case, should undergo urgent surgical repair following a diagnostic cardiac catheterization because of the unpredictable risk of rupture. However, the risk of early repair is significant. Older false aneurysms are treated based on symptoms. Linear repair may be feasible because of the narrow neck, but most often the best surgical repair of a false aneurysm utilizes a patch closure technique. Geometry of the ventricle is well maintained, which minimizes the risk of post-repair mitral regurgitation. Several recent articles promote sutureless external patch and glue reinforcement as an alternate technique.

Some variety of myocardial rupture (free wall, septal, or papillary muscle) complicates up to 10% of all acute myocardial infarctions (AMI) and is responsible for 15% of in-hospital mortality following AMI. Reports indicate that early reperfusion for coronary disease (either PCI or CABG) minimizes such complications. Myocardial rupture is more common among patients older than 60 years and women as compared to men (1.4:1). Most myocardial ruptures occur between 1 and 5 days following AMI. Echocardiography offers rapid, accurate diagnosis of these conditions. In the described case the findings were near-complete papillary muscle rupture, which can manifest as acute pulmonary edema with associated tachycardia, tachypnea, rales, respiratory distress, and hypotension. In roughly 2/3 of cases of acute papillary muscle rupture the posteromedial papillary muscle is involved. The posteromedial papillary muscle usually receives blood supply from a single source -- either the right coronary artery or the circumflex coronary artery in a left dominant system. The anterolateral papillary muscle receives dual blood supply from the left anterior descending and circumflex coronary arteries.

The presentation of acute MR represents only 1-2% of all cases of ischemic MR. Rapid diagnosis is essential to survival. A murmur may be absent following papillary muscle rupture given a rapid equalization of pressure between the left atrium and ventricle. "Medical" therapy includes afterload reduction with vasodilators and/or insertion of an intra-aortic balloon pump. However, often these patients develop acute, severe cardiogenic shock that is unresponsive to inotropic and IABP support. Mitral valve replacement is the best surgical option in most cases. It is associated with 10-40% mortality depending on patient comorbidities, but without valve replacement this condition is fatal.

critique:
A patient with papillary muscle rupture may present a few hours to 14 days following an acute myocardial infarction (typically 2-7 days). Abrupt chest pain and shortness of breath are the most common symptoms, and 90% of patients have hemodynamic instability, commonly shock, pulmonary edema, hypotension, oliguria and acidosis. On physical exam a holosystolic murmur radiates to the axilla. The differential diagnosis includes ischemic ventricular septal defect, massive myocardial infarction, free wall rupture and ruptured papillary muscle. Acute mitral regurgitation from a ruptured papillary muscle is not well tolerated and represents a surgical emergency. The mortality for medical management is 50% at 24 hours and 75% at 48 hours.

This patient's EKG shows an acute inferior infarction with elevated ST segments in leads II, III, and aVF. The echo clip shows the tip of the posteromedial papillary muscle flail within the left atrium during systole. The posteromedial papillary muscle is involved two-thirds of the time, primarily because the blood supply to this muscle is poorly collateralized and comes from either the right coronary artery or from the circumflex coronary in a left-dominant system. The anterolateral papillary muscle blood supply comes from both the left anterior descending artery and the circumflex coronary.

Placing an intra-aortic balloon pump is helpful to stabilize a decompensating patient. Circumstances dictate whether preoperative cardiac cath is essential for best outcome since 50% of patients presenting with acute papillary rupture have single-vessel disease. "Prophylactic" bypass of all major epicardial vessels does not improve survival. If the patient's stability permits catheterization then all diseased vessels should be bypassed. Most surgeons advocate mitral valve replacement and many favor using a low-profile mechanical valve since ventricular size is typically small since anticoagulation for the infarct and residual dysfunction is likely to be recommended. However, repair in the acute setting has be reported with good results, especially in the setting of a ruptured single papillary muscle head.

The most significant factor influencing postoperative mortality is poor left ventricular function before operation. Other factors that predict post-repair mortality include three-vessel disease, preoperative malignant arrhythmias, and advanced age. "Circular" repair (Dor, Jatene, others) is generally favored over linear closure, but the influence on outcome of the method of repair remains somewhat controversial. Ejection fraction will improve following repair for almost all patients. However, primary heart transplantation should be considered if the ejection fraction is less than 20%, if symptoms are NYHA class IV, and if the patient is a good candidate for transplantation. The causes of death for medically managed patient are: arrhythmia (44%), heart failure (33%), and recurrent MI (11%).

question_text: Which of the following statements about cold blood cardioplegia is true?
critique:
Characteristics of cold blood cardioplegia, the strategy used most often in the United States, include real time mixing with perfusate at a ratio between 1:2 and 1:8, alkaline pH (approximately 7.8), robust buffering via blood proteins and added THAM or bicarbonate, citrate-phosphate-dextrose (CPD) to control calcium flux, and elevated potassium (approximately 30 mmol/L) to induce diastolic arrest. The importance of hypothermia is critical to effective blood cardioplegia protection, and the hematocrit of the solution varies with the blood:crystalloid additive ratio selected. Different ratios have been used with good success. Modest initial (1-2 min) antegrade delivery minimizes myocardial cellular edema, and the pressure of intermittent retrograde delivery is always kept around 40 mmHg.

Most protocols specify intermittent infusions at 20-minute intervals, but continuous delivery has reported advantages. In studies of continuous retrograde delivery (50 mL/min) authors claim less enzyme release, better maintenance of non-acidic myocardial pH, improved left and right ventricular stroke work index during the first 20 hours after coronary artery bypass. Trends in favor of improved measured parameters have been show, but no study has been adequately powered to demonstrate significant clinical outcome advantages. In these studies, a higher blood:crystalloid cardioplegia ratio was used (8:1) such that the maintenance potassium concentration was 10-12 mEq/L. Overall potassium delivery was higher with continuous administration, but significant postoperative hyperkalemia was not observed.

critique:
Fortunately, the need for post-cardiotomy ventricular assistance in patients with reasonable preoperative function appears to have decreased because of improved myocardial protection strategies. However, the relative number of patients with poor preoperative cardiac function has risen and thus the need for unexpected post-cardiotomy support remains essential. The most effective strategy to deal with this scenario is early institution of ventricular support prior to end-organ damage. This requires considerable judgment, experience with device options and dogged attention to care details. Creating and following guidelines and established protocols for institution of extraordinary mechanical ventricular support (beyond inotropes and/or intra-aortic balloon pump) improve survival dramatically. Samuels, et al showed that early (within 3 hours) institution of VAD support once two or more high-dose inotropes are required produced improved survival. Several current ventricular support devices are readily available and can be inserted without extensive previous experience.

The described patient has profound left ventricular failure and ample evidence of inadequate systemic perfusion. Correcting the acidosis may optimize the response to pharmacologic support, but the underlying muscle dysfunction is global and severe. The man's pulmonary hypertension is a reflection of left ventricular failure, and response to nitric oxide is unlikely. Functional grafts are documented, so additional bypass conduits are not indicated. Contractility will not return quickly and aggressive inotropic stimulation will worsen the chance of recovery. Venoarterial ECMO is an option, but it is not necessary if mechanical support is instituted early enough to prevent lung damage. Isolated LVAD placement will probably suffice for univentricular failure, although occasionally biventricular support becomes necessary. critique:

Overall, 16% of the LVAD patients had a stroke (0.19 per year) compared to 0.052 per year in the medical group. The mean interval from LVAD implantation to stroke was 221.8 days, although many occurred in the early postop recovery.

question_text: Regarding using an LVAD as bridge to transplantation, which of the following statements is correct?
critique:
Bleeding is the most common complication associated with LVAD implantation. Excessive bleeding (> 4 units) occurs in most patients, and returning to the operating room for control is frequent (up to 60%). Preoperative comorbidities such as renal insufficiency, hepatic congestion, and low flow state contribute to the high incidence of bleeding. Strategies to manage coagulopathy include preoperative Vitamin K, preoperative plasmapheresis, priming the cardiopulmonary bypass circuit with fresh frozen plasma, and use of antifibrinolytics. Some surgeons routinely perform delayed chest closure so tamponade and emergency reoperation can be avoided. Planned, early post-pump treatment of coagulopathy with FFP, cryoprecipitate and platelet transfusions is routine in many centers. Recombinant factor VII has been used effectively both intra- and postoperatively in VAD patients, but several reports caution against routine use of this drug and component therapy because of potential pro-thrombotic consequences. After LVAD placement the reported rates of stroke and thromboembolism vary from 10-30%. The type of device, anticoagulation regimen, and various definitions of "neurological event" each influence statistical reports of these complications.

Excessive transfusion of blood products is associated with several postoperative complications, including right ventricular (RV) failure, which is reported to occur in up to 30% of patients who require an LVAD. RV function in the initial postoperative phase often determines mortality after LVAD. A typical LVAD patient requires one or two inotropes and either inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin to achieve and maintain adequate LVAD flows. All agents usually can be weaned off slowly over a few days. Despite this anticipated outcome, a right-side VAD is required in approximately 10% of LVAD patients. The incidence of RVAD use has not been higher with the use of newer generation rotary pumps.

Outcome reports indicate similar results for nearly all bridge LVAD devices, with survival to transplantation in 60% to 70% of patients and survival to discharge after transplantation of 50% to 60% of the total population. For comparison, 84% of non-bridged listed patients receive a transplant (UNOS, 2008; USA patients 07/01/2004-12/31/2006). Despite increased immunologic sensitization in bridged patients, contemporary post-transplant survival is similar to non-bridged patients, which is 85-90%.

Overall infectious complications are less with continuous flow VADs. Bacteremia (25%) and pump endocarditis (3%) are equivalent. However, driveline, pocket, wound, and local device infections and sepsis are all substantially lower with axial flow devices.

critique:
Axial and centrifugal pumps, the newest generation of LVADS, function by a different method to achieve mechanical support. Each of these two pump types has a rotor that constantly spins, allowing uninterrupted unloading of the ventricle. With axial pumps the overall direction of blood flow from the inlet to the outlet is linear. With centrifugal flow, the direction of inflow is perpendicular to the outflow.

All continuous flow pumps produce minimal pulse pressure, but in clinical application pulsatility is usually maintained as a result of native ventricular contraction and output. Although these devices are often called non-pulsatile, they should be considered low pulsatility, continuous flow pumps (c-LVAD). If the device inflow cannula is well-positioned, then device rotation speed (rpm) determines the degree of ventricular emptying (unloading) and the potential for native output. Current pulsatile (volume displacement) and continuous flow devices, when operated at fixed rates or rpm respectively, produce equivalent ventricular unloading. Each reduces intrinsic cardiac output and its pulsatility. However, sustained high speed c-LVAD settings can completely unload a ventricle throughout the cardiac cycle, which invites septal shift and a "suction event." This potential complication is unique to these pumps and can result in very low pump output with slow recovery, especially in the setting of hypovolemia or limited right heart output.

Although the long-term effects of low pulsatility on end organ function are not certain, growing experience and observations suggest that both end-organ recovery and success as a bridge to transplantation are at least equivalent to traditional pulsatile devices. Current reports indicate good durability and limited device failure in bridge-to-transplant applications (median support time 126 days, maximum 600 days in one study). Destination therapy trials are not mature.

question_text: According to current CMS guidelines, which of the following patients is eligible for a VAD as destination therapy?
critique:
The term "destination therapy" refers to implantation of an LVAD or total artificial heart as a permanent device for to treat end-stage heart failure. The initial approval of this application for the Heartmate electric, pulsatile pump (currently designated as Heartmate XVE) required that patients be on optimal medical therapy for at least two months. This involves current standard treatments, which may include any or all of the following: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, Œ≤-blockers, vasodilators, aldactone antagonists, and ICD/Biventricular pacemakers. Patients must not be eligible for cardiac transplantation and have a life expectancy of less than two years. The approval of this device was based on the landmark REMATCH trial (see below) that showed a survival advantage for patients receiving the Heartmate device compared to continued medical therapy.

Age over 65 is a relative contraindication to transplantation and many centers now transplant older patients if they do not have significant comorbidity. The REMATCH trial included only patients who were in NYHA Class IV heart failure on medical therapy (2/3 were dependent on inotropes), with EF < 25%, VO2max< 14 ml/(kg*min), and who were ineligible for transplantation. The trial only involved patients with chronic heart failure and was not meant to enroll patients with acute heart failure from acute myocardial infarction or post-cardiotomy shock. Although recent data and interest is directed at applying destination therapy for Class III heart failure (particularly class IIIB), no data is yet available from ongoing clinical trials.

Evaluation of patients for destination therapy VAD should include a complete and systematic workup equivalent to evaluation for cardiac transplantation. Comorbid factors associated with poor survival include severe right heart dysfunction, coagulopathy associated with liver dysfunction, renal insufficiency, poor nutritional status (albumin < 3.3 mg/dl), inability to undergo cardiopulmonary testing (often due to dependence on inotropes). In addition, a stable psychosocial condition is necessary for care associated with ventricular assist devices, whether for bridge-to-transplant or destination therapy.

 

Current CMS guidelines for VAD destination therapy relate to patients who have chronic end-stage heart failure (NYHA Class IV left ventricular failure for at least 90 days with a life expectancy of less than 2 years).  They must not be candidates for heart transplantation, and must meet all of the following conditions:  
a. The patient’s Class IV heart failure symptoms have failed to respond to optimal medical management, including dietary salt restriction, diuretics, digitalis, beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors (if tolerated) for at least 60 of the last 90 days.
b. The patient has a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <25%.
c. The patient has demonstrated functional limitation with a peak oxygen consumption of <12 ml/kg/min; or the patient has a continued need for intravenous inotropic therapy owing to symptomatic hypotension, decreasing renal function, or worsening pulmonary congestion.
d. The patient has the appropriate body size (>1.5 m2) to support the VAD implantation.
 
The acute course of several of the patients described excludes them from consideration.  Adriamycin-induced cardiomyopathy is a lethal condition, but a new diagnosis dictates maximal medical therapy as primary treatment.  Transplantation for this condition may be possible depending on cancer status and intervals, which must be resolved before destination VAD can be considered.  Imatinib therapy for CML has improved outcomes dramatically, and bone marrow or stem cell transplantation is an option for recurrent disease.

question_text: A 59-year-old man experienced increasing angina during routine activities. He had two episodes during hemodialysis last week and was admitted for further workup. A high resolution CT slice is shown. These findings are significant for
critique:
The pattern of coronary blood flow during the coronary cycle is unique. Epicardial coronary vessels serve as capacitance vessels, primarily filling during the period of diastole (as much as 85% of total flow), and intramural pressure and resistance to myocardial perfusion progressively increase from the outer to inner layers of the heart. Myocardial arterioles have tremendous vasodilatory reserve capacity and enable high flow with low resistance in response to exercise. Two mechanisms of vasodilatation may be available: larger proximal vessels by endothelium-derived nitric oxide, and direct stimulation of smooth muscle cell alpha2-receptors by adenosine and other metabolites.

A coronary artery with an oblique origin, an intramural (within the wall of the aorta) course, or a position between the great arteries (as seen in this patient's CT) may be compressed and its reservoir capacity may be severly limited. The law of Laplace (tension = pressure x radius) dictates that comparable pressure in larger vessels creates greater wall tension. Thus the aorta and main pulmonary artery can compress smaller vessels that course between them or are intramural.

Signs and symptoms in older patients can include angina, syncope, arrhythmias, MI, enlarged heart, and sudden death, which is most often associated with activity. Sudden death is frequently observed in association with anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the right sinus of Valsalva. This pattern is associated with an oblique origin, a slit-like ostium, and an intramural, inter-arterial course. Each of these features (oblique origin, ostial stenosis, intramural and intra-arterial compression) can diminish flow and result in coronary ischemia. Limited flow and loss of reservoir capacity cannot meet the increased myocardial oxygen demands associated with exercise.

He has been compliant with his Œ≤-blocker regimen but he is concerned because his sister had an aortic dissection at age 26. An echocardiogram shows normal aortic valve function and normal ventricular function. The most appropriate management is to
critique:
All patients with Marfan syndrome require aggressive cardiovascular imaging surveillance including echocardiograms obtained at regular intervals. Patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk of acute aortic dissection even when the aorta is only modestly dilated, and this is particularly true in patients with a family history of dissection. Therefore, aortic root replacement is recommended when the ascending aortic diameter exceeds 5.0 cm in patients with Marfan syndrome, in contrast to the 5.5-cm threshold generally used in non-Marfan patients. When patients with Marfan syndrome undergo isolated graft replacement of the tubular portion of the ascending aorta, progressive disease of the aortic root -- including annuloaortic ectasia, aortic valve regurgitation, and acute dissection -- invariably develops, necessitating complex reoperation. Therefore, ascending aortic repair should always involve full root replacement using either valve-replacing or valve-sparing techniques, even if the sinuses of Valsalva are not yet dilated and the aortic valve is competent.

Although treatment with Œ≤-blockers is currently standard for Marfan patients, the effectiveness of this therapy has not yet been proved. Recent experiments show that losartan, an angiotensin II type 1 receptor antagonist, prevents aortic dilatation in a mouse model of Marfan syndrome. This work has generated a current randomized clinical trial. Regardless of losartan's efficacy in preventing aneurysms, however, it will not replace surgical treatment for patients who have indications for aortic replacement.

question_text: The mutation causing Marfan syndrome most frequently involves the gene for
critique:
Marfan syndrome is a heritable connective tissue disorder associated with severe orthopedic, ophthalmologic, and cardiovascular manifestations. The most common cardiovascular problem in patients with Marfan syndrome is aortic root aneurysm caused by progressive annuloaortic ectasia. If untreated, such aneurysms ultimately rupture, dissect, or cause severe aortic valve regurgitation. In addition to aortic root aneurysms, patients with Marfan syndrome are prone to mitral valve prolapse and to aneurysms and dissections involving the aortic arch and thoracoabdominal aorta. This propensity for developing multiple aortic aneurysms mandates that periodic aortic imaging be continued for life, even after a patient has undergone successful aortic root replacement.

In most patients who meet the clinical diagnostic criteria for Marfan syndrome (ie, the Ghent criteria), the disease is attributed to a mutation in the gene for fibrillin-1. Fibrillin-1 is a glycoprotein component of microfibrils, which are key structural components of the extracellular matrix within the media of the aortic wall. Elastin and collagen are the major components of the aortic wall matrix, conferring resilience and strength, respectively. Mutations that affect these proteins are responsible for other cardiovascular conditions. For example, the vascular form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by mutations affecting type III collagen, and supravalvular aortic stenosis is caused by mutations affecting elastin. Mutations that affect a receptor for transforming growth factor-Œ≤ have been described in patients with clinical features of Marfan syndrome, and these mutations have been recently shown to cause Loeys-Dietz syndrome, a condition associated with particularly severe aortic and peripheral vascular manifestations that require aggressive surgical treatment.

critique:

The presence of symptoms is the most important consideration, and the lesion causing the most life-threatening symptoms should be repaired first. Second, the presence of correctable cardiac disease is an issue because clamping the descending thoracic aorta induces substantial cardiac stress. Addressing correctable coronary and valvular disease first reduces the risk of cardiac complications during the thoracoabdominal aortic repair. A third consideration relates to assessing the relative sizes of the aneurysms. When one aneurysm is disproportionately larger than the other, the larger aneurysm is treated first.

critique:
Myocardial protection during prolonged cooling for circulatory arrest can be challenging in patients with ascending/arch aneurysms and aortic valve regurgitation. The incompetent valve allows pump flow to distend the fibrillating left ventricle and causes a marked increase in sump drainage. If not corrected, ventricular distention will cause increased myocardial oxygen demand and decreased subendocardial perfusion. The resulting inadequate myocardial preservation will lead to severely impaired postoperative cardiac function. Adding another ventricular sump may lessen distention but will not correct or reliably control this problem.

The best way to protect the myocardium is to induce cardioplegic arrest as rapidly as possible after fibrillation. When anatomically feasible, the aneurysmal ascending aorta should be clamped. This will stop the inflow into the distended left ventricle, increase systemic flow, and allow delivery of cardioplegia. In the described patient, the ascending aorta is not dissected and atheromata are not prominent so it can be clamped safely. Placing a needle in the ascending aorta is unlikely to allow adequate cardioplegia delivery, as the cardioplegia will flow through the regurgitant valve instead of pressurizing the root and perfusing the coronary arteries. The best approach is to open the ascending aorta and deliver cardioplegia directly into the coronary ostia. When clamping the aorta is not possible (e.g., in patients with enormous aneurysms, see figure) delivering continuous retrograde cardioplegia while manually decompressing the ventricle and continuing rapid cooling may be the only option.

critique:
The CT angiogram shown reveals a Type B intramural hematoma (IMH) with a penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (PAU). As the name implies, PAU is associated with severe atherosclerotic disease and the radiologic appearance is similar to ulceration in the GI tract. The natural history and best treatment of PAU is somewhat controversial. Recent studies suggest that conservative treatment is appropriate under most conditions. However, close clinical follow-up is mandatory as thin-walled saccular pseudoaneurysms or rupture may occur. This patient's ipsilateral pleural effusion heightens concern for such complications, and TEE may define the local anatomy more precisely. While endoaortic stent grafting might appear to be well suited for a localized PAU, severe atherosclerosis in the aorta and the embolic risk of manipulation, the risk of paraplegia and access difficulties moderate these considerations. The current clinical experience with endografting for IMH-PAU is meager.

Intramural hematoma was initially thought to result from rupture of vasa vasora, though there is little evidence to support this theory. Others believe that IMH is always associated with some degree of intimal tear that may go undetected. The case of PAU with IMH, as is in this patient, appears to contradict that theory. On CT or MRI imaging IMH appears as a crescentic or concentric wall thickening greater than 0.5-0.7 cm. This represents medial degeneration with hematoma within the media, though at a location closer to the adventitia compared to the pathology of aortic dissection.

The natural history of IMH is more benign than aortic dissection, perhaps due to a lower associated incidence of malperfusion syndromes. Aortic dissection, rupture or late progression to aneurysm may evolve from IMH. Like aortic dissection, IMH is categorized as type A (involving the ascending aorta) or type B (isolated to the descending aorta). Type B, as in this case, has a less malignant course. Complete resolution of the hematoma has been observed in 50-80% of cases with conservative management. Predictors of progression include the presence of PAU, older age, aortic diameter greater than 4.0-4.5 cm, and hematoma thickness greater than 1 cm. Nonoperative management of type B IMH is widely accepted. Controversy exists regarding the management of type A IMH, with some advocating intervention only in cases of complication (dissection, expansion, rupture) while others propose a more aggressive approach. If conservative management is chosen, patients require inpatient observation in the ICU with bed rest for 2 weeks and vigilant blood pressure control. Repeat imaging by CT or MRI is mandatory every few days, as is repeat echocardiography.

This man has developed acute, delayed paraplegia following thoracoabdominal aortic replacement that is likely secondary to hypotension caused or exacerbated by starting a propofol infusion for sedation. Delayed paraplegia is a well-known phenomenon that occurs after thoracoabdominal aortic surgery and is often due to hypotension in a watershed zone of devascularized spinal cord. If treated immediately it can often be reversed by improving spinal perfusion pressure. This is best achieved by a combination of hypertensive treatment and lumbar CSF drainage. Vasopressors (e.g. norepinephrine, neosynephrine, or vasopressin) can be used to initiate hypertension. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) should be increased stepwise every few minutes until an improvement in the lower extremity neurologic exam is noted (initial MAP target pressure is above 90 mmHg). Several factors are involved with most cases of delayed onset paraplegia, and its prognosis is much better than paraplegia noted immediately at the end of aneurysm repair.

In this case, the spinal (or cerebral) perfusion pressure was only 41 mmHg (MAP-CVP) when neurologic changes were noted. The propofol infusion should be discontinued immediately and a vasopressor infused to reverse the hypotension. There is already a lumbar CSF drain in place because the intrathecal pressure is provided, but a new drain is indicated if there is a question about its function. The drain should be opened to drop intrathecal pressure to below 10 mmHg to further improve spinal perfusion pressure.

MR angiography might help define a region of infarction, but it is an inappropriate first step in management because treatment would be delayed. Nicardipine is an antihypertensive drug, which is contraindicated in this setting. Naloxone (Narcan) has been used in the setting of acute paraplegia following thoracoabdominal aortic replacement, but its efficacy is not well-established. Its use as an adjunct would be secondary to the primary therapies (hypertensive therapy and CSF drainage).

Normal atrioventricular (A-V) conduction directs the electrical impulse from the SA node though the AV node to the His bundle and down the Purkinje cells. The A-V node creates an electrical delay prior to the impulse entering the His bundle. The central fibrous body normally acts as a functional electrical insulator from abnormal A-V conduction. If there is an accessory A-V conduction connection (Kent bundle), then more rapid antegrade conduction down this pathway may occur. This pre-excitation translates to a short P-R interval and a delta wave noted on the ECG. These features are apparent in the augmented figure. This patient has Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome.

Reciprocating tachycardia can develop if an accessory pathway functions as part of a re-entrant conduction loop. Either the Kent bundle or the normal A-V node can conduct these impulses, but each can function in one direction only. If A-V conduction is normal and the impulse returns via the accessory bundle it is termed orthodromic. If antegrade conduction is via the accessory pathway and re-entry is backward through the A-V node, it is antidromic. Rapid tachycardia can occur in either case, with the upper rate limited only by the refractory periods of the pathways. The ventricular response may be fast enough to be inefficient and cause low cardiac output symptoms or sudden death. Development of atrial fibrillation can certainly be dangerous.

WPW and other accessory pathway-mediated tachycardias were once surgical diseases, but now they are best treated by percutaneous mapping and ablation of the accessory pathway. A MAZE procedure or unmapped left atrial ablation will not offer the requisite precise identification or destruction of this patient's accessory pathway. Since the A-V node is not the abnormality, node ablation and permanent pacing is not appropriate. Most patients with WPW syndrome have few symptoms and chronic drug therapy is undesirable and not reliably effective. A primary challenge is to determine when ablation is warranted.
