title: cardiac transplantation; recipient contraindications
question_text: Which of the following recipient characteristics is an absolute contraindication to cardiac transplantation?
critique:
Cardiac transplantation has traditionally been offered to patients less than 66 years of age due to organ availability and historical reports of worse survival. With improved patient selection and postoperative management excellent early survival and good mid- and long-term outcomes are now seen in well-selected older patients. However, careful selection is still advised for all recipient candidates over age 55. Renal insufficiency is often seen with end-stage heart failure. The causes can be multifactorial although a pre-renal component is common. Determining the potential for renal function recovery is difficult, especially when nephrotoxic immunosuppressants are used. Preoperative 24-hour creatinine clearance and renal biopsy are often needed. A creatinine clearance under 30 mL/min is an indication for combined heart/kidney transplant.

Recently diagnosed malignancy of any kind is an absolute contraindication to a solid organ transplant. However, a remote history of treated cancer (more than 5 years disease-free) is not an absolute contraindication and should be assessed cautiously and case by case. Many programs match hepatitis C virus (HCV) positive recipients with HCV positive donor organs because of survival concerns, although HCV status is unknown for many recipients and the actual effects of recipient HCV positivity are not striking. Hearts from hepatitis C-positive donors are associated with decreased recipient survival (hazard ratio 2.1 for HCV negative recipients), but outcomes do not prohibit use of these organs, and survival is independent of recipient age and HCV status.

Secondary pulmonary hypertension is commonly seen in end-stage heart failure patients. Preoperative preparation of the recipient includes decreasing the pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) to under 3 Woods units. The donor (normal) heart is rarely able to generate and sustain enough pressure to accommodate PVR elevation beyond this. Strategies to reduce PVR include chronic afterload reduction and long-term LVAD use.

critique:
An atrial myxoma (as seen in the specimen) is most commonly sporadic, isolated, of left atrial origin, and rarely recurrent. However, familial forms of atrial myxoma exist and should be suspected when tumors are multiple, recurrent, or atypically located. Carney complex is a rare autosomal dominant multiple endocrine neoplasia-like syndrome with nearly complete penetrance. Previously acronyms include LAMB (lentigines, atrial myxomas, mucocutaneous myxomas, and blue nevi), and NAME (nevi, atrial myxomas, and ephelides). Defects in the PRKAR1A gene on chromosomes 17 and 2 lead to erratic protein kinase activity due to a faulty cAMP subunit. Patients manifest with cardiac myxomas that may occur in any chamber. They are often multiple and may recur. Extracardiac myxomas also occur, and are seen in the skin and mucosa of the eyelid, ear, breast and nipples. Spotty skin pigmentation (lentigenes or liver spots) are seen on the eyelids (as shown in the photograph of this patient), ears, conjunctiva, lips, or genital mucosa of 95% of patients and should alert the astute clinician to this possible diagnosis. Blue nevi and cafe au lait spots may also be seen. Importantly, these patients can share characteristics of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes I, IIA and IIB. Abnormalities of thyroid (most commonly follicular adenoma, but thyroid cancer in 10%), adrenal (Cushing's syndrome), pituitary (acromegaly, elevated growth hormone and IL-1), testicle (sertoli cell tumors), and breast (ductal adenoma) have been reported.

Peutz-Jegher syndrome is an inherited polyposis of the intestinal tract characterized by multiple hamartomas, especially in the jejunum. It is also associated with melanin spots on the lips and buccal mucosa, but not with familial atrial myxomas. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease) is another genetic syndrome associated with multiple soft tissue tumors (neurofibromas) of the skin and nervous system. Skin pigmentations known as cafe au lait spots are associated with this disorder, but they appear different from those in the photograph of this patient. Neurofibromatosis has no association with recurrent atrial myxomas. The skin lesions of melanoma are distinguished by asymmetry, irregular border, heterogeneous color, and diameter greater than 6mmm which differ from those in the picture. Metastasis to the heart, while possible, is unlikely.

question_text: A 72-year-old man is in the coronary care unit in pulmonary edema. He was generally healthy until the preceding two weeks of shortness of breath on exertion, malaise, low grade fevers, and night sweats. On examination he has a loud apical systolic murmur and scattered bilateral rales. A recent echocardiogram revealed an anterior leaflet perforation and a mobile vegetation that measured one cm in diameter. Lab results include an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 81 mm/hr and a WBC of 32,000. Multiple blood cultures drawn 24 hours ago in his primary care physician's office are now positive for Streptococcus bovis. critique:
ACC/AHA guidelines are classified both by the strength of recommendation and the quality of evidence supporting the recommendation. Class I recommendations are those for which "there is evidence for or general agreement that the treatment is beneficial, useful, and effective." Class II recommendations are those for which there is conflicting evidence or a divergence of opinion about the efficacy of a treatment. If the weight of opinion is in favor of the treatment these recommendations are graded Class IIa. Class IIb recommendations are those for which treatment efficacy is less well established. The internet link supplied outlines current guidelines for care of patients with valvular heart disease.

The timing of surgery is a key part of optimizing surgical management of endocarditis. Patients should be taken to the operating room regardless of the duration of antimicrobial therapy when there is an indication for surgery. Current ACC/AHA class I indications for surgery in native valve endocarditis include:
1) any acute valve lesion resulting in heart failure
2) aortic or mitral regurgitation with hemodynamic evidence of elevated left ventricular end-diastolic or left atrial pressures or moderate pulmonary hypertension
3) structural complications such as annular or aortic abscess, or other destructive penetrating lesions including fistulae and "kissing lesions"
4) fungal or other highly resistant organisms

Native valve endocarditis complicated by recurrent emboli and persistent vegetations despite appropriate antibiotic therapy is a class IIa indication for surgery, and the presence of mobile vegetations in excess of 10mm with or without emboli is classed by the ACC/AHA guidelines as a class IIb indication for surgery. In this patient, heart failure with pulmonary edema is an urgent indication for surgery. Other indications exist, but they do not justify emergent operation: anterior leaflet perforation will eventually need surgery; a mobile vegetation without embolization is likely to be watched in an elderly patient; Streptococcus bovis is a sensitive organism which can often be eradicated by antibiotic therapy; and an elevated WBC at this point in his treatment does not constitute uncontrolled sepsis.

1 - prepare for discussion by ensuring all information/facts/data are available
2 - deliver an analysis in person in a private area without interruptions
3 - establish patient and/or family knowledge and understanding of the illness
4 - establish what/how much the patient and/or family want to know
5 - deliver information in a sensitive, straightforward manner, avoiding technical language and euphemisms
6 - check for understanding and clarify concepts and terms
7 - respond by using active listening, encouraging expression of emotions
8 - organize an immediate therapeutic plan that addresses the patient's and family's concerns and agenda
9 - reassess understanding of the condition and treatment plan and determine the need for further education and follow-up

critique:
Several names describe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), including hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), and idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis (IHSS). The most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young people is related to HCM, but a minority of all HCM patients is susceptible to this risk (10%-15%). Treatment for HCM remains controversial. When recognized, the associated arrhythmias and sudden death risk can be treated with an ICD. Drugs, dual-chamber pacing, and percutaneous alcohol septal ablation have all been touted as optimal strategies for these patients, but each of these options carries unique risks. Septal alcohol injection done via percutaneous retrograde injection was first reported in 1995. Current follow-up studies in multiple centers report an effectiveness of 75%-80%. Patient selection factors include severe heart failure symptoms (NYHA classes III or IV) refractory to medications as well as a subaortic gradient of at least 50 mmHg. In this procedure 1-3 cc of absolute alcohol is injected through a small catheter impacted into the first septal branch of the LAD. Improvement of the gradient takes 6-12 months, and echocardiography is used to monitor progress.

The history of surgical resection for HCM is rich, and the reference article by Morrow is a classic that should be read by all surgeons. The described retrograde approach through the aortic valve has not been improved upon. A recent 10-year experience at Cleveland clinic involved 323 patients, with no hospital mortality and sustained relief of outflow tract gradients. Heart block requiring permanent pacing and iatrogenic VSD (all repaired) were the most notable complications. Reoperation was required in 3% for HCM related causes. In this and other surgical series the risk of sudden death was reduced to that of the general population, and ICD requirements are reduced, both of which benefits are not seen with other types of treatment. A 2005 Canadian study compared outcomes of 48 patients who had myomectomy with 60 that underwent alcohol injection. The surgical group had superior outcomes in virtually every measure including functional class, survival, freedom from pacemakers, pressure gradient, and mitral systolic anterior motion. The measured septal thickness and the incidence of mitral regurgitation were similar at an average follow-up interval of 2.2 years.

critique:
Criteria for catheter intervention for mitral stenosis are based on symptoms, valve characteristics and pulmonary artery pressures. A symptomatic patient (NYHA class II or worse) must have favorable valve morphology and moderate or severe mitral stenosis and/or PA systolic pressure > 50 mmHg at rest (or > 60 mmHg with exercise to satisfy ACC / AHA Class I indications for percutaneous mitral balloon valvotomy/valvuloplasty. Favorable valve morphology includes non-calcified, pliable mitral valve leaflets.

Mitral valve morphology is most important determinant of immediate post-valvotomy hemodynamic results and long-term clinical outcomes. Patients with valvular calcification, thickened and fibrotic leaflets with decreased mobility, and subvalvular fusion have a higher incidence of acute complications and a higher rate of recurrent stenosis on follow-up. Therefore, marked fusion of the leaflets and subvalvular apparatus and severe commissural calcification are relative contraindication to percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy. The Wilkins scoring system grades mitral valve morphology using four echocardiographic characteristics:  leaflet mobility, leaflet thickening, valve calcification and involvement of the subvalvular apparatus. Each parameter is graded from 0-4. A total score of more than 8 predicts a low success with percutaneous mitral valvuloplasty. Other relative contraindications to this procedure include left atrial thrombus and mitral regurgitation that is worse than mild.

The thresholds for mitral valve surgery for stenosis have historically been more conservative than for regurgitation. The potential for durable repair is much lower, and MVR is generally reserved for symptomatic patients or those with severe pulmonary hypertension. The described patient has NYHA class II symptoms and moderate mitral stenosis. Scoring contraindicates percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy, and conventional recommendation is medical management with follow-up in six months (see figure).

Tools available to treat mitral systolic anterior motion (shown in the video clip) include discontinuation of inotropic agents, additional volume, added alpha agents and, possibly, Œ≤-blockade. When these maneuvers fail to reverse SAM the cause is usually a discrepancy between the residual anterior and posterior leaflet heights and the septal-lateral diameter of the mitral annulus following ring annuloplasty. The type of ring annuloplasty does not influence the risk of SAM, and this condition has been reported with essentially all types of annuloplasty rings (flexible, rigid, semi-rigid rings and partial or complete designs). This complication can occur in the absence of an annuloplasty ring, so changing the ring to an incomplete band is unlikely to resolve SAM. Sizing the ring is a more critical issue, but since a 40 mm ring is the largest commercially available size, a larger ring is not an option in the described case. Removing the ring could resolve the SAM, but absence of a ring in degenerative repair can predispose to recurrent mitral regurgitation in the long term.

The likely cause of SAM in this case is excess residual posterior leaflet tissue. Although the posterior leaflet is tall, the repair was undertaken with minimal resection techniques (triangular resection and artificial chordae). The residual posterior leaflet height is likely displacing the anterior leaflet into the left ventricular outflow tract. A sliding posterior leaflet plasty would have been appropriate during the initial operation to minimize the risk of SAM. At this point, however, it would be necessary to remove the ring and a longer period of cross clamping and bypass would be required. Mitral valve replacement is usually not necessary and it should be avoided in this young woman. Repair is better because valve replacement would shorten her life expectancy, increase the lifetime risk of stroke and potentially complicate childbirth. One effective solution is to shorten the anterior leaflet. This is achieved by making a transverse incision toward the base of the anterior leaflet and re-suturing (which will shorten the leaflet by 5 to 7 mm) or to resect a 2 to 3 mm transverse ellipse of the leaflet before re-suturing (which will shorten the leaflet by 7 to 10 mm). A triangular resection of A2 is another option to shorten its length. Another option is to use a shorter PTFE chord to lower the margin of the posterior leaflet further down into the ventricle, moving the closure line more posteriorly and aligning the anterior leaflet away from the outflow tract. Finally, a recently proposed technique of posterior leaflet shortening by pledgeted sutures through the leaflet and under the annuloplasty ring has promise as an equivalent to sliding plasty.

critique:
Mitral valve repair offers superior long-term survival, freedom from cardiac morbidity, and better quality of life in most patients with severe mitral regurgitation compared to medical management and mitral valve replacement. It is the treatment of choice in these patients because it is the only treatment that restores normal life expectancy to otherwise healthy patients with advanced degenerative mitral valve disease.

(1) a prior history of myocardial infarction
(2) tethering of predominantly P2 and P3

Several clinical trials demonstrated clinical improvement when selected patients with systolic ventricular dysfunction and heart failure were treated with CRT. Using these "standard" selection criteria 60-70% of patients benefited symptomatically from biventricular pacing. Conversely, a patient with an EF of 40% likely has diastolic heart failure from hypertension and conventional medical therapy is indicated. question_text: A 62-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis presented with shortness of breath and lower extremity edema. Physical exam revealed a positive Kussmaul's sign, marked jugular venous distension, and no significant pulsus paradoxus. Pressure tracings from his heart catheterization are shown. critique:
Catheterization hemodynamics in pericardial constriction reveal three key features: (1) elevation and equalization of diastolic pressures in each of the cardiac chambers; (2) early diastolic "dip-and-plateau" or "square root-sign" configurations in the right and left ventricular tracings; and (3) a prominent y-descent in the right atrial pressure tracing. The constrictive effect of the thickened pericardium results in elevated, equalized diastolic pressures all cardiac chambers. Early diastolic filling is unimpeded and elevated venous pressures lead to abnormally rapid filling, while ventricular pressure decreases during this time. This rapid early diastolic filling then abruptly stops and ventricular pressure increases abruptly as intracardiac volumes approach the volume limit set by the noncompliant, thickened pericardium. The dip-and-plateau pattern (a.k.a. square root sign) of the ventricular waveform reflects rapid filling and arrested volume accumulation respectively. Equalized cardiac diastolic pressures and volumes translate to limited stroke volume and cardiac output.

Increased sensitivity and specificity of hemodynamic testing can be augmented by provocative maneuvers. Intracardiac pressure dissociation is a phenomenon whereby inspiration leads to increased RV inflow and intraventricular septal shifting to the left, which reduce left ventricular filling. This creates a preload mismatch between the left and right sides of the heart, with elevated preload on the right compared to the left. Simultaneous right- and left-sided ventricular pressure tracings become discordant and begin to separate as a consequence, with LV pressures falling while RV pressures increase. The opposite occurs during expiration. This discordant response does not occur with restrictive disorders or congestive heart failure. Examination of the right atrial wave forms shows an exaggerated and deep y-descent compared to the x-descent, forming a characteristic M or W configuration. This is in contrast to cardiac tamponade in which the y-descent is attenuated or up sloping. Cardiac tamponade is the result of generalized cardiac compression throughout diastole. As such the diastolic surge that is seen in a constrictive pericardial patient is absent. Atrial filling occurs during ventricular ejection in early systole and the venous pressure tracing shows an absent or blunted diastolic y-descent.

question_text: A 59-year-old woman has elevated 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) serum levels and consequent systemic symptoms. Examination shows significant lower extremity edema and ascites. critique:
Midgut carcinoid tumors may secrete 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin), tachykinins, and prostaglandins. The liver effectively inactivates these compounds from the portal circulation, but when disease advances to include hepatic or distant metastases the vasoactive substances produced are able to reach the systemic circulation. Clinically, this is characterized by flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm. It is believed that these same substances induce fibrous tissue plaques on the endocardial surfaces of the heart, predominantly on the right side (15% have left side involvement). Typical tricuspid involvement includes thickened and fused commissures and chordae tendineae. Similarly, tricuspid and pulmonary valve leaflets are thickened and retracted, resulting in combined stenosis and regurgitation. Up to 70% of patients with carcinoid syndrome have evidence of carcinoid heart disease with peripheral signs of right heart failure.

When symptoms are severe or if right ventricular dysfunction is demonstrated, valve replacement offers marked improvement and a possible survival benefit. Repair of such complex involvement, however, is unreliable. Previous reports favored use of mechanical prostheses because of potential early failure of bioprostheses from carcinoid plaque formation. However, the use of warfarin in the face of liver dysfunction poses an elevated bleeding risk and some patients will undergo subsequent hepatic resection, hepatic artery embolization or other surgery. Treating symptoms with somatostatin analogues (octreotide) seems to minimize plaque formation on tissue valves, and placing a bioprosthesis eliminates the risk of mechanical valve thrombosis. Although no large comparative series of different valve types is available, the use of tissue valves for carcinoid heart disease is presently favored.

Class I:
Severe TR in patients with MV disease requiring MV surgery (level of evidence B)

title: tricuspid valve; diagnosis; stenosis vs. regurgitation; physical examination
question_text: A 54-year-old woman complains of fatigue and weakness. On physical exam, she has a parasternal pansystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. There is jugular venous distention with fused c- and v-waves followed by a prominent y-descent. A chest radiograph demonstrates cardiomegaly, increased right atrial and ventricular size and a prominent azygos vein. Echocardiography will most likely demonstrate
critique:
The signs and symptoms of tricuspid regurgitation and stenosis overlap. However, there are distinct characteristics of each.

Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is often due to left-sided heart failure and evolves with symptoms of fatigue and weakness that result from reduced cardiac output. Right-sided heart failure leads to ascites, congestive hepatosplenomegaly, a pulsatile liver, pleural effusions, and peripheral edema. In the late stages, these patients are wasted with cachexia, cyanosis and jaundice. Impressive jugular venous distention with an s-wave or fused c- and v- waves, followed by a prominent y- descent, is present. During inspiration, this finding is accentuated because of the physiologic increase in venous return. Not surprisingly, atrial fibrillation is common. Auscultation of the heart is notable for an S3 that increases with inspiration and decreases with a Valsalva maneuver, an increased P2 if pulmonary hypertension has developed, and a parasternal pansystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. The chest radiograph demonstrates cardiomegaly, increased size of the right atrium and ventricle, a prominent azygos vein, possible pleural effusion and upward diaphragmatic displacement owing to ascites.

Tricuspid stenosis (TS) is most commonly rheumatic. It is rare to have isolated tricuspid stenosis, as some degree of TR is always present and coexisting mitral and aortic disease are occasionally seen. The incidence of rheumatic tricuspid valve disease in underdeveloped countries is still significant. Patients with TS also have presenting symptoms of fatigue and weakness related to reduced cardiac output. This lesion is more common in young women. A diastolic gradient across the valve causes the right atrium to thicken and dilate, while the right ventricle remains relatively normal in size, but underfilled. However, the clinical picture, similar to pure TR, features jugular venous distention, ascites, pleural effusions and peripheral edema. In sinus rhythm, the right atrial tracing and jugular venous pulse have prominent a-waves that accentuate with inspiration. The cardiac murmur is mid-diastolic and increases with inspiration. There may be an opening snap that is best heard along the left sternal border. The chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly with accentuated right atrial and pulmonary artery profiles.

Although it is preferable to wait until patients have conquered their drug dependence prior to valve replacement, at times a one-stage procedure is required. Many techniques have been described, including partial excision, prosthetic replacement, and replacement with homograft tissue or a stentless porcine valve, but no technique has proven to be superior. The main principal of treatment is the same for all endocarditis, which is complete elimination of infection.

The advantages of mitral valve repair over replacement should dominate decision making about patients with mitral regurgitation, and every effort should be made to repair the tricuspid valve when indicated. Since there is no overwhelming advantage to either mechanical or bioprosthetic valves in the tricuspid position, patient specific factors need to be considered. Some of these include age, expected survival, arrhythmias, need for right ventricular access (biopsy post-transplant, hemodynamic monitors in CHF, need for pacemaker), status of liver function (for future anticoagulation) and contraindications to anticoagulation.

In this case, severe right heart failure is obvious but tricuspid repair is not possible. A mechanical valve would commit the patient to long-term anticoagulation. A bioprosthetic valve would be a better choice for this patient or even a younger one, especially if the patient is a woman of a child-bearing age. No survival benefit (approximately 60% actuarial survival at 5 years) or difference in freedom from reoperation (> 90% at 5 years) has been demonstrated for either mechanical or bioprosthetic valves in the tricuspid position. Because of the relatively low pressure of the right side, bioprosthetic valves are more durable in the tricuspid position as compared to the mitral. Freedom from structural degeneration is nearly 100% at 9 years, but non-structural dysfunction is high (73%) due to pannus formation on the ventricular side of the cusps. This remains a concern that needs further investigation.

However, prosthetic tricuspid replacement is not complication-free, and mortality approximates 10%. The risk of complete heart block is approximately 6%. Pulmonary embolization rates following tricuspid replacement has been reported to be less than 1%.

Postinfarction ventricular septal rupture complicates 1-2% of patients after myocardial infarction. A patient may be minimally symptomatic or present in cardiogenic shock depending on the size and location of the infarct and the size of the left-to-right shunt. A new pansystolic ejection murmur is notable on physical examination and a precordial thrill is detected in 50% of patients. Late presentation with minimal symptoms is possible for a patient with a small defect, but in all other patients an intra-aortic balloon pump helps to stabilize hemodynamics in the pre- and peri-operative period. Percutaneous device closure is presently a plausible option for a recurrent ventricular septal defect following surgical closure or for a small defect detected late after infarction. critique:
For patients with severe coronary disease, tight proximal lesions may prevent adequate distribution of cardioplegia when given antegrade into the aortic root. Aortic valve regurgitation prohibits predictable coronary perfusion and risks left ventricular distention when antegrade delivery is attempted. A ventricular vent prevents this distention but does not permit quantification of actual cardioplegia delivery. Opening the aorta is required for direct ostial cannulation in these circumstances, and native coronary disease may still cause maldistribution and inadequate myocardial protection.

The use of retrograde cardioplegia has become a cornerstone tool for myocardial protection in many cardiac procedures in which a safe, and often prolonged, arrest in desired -- especially in complex cases. During complex operations on the aorta or aortic valve, continuous retrograde cardioplegia can be given not only for the benefit of myocardial protection but also to visualize the coronary ostia to prevent injury and to wash out any potential embolic particles. Retrograde delivery through the coronary sinus requires less manipulation within the operative field and less interruption of the work at hand. During aortic valve replacement and reoperations on patients with previous bypass grafts, retrograde delivery may reduce the risk of embolic complications and myocardial injury from debris resulting from manipulation of old, diseased grafts.

Despite its benefits, retrograde cardioplegia delivery can result in inadequate protection of the anterior surface of the right ventricle. The venous drainage of this portion of the heart is typically not into the coronary sinus and variability in coronary sinus anatomy can limit flow to the right ventricle. Hence, in patients with severe right ventricular dysfunction, additional protection techniques (such as topical cooling or additional antegrade cardioplegia) may be required to achieve optimal myocardial protection. Inadequate protection in the presence of a left superior vena cava and from a ruptured coronary sinus are unique shortcomings of retrograde delivery.

Cerebral oxygen consumption decreases more than 50% with a 10o C drop in temperature. However, brain activity cannot easily be arrested, glucose is the only substrate that can be utilized, and energy storage in neurons is negligible. Endothelial injury is also a concern, and cerebral vasospasm cannot be precisely controlled. Gross blood flow disturbances to the brain are not tolerated well. However, current techniques for profound hypothermia and circulatory arrest are well established for children and adults. Available strategies and interventions to minimize brain activity include hypothermia (both perfusion and topical) and pharmacologic (anti-inflammatory drugs and barbiturates). Operations for complex aortic disease are increasing, and hybrid strategies are evolving to minimize brain ischemic time and to afford maximal protection against anoxic and embolic damage.

Any increased cerebral activity during either cooling or warming may be a sign of unequal temperature distribution or neuronal injury and must be treated aggressively with increased cooling and/or deeper anesthesia. External warming is an important adjunct to achieve and maintain normothermia after an arrest period.

critique:
"Reperfusion injury" represents a spectrum of pathologies associated with re-establishing blood flow to ischemic myocardium. Myocyte and tissue damage may manifest as stunning, defined as "prolonged post-ischemic dysfunction of viable tissue salvaged by reperfusion." Various mechanisms have been proposed to explain the biochemical environment at the time of reperfusion that can account for the clinical findings. The "free radial hypothesis" suggests that oxidative stress and generation of free oxygen radicals (and depletion of antioxidants) results in cell damage. The "calcium hypothesis" stresses the importance of accumulated intracellular ionized calcium from low pH activated opening of Na-Ca channels during reperfusion. Depletion of intracellular energy stores (i.e., ATP) and disruption of phosphorylation ratios can also have a significant impact on myocardial contractility.

Myocardial cells can withstand severe hypoxia for about five minutes without significant lasting damage. More severe insults cause "stunning," which results from free radical generation, alteration of endothelial vasodilation capacity, release of platelet activating factor, increased intracellular calcium and its handling, increased intracellular protease activity, lactate accumulation, and imbalance of several fragile intracellular metabolic equilibria. Endothelial cells are exquisitely sensitive to anoxia, and damage results in vasoconstriction, increased platelet and WBC adhesion and activation, further thrombosis, and loss of vascular integrity. When microvascular dysfunction is severe, reperfusion may not be possible, a phenomenon termed "no-reflow." Even when myocardial protection seems adequate there is some degree of ischemia-reperfusion injury. It is worth noting that inotropic stimulation does not necessarily worsen reperfusion injury. When the balance of increased perfusion vs. work is favorable, inotropic agents are effective and do not worsen chances for ultimate functional recovery.

question_text: Several hours after an uneventful LVAD placement the initial flow of 6.5 L/min has dropped to 4 L/min. Each of the following may cause a low flow state EXCEPT
critique:
An acute decrease in LVAD flow must me immediately investigated and corrective action taken. Standard hemodynamic indices may explain the change, but several factors must be considered together. Almost all LVAD cannulations involve inflow from the left ventricle and outflow to the aorta. Causes of reduced flow of blood to the left ventricle include inadequate intravascular volume, tamponade, RV failure and mechanical factors.

Hypovolemia is often secondary to excessive bleeding and manifested by decreasing CVP, with or without changes in the pulmonary artery pressure. A fluid challenge will readily improve this problem. Cardiac tamponade is most typically indicated by elevated pulmonary wedge, PA and CVP pressures along with widening on the chest radiograph. More insidious and difficult to establish is focal tamponade from left atrial compression, which can occur without marked CVP elevation. Mechanical obstruction causing LVAD dysfunction is uncommon, but kinked cannulas and suboptimal LV cannula orientation have been reported. Operative exploration to clear the pericardial space and to reposition or reorient is necessary to remedy such problems.

Acute or progressive right ventricular failure is the most ominous cause of low LVAD output. Transfused blood and components, the systemic inflammatory response, volume expansion, tissue edema, right-to-left ventricular septal shift and low systemic blood pressure can contribute to acute RV failure despite adequate initial LVAD flows. A rising CVP in the setting of unchanged or low pulmonary artery pressure requires compulsive attention to minimize PA pressure, which is elevated by hypoxia, acidosis, hypercarbia, pneumothorax and pleural blood. In addition to inotropic support (phosphodiesterase inhibition is typical), inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin is often used to optimize transpulmonary flow.

Echocardiography will often clarify problems, although a transesophageal study may be necessary due to hardware, chest tubes and wound dressing congestion. Excessive "suction" by a continuous flow VAD or use of high vacuum on a pneumatic VAD can result in a right-to-left septal shift that impairs RV function and LV filling. Despite best efforts to characterize problems, however, when low LVAD flow fails to improve, returning to the operating room for open assessment is prudent. Implantation of an RVAD may be necessary, and a delay in making this decision is associated with very high mortality.

critique:
Selection of a donor allograft must consider organ quality and absence of transferable disease. Optimal donor management optimizes and maintains the quality of the organs and their utility. Organ quality is assessed with a thorough donor history that includes mechanism of brain death, malignancy, and infectious exposures (Hepatitis B, C, HIV). Accurate diagnostic studies (echocardiography, chest radiograph, and possible catheterization) are also critical.

A depressed global left ventricular ejection fraction (40%) may improve following a standardized hormonal resuscitation package consisting of methylprednisolone, triiodothyronine, and arginine vasopressin. However, segmental wall abnormalities with a moderate decrease in ejection fraction suggest direct myocardial injury, which is a relative contraindication to organ use. Donor heart left ventricular hypertrophy ( > 1.4 cm) is a predictor of increased mortality and increased vasculopathy after three years. Donor bacteremia poses an unacceptable risk of carrier septic inoculation of an immunocompromised host. Acoustic neuromas are benign cranial nerve tumors that pose no risk for transmission of malignancy.

critique:
Coordinating and addressing donor organ management with the needs of different procurement teams is challenging. The renal and liver harvesters prefer generous intravascular volume and the thoracic organ team members prefer a "dry" donor. Brain stem death results in severe hemodynamic instability, caused by vasomotor autonomic dysfunction, hypovolemia, hypothermia, and dysrhythmias. With specific respect to the cardiac donor and harvesting details, the two overarching goals are to optimize organ preparation for successful transplantation and to expand the donor pool. The best success has been achieved with compulsive donor evaluation with echocardiography to assess cardiac structure and function, and donors over age 45 should undergo cardiac catheterization to identify occult coronary occlusive disease. A PA catheter is useful for intravascular volume optimization and a standardized hormonal resuscitation package consisting of methylprednisolone, triiodothyronine, and arginine vasopressin.

Other management issues include maintaining normal values for temperature, electrolytes, osmolarity, acid-base balance, and oxygenation. Diuretics may be required to correct overzealous volume resuscitation. Vasopressin is useful because it addresses diabetes insipidus, which develops in nearly 50% of brain dead donors. This drug independently improves arterial blood pressure and it reduces exogenous inotrope requirements. When management is complicated, synthetic arginine vasopressin (DDAVP) may prove useful in addition to "standard" vasopressin infusion. Topical cooling is used for explanted organ preservation but not for donor management.

title: cardiac transplantation; technique; bicaval anastomoses; outcomes
question_text: Benefits of the bi-caval technique of orthotopic cardiac transplantation over the bi-atrial technique include each of the following EXCEPT
critique:
The original Lower-Shumway technique of cardiac transplantation involved leaving moderate-sized right and left atrial cuffs. The donor cardiectomy was performed by incising pulmonary veins and each vena cava. At implantation the donor pulmonary veins were connected and anastomosis to the left atrial cuff completed. The donor right atrium was incised vertically and onto the right atrial appendage, and a large right atrial chamber was created from the recipient cuff and the entire donor atrium. End-to-end aortic and pulmonary artery anastomoses completed the operation. Early and mid-term tricuspid regurgitation is frequent after this "conventional" orthotopic heart transplantation. Several mechanisms for this complication have been proposed, including asynchronous contraction of the donor and recipient atrial compartments and disturbed geometry of the right atrial anastomosis with subsequent impairment of the functional integrity of the tricuspid valvular apparatus. Supraventricular arrhythmias were common as was the requirement for chronic atrial pacing early post-transplant.

An alternate implantation technique, bicaval anastomosis, is performed after complete recipient right atrial cardiectomy, which thus preserves the entire right-sided geometry of the implanted heart. The resulting right atrial chamber is of normal size, and wall tension is normal as well. A more tedious variation on the bicaval technique involves separate left atrial cuff anastomoses. Claimed advantages of bicaval anastomotic technique include decreased diuretic requirements, lower incidences of atrial arrhythmias, less conduction disturbance, decreased A-V valve regurgitation, more efficient atrial transport, less right ventricular failure, and reduced length of stay. Long-term comparisons and randomized evaluations of the differences between standard and bicaval implantations are yet to come. Late tricuspid regurgitation is seen after both techniques, and it is most commonly caused by chordal and leaflet disruption from frequent right ventricular endomyocardial biopsies.

The CardioWest Total Artificial Heart (TAH) was approved as a bridge-to-transplantation device by the United States FDA in October, 2004. question_text: The AV node is most at risk for injury during repair of which of the following types of atrial level communication?
critique:
The conduction system of the heart may be at risk for injury during the repair of many intracardiac defects. The sinus node is located at the medial aspect of the superior vena cava-right atrium junction. Its blood supply usually originates as a proximal branch of the right coronary artery and may course around the vena cava to reach the sinus node or take a more direct course. The AV node lies in the triangle of Koch, bounded by the coronary sinus, the tricuspid valve annulus and the tendon of Todaro. The bundle of His originates from the AV node, traversing the atrioventricular junction to the left side of the ventricular septum where it divides into right and left bundle branches. Repair of atrial septal defects, while associated with a very low incidence of complications in most centers, may injure the conduction system or its blood supply and result in postoperative dysrhythmias.

Secundum atrial septal defect and patent foramen ovale, the most commonly seen atrial septal defects, are centrally located in the fossa ovalis of the atrial septum and distant from any of the major components of the conduction system. Ostium primum ASDs (also referred to as partial AV canal defects) are located in the inlet septum, which is in continuity with the atrioventricular junction. Patch repair of these defects may expose the AV node or His bundle to injury. Sinus venosus defects, most commonly located superiorly adjacent to the superior vena cava, and often associated with anomalous drainage of the right superior pulmonary veins, may be repaired by a number of patching techniques, virtually all of which involve suturing near the SA node or its blood supply.

Ostium primum atrial septal defect, a type of atrioventricular septal defect or AV canal defect, is also referred to as a partial AV canal. It is distinguished from complete and transitional AV canal defects by the lack of any ventricular level communication. Similar to other forms of AV canal defect, in a primum ASD the inlet portion of the ventricular septum is deficient, which leads to an elongated, "goose-neck" deformity of the LV outflow region. There are also typical abnormalities of the atrioventricular valves that may include a cleft anterior leaflet of the left AV valve, and regurgitation due to imprecise coaptation of this "zone of apposition" can result.

Suturing the patch inferiorly, in the vicinity of the coronary sinus, places the AV node and/or His bundle at risk of injury, though in modern series the risk of complete heart block requiring pacemaker placement is very low (about 1-2%). Residual atrial communications are rarely seen, but when present, they are typically due to patch dehiscence. Repair of ostium primum ASD typically involves patch closure of the defect and closure of any identified AV valve cleft (bileaflet repair) should be considered. Residual left-sided atrioventricular valve regurgitation is commonly seen, but cleft closure appears to lessen this problem. Its severity is best predicted by the degree of insufficiency both preoperatively and immediately postoperatively. In approximately 10% of cases reoperation is required to repair or replace the left AV valve. Although virtually all patients with partial AV canal defects have an elongated and somewhat narrow LV outflow tract, the incidence of late subaortic stenosis is only 3-7%.

question_text: The figure depicts a heart with a complete atrioventricular septal defect (complete AV canal). The view is taken from the cardiac apex, looking up at the common AV valve. The name of the structure marked with the "?" is the
critique:
Synonyms for atrioventricular canal defect include endocardial cushion defect and atrioventricular septal defect. Atrioventricular canal defects are characterized by the presence of a common atrioventricular junction. Atrioventricular canal defects are a spectrum of cardiac anomalies subdivided into partial, transitional, and complete forms. Complete atrioventricular canal has defects in both the atrial septum just above the atrioventricular valves (ostium primum atrial septal defect) and in the ventricular septum just below the atrioventricular valves. In complete atrioventricular canal there is a single common A-V valve that bridges both the right and left sides of the heart, creating superior (anterior) and inferior (posterior) bridging leaflets. The zone of apposition between the left superior leaflet and the left inferior leaflet represents what was previously termed the "cleft" of the left atrioventricular valve.

critique:
Pulmonary hypertensive crisis can be a life threatening postoperative complication, and is defined as "a serious syndrome characterized by an acute increase in pulmonary arterial pressure followed by a reduction in cardiac output and a decrease in oxygen saturation." This problem occurs most commonly in neonates and infants after repair of congenital cardiac malformations that are associated with large left-to-right shunts and elevated pulmonary artery pressures. Examples of such defects include atrioventricular septal defect (A-V canal defect) and truncus arteriosus. After surgical repair, patients may have essentially normal pulmonary arterial pressures until pulmonary hypertension occurs suddenly. This acute elevation in pulmonary arterial pressure is commonly preceded by a stimulus such as suctioning the endotracheal tube. Other potential etiologies of pulmonary hypertensive crisis include hypothermia, hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, and the use of alpha-adrenergic inotropic or vasopressor medications.

Pulmonary hypertensive crisis can progress to right ventricular dysfunction and low cardiac output. Therapy for pulmonary hypertensive crisis includes the following interventions: 1. hyperventilation with 100% oxygen 2. sedation with fentanyl or morphine 3. chemical paralysis with vecuronium or pancuronium 4. alkalinization (correction of acidosis) 5. initiation of inhaled nitric oxide The single most important intervention to treat and prevent pulmonary hypertensive crisis is inhaled nitric oxide. This selective pulmonary vasodilator has essentially no systemic effects. Standard dosing ranges from 5 parts per million to 20 parts per million, with a useful range of 1-40 ppm. Inhaled nitric oxide may decrease otherwise refractory pulmonary arterial hypertension. Epinephrine is an intravenous inotrope and vasopressor with both alpha and beta adrenergic actions. At doses higher than 0.2 Œºg/(kg*min) this drug has marked alpha adrenergic activity and can lead to decreased renal perfusion. Patients with fixed pulmonary arterial hypertension may undergo surgical palliation with a fenestrated VSD closure to prevent right ventricular failure. After surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot, many surgeons leave open a small patent foramen ovale to function as a "pop-off valve" in the setting of postoperative right ventricular dysfunction. This strategy does not apply to pulmonary hypertensive crisis, in which the problem lies within the pulmonary vascular bed.

title: CCTGA; initial treatment; PA banding
question_text: A 12-month-old girl presented with tachypnea and failure to thrive. A chest radiograph shows pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly, and an echocardiogram demonstrates atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. She has moderate-to-severe tricuspid valve regurgitation. Her systolic pulmonary artery pressures are half systemic. Her morphologic right ventricular function is moderately depressed. Which of the following is the best surgical option for this patient?
critique:
Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (CCTGA) is characterized by atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. In this condition, the morphologic right atrium receives the systemic venous return which then enters the morphologic (right-sided) left ventricle via the mitral valve. Similarly, the morphologic left atrium receives the pulmonary venous return which then enters the morphologic (left-sided) right ventricle via the tricuspid valve. The left ventricle is connected to the pulmonary artery and the right ventricle is connected to the aorta. A physiologically "normal" circulation results as deoxygenated systemic venous return enters the pulmonary circulation and oxygenated pulmonary venous return enters the systemic circulation.

Most patients present as a consequence of an associated condition. Those with significant left A-V valve (tricuspid) regurgitation or a large VSD with minimal left ventricular outflow tract obstruction develop congestive heart failure symptoms early in life. Tricuspid valve regurgitation is an important determinant of long-term outcome. Traditional approaches to repair underlying anomalies associated with CCTGA result in unsatisfactory long-term outcomes with high late mortality rates, progressive right ventricular dysfunction, and progressive tricuspid valve regurgitation. Tricuspid valve replacement with existing right ventricular dysfunction entails high operative risk and poor long-term survival.

In the 1990's the operative focus shifted toward anatomic repair that would allow the morphologic left ventricle to support the systemic circulation. Retraining the left ventricle to function at systemic pressure is necessary, and this can be achieved by pulmonary artery banding. It is essential to gradually increase LV pressure to avoid dysfunction. When initially placing the band, a reasonable goal is to achieve an LV pressure of 50% systemic, which is accompanied by a shift of the ventricular septum to the left. Tricuspid valve regurgitation often improves as the septum moves toward the morphologic RV. Typically, it is not possible to achieve adequate LV pressures at the initial band due to LV dysfunction, and repetitive banding procedures are required. Anatomic repair can be carried out when the LV/RV ratio is > 80% and LV function is normal. The left ventricle and mitral valve, better suited for long-term performance under high pressure, are placed in the systemic circulation. The Senning/arterial switch operation can be performed with acceptable morbidity and mortality.

critique:
Near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) monitoring measures cerebral cortical tissue oxygen saturation (regional SO2 or rSO2). Because the cerebral tissue bed sampled is predominantly venous, rSO2 has been shown to be positively correlated with mixed venous saturation. Thus, it represents a noninvasive method to monitor the balance between oxygen delivery and oxygen consumption.

In the described scenario, pre-bypass data reflect a stable patient with good oxygen delivery -- there is no significant metabolic acidosis and rSO2 is 70. After uneventful initiation of bypass, the rSO2 reading fell to 30, indicating either inadequate oxygen delivery or increased consumption. There would be no reason for consumption to have suddenly increased, though through cooling this could be decreased with a likely improvement in rSO2. Cerebral venous congestion may affect regional blood flow, and thus oxygen delivery. With single atrial venous cannulation this would be extremely unlikely, but it is observed more commonly with direct caval cannulation.

Blood gas management strategy may impact cerebral blood flow, though at normothermia both alpha stat and pH stat strategies are equivalent. Increasing pump flow will increase oxygen delivery and thus improve rSO2, although the initial pump flow of 2.5 L/(min*m2) should represent a sufficient cardiac output for support. With a baseline hematocrit of 31% and the use of an asanguinous prime, the patient's hematocrit on bypass would have fallen into the high teens. Given the modest blood loss associated with the mammary artery injury, it is likely the hematocrit would be in the mid teens, thus markedly decreasing oxygen carrying capacity. This is the most likely reason for the marked fall in rSO2. In most pediatric cardiopulmonary bypass cases, the target on-bypass hematocrit is 30%.

critique: Dislodgement of an aortic cannula during cardiopulmonary bypass is a rare event, but one that can be quite stressful. The safe time period to re-establish flow depends on the temperature of the patient at the time of the dislodgement. At normothermia, the probability of recovery from 2 minutes of circulatory arrest is almost 100%. However, after 10 minutes that probability is only 10%. At 28oC, the probability of safe circulatory arrest is almost 100% after 10 minutes, but the probability of full recovery is only 50% after 20 minutes. In the scenario described, the surgeon does not have to rush to reinsert the cannula, but action should be expeditious to re-establish flow within 10 minutes. It is more important to take appropriate time to adequately purge air from the cannula and aorta than to rush reconnection to bypass. Of course, cannula dislodgement at normothermia must be handled much more rapidly.

title: Ebstein's malformation; neonatal management

question_text: A full-term 3.1 kg girl developed increasing respiratory distress and profound cyanosis within 12 hours of delivery. Her chest radiograph is shown. She was intubated and started on prostaglandins. An echocardiogram showed no obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract. After two weeks, she cannot be weaned off of prostaglandins without profound cyanosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial surgical intervention?
critique:
Ebstein's malformation is a disease of development of the tricuspid valve and the entire right ventricle. It appears as a spectrum of anatomical abnormalities of variable severity, which include apical displacement of the septal and mural leaflets of the tricuspid valve, which have failed to delaminate from the underlying myocardium. There is also thinning or atrialization of the inlet component of the right ventricle with variable dilation, and malformation of the antero-superior leaflet with anomalous attachments, redundancy, and fenestrations. Patients who present in infancy have the poorest prognosis. There is a high rate of fetal death, hydrops, and pulmonary hypoplasia when the diagnosis is made during fetal life.

Cyanosis is the most common presentation of Ebstein's malformation in infancy. These patients have severe tricuspid regurgitation with a poorly functioning right ventricle in the face of elevated pulmonary arterial resistance. The result is a state of low cardiac output dependent upon right-to-left shunting across the fossa ovalis. The chest radiograph can vary from normal (patients with mild anatomic abnormalities), to the classic "wall-to-wall" heart, as seen in this infant's chest film. Neonates may require prostaglandins to maintain adequate flow of blood to the lungs soon after delivery when pulmonary resistance is high.

It is important to distinguish functional from anatomic pulmonary atresia. In infants with functional atresia, it may be possible to wean prostaglandins while maintaining adequate saturations off oxygen as pulmonary resistance falls. These patients can then be followed for development of further symptoms. In neonates who cannot be weaned from prostaglandins due to unacceptable levels of hypoxemia, or in those with anatomic pulmonary atresia, it is necessary to construct a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt to maintain adequate pulmonary blood flow.

For those neonates who also develop symptoms of congestive heart failure while on prostaglandins, it is necessary to address the underlying valvular pathology. The options include patch closure of the tricuspid valve, with or without fenestration (along with construction of a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt) or repair of the tricuspid valve in selected cases. Heart transplantation is rarely necessary, especially if LV function is good. The pulmonary vascular resistance in a neonate is too high for a successful cavopulmonary anastomosis.

Stasis, atrial thrombus, and limited forward cardiac output are often present. Conversion to an extracardiac Fontan may improve hemodynamics, but this does not eliminate the anatomic substrate for arrhythmia. Therefore, the presence of atrial tachycardia should be viewed as an electromechanical problem that will not be adequately addressed by either arrhythmia therapy or hemodynamic repair alone. Fontan conversion with a MAZE procedure can be performed with a mortality under one percent, including patients with complex functional single ventricle morphology. Late recurrence of arrhythmia is approximately 15%.

Heart transplantation is not indicated in this patient with good left ventricular function and a low trans-pulmonary gradient. Epicardial anti-tachycardia pacemaker placement, amiodarone therapy, or thoracoscopic MAZE procedure do not address the hemodynamic problems associated with a failing Fontan.

Potential benefits of the Sano shunt (RV-to-PA) over the modified Blalock-Taussig shunt (systemic-to-PA) include an easier postoperative course after the Norwood procedure because of a better balance of pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow. In addition, it is thought that there is better long-term myocardial preservation as a result of higher diastolic pressures and improved myocardial perfusion. Despite the early benefit, many centers have reported the need to perform the Stage 2 palliation (bidirectional Glenn or hemi-Fontan procedure) at an earlier age because of progressive cyanosis.

Numerous studies have demonstrated that coronary perfusion is greater in patients with RV-to-PA shunts. However, enhanced coronary perfusion does not necessarily translate into improved ventricular function. The negative effect of the ventriculotomy may have greater impact on long-term outcome than the higher coronary perfusion pressure. Coronary ¬ìsteal¬î has been postulated to be a critical factor in the demise of patients with Blalock-Taussig shunts, but this claim is difficult to substantiate. Nonetheless, it is believed that the benefits seen with the Sano shunt are related to higher diastolic blood pressure and enhanced coronary perfusion. question_text: A 6-month-old with hypoplastic left heart syndrome is in the ICU 8 hours after a bidirectional cavopulmonary anastomosis was done. The patient is mechanically ventilated, tachycardic, oliguric, and extremities are cool. The arterial blood pressure is 60/35 mmHg, the superior vena cava pressure is 26, and the common atrial pressure is 4. The arterial and superior vena caval oxygen saturations are 70% and 35% respectively, and hematocrit is 41%. Arterial blood gas values are: pH 7.38, pCO2 49, pO2 42. critique:
The patient scenario suggests inadequate systemic cardiac output and inadequate ventilation. One systematic approach to optimize oxygen delivery is to optimize each variable that affects oxygen delivery (DO2). DO2 = total arterial oxygen content x cardiac output. The factors that influence these two factors include hemoglobin, arterial saturation, heart rate, preload, afterload, and contractility.

The patient is already tachycardic. After confirming sinus rhythm, there is little to be gained by further increasing the heart rate. The target hematocrit for optimal oxygen carrying capacity after bidirectional Glenn is 45%. The level of 41% in this patient is not critically low. Myocardial contractility can be diminished in neonates and infants after cardiac surgery. In the described patient the low common atrial pressure suggests congestion is minimal and that contractility is adequate.

After cavopulmonary anastomosis, it is important to modify the ventilation parameters to maximize cerebral blood flow and to minimize pulmonary vascular resistance. Paradoxically, however, maneuvers that decrease pulmonary vascular resistance (including low pCO2) tend to diminish cerebral blood flow. The opposing effects of these maneuvers have been studied in post-cavopulmonary anastomosis patients and induction of a mild respiratory acidosis while mechanically ventilated optimizes distal oxygen delivery.

Preload must be optimized after cavopulmonary anastomosis, and this patient's CVP is quite high. The gradient between the SVC and common atrium is concerning for an anastomotic problem. A stenotic Glenn anastomosis restricts systemic return and therefore limits effective right heart output, which limits left heart preload. Accurate confirmation can be obtained from cardiac catheterization, as in this case. The problem may be treatable with balloon dilation, but reoperation and anastomosis revision is definitive care.

question_text: A 16-year-old boy with a history of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy underwent a septal myectomy five years ago. His father died suddenly at 49 years of age. critique:
Surgical myectomy is currently the treatment of choice for symptomatic patients with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM, HCM) who are unresponsive to medical therapy. A high resting gradient in the left ventricular outflow tract is also an indication for surgery. The typical approach is transaortic, and myomectomy results in relief of the outflow tract obstruction and resolution of symptoms in the majority of patients. In nearly all circumstances, mitral valve regurgitation due to systolic anterior motion will resolve without the need for mitral valve replacement. Operative mortality in experienced centers approaches 1%. Late survival may be improved when compared to HCM patients not receiving surgical myectomy.

A minority of patients will have recurrent left ventricular outflow tract obstruction after septal myomectomy, and reoperation should be considered. The most common mechanisms for obstruction are incomplete myomectomy at initial surgery or mid-ventricular obstruction. Children are more susceptible to initial operative failure secondary to difficult access through a small aortic valve. Redo septal myectomy is an effective treatment for recurrent left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in HCM.

Although surgical myomectomy may reduce the risk of sudden death, it does not eliminate it. ICD placement is recommended for high risk patients including those with non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, a family history of sudden death, massive septal hypertrophy (> 30 mm), or a history of syncope.

Decision-making in neonates with critical left ventricular outflow tract obstruction can be challenging, as a choice between pursuing a one- or two-ventricle repair strategy is frequently required. Considerable morbidity and mortality attends inappropriate pursuit of a two-ventricle repair in a subset of patients in which either strategy appears, at first glance, to be feasible.

In order to assist with decision-making, numerous investigators have developed scoring systems to integrate data from multiple aspects of the patient'¬ís physiologic and anatomic characteristics. In the most commonly cited scoring systems, the presence of severe endocardial fibroelastosis is an important predictor of unfavorable outcome with a two-ventricle repair strategy. Other commonly reported risk factors for poor results after two-ventricle repair include: a left ventricle which is non-apex forming, small left ventricular outflow tract dimensions at multiple levels, and poor left ventricular function. Small mitral annulus size and/or submitral obstruction (e.g., parachute mitral valve) also contribute to poor outcomes in patients undergoing two-ventricle repair.

Shunting across the atrial septum makes determination of the functional status of the mitral valve difficult in the described neonate. A gradient across the valve may not be present due to the combination of poor left ventricular filling and left-to-right shunting. If the atrial level shunt was eliminated, then left ventricular compliance could improve and a gradient across the valve could be revealed.

Neonatal Ross/Konno procedures can be performed in patients with complex left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. However, care must be taken to determine that the functional characteristics of the left ventricle and mitral valve will be satisfactory after removal of the outflow tract obstruction. The presence of a small left ventricle, endocardial fibroelastosis, and a questionable mitral valve add significant risk to this approach. Improved left ventricular compliance following resection of endocardial fibroelastosis has been rarely reported and may offer promise in the future. This approach does not, however, alter the left ventricular size and mitral valve limitations of patients with multi-level hypoplasia of the left ventricle.

This is then further enlarged and closed with a patch. Using these landmarks, the incidence of postoperative conduction block is very low.

Initial inspection of the subaortic region and placement of the ventricular septal incision is facilitated through open aortotomy. Thereafter, the extension of the ventricular septal incision, additional resection, and subsequent patching of the VSD is performed through a right ventricular infundibular incision. Approximately half of these children will need a single ventricle management strategy while the others will achieve a two-ventricle cardiac reconstruction.

With mild-to-moderate degrees of RV and tricuspid valve hypoplasia, early RV decompression by opening the RV-to-PA connection may result in satisfactory RV growth to allow an ultimate two-ventricle circulation. When right ventricle-dependent coronary blood flow is confirmed by prominent right ventricular-to-coronary artery fistulae and when there is associated stenosis of proximal native coronary arteries, then RV decompression must not be done. Either severe right-sided hypoplasia or right ventricle-dependent coronary circulation may indicate that an Infant with PA/IVS is best managed with a single ventricle reconstruction strategy. In these patients first-stage palliation utilizing a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt is necessary to create a source of pulmonary blood flow which has been denied by the pulmonary atresia.

The right ventricular outflow tract in PA/IVS is completely occluded, so virtually all right atrial return must shunt right-to-left through the (typically) large atrial septal defect. While ASD closure may ultimately be a late component of a two-ventricle repair in suitable hearts, the presence of the ASD in infancy is essential for survival in this anomaly. Transplantation has been advocated by some centers for selected patients with this anomaly, especially in the presence of severe coronary anomalies such as aortocoronary atresia.

question_text: A patient with total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage underwent repair as a neonate. At one year of age, the baby is asymptomatic but a chest radiograph demonstrates diffuse congestion of the left lung field. An MRI demonstrates tight localized stenoses of the left pulmonary veins at the junction with the left atrium. Which of the following statements is correct?
critique:
After repair of total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, approximately 10% of patients develop post-repair pulmonary vein stenosis. The onset of this complication can be insidious, but pulmonary vascular congestion is evident on chest films. Any or all of the pulmonary veins may be affected and three categories of involvement are recognized. A stenosis can be limited to the site of anastomosis, which likely represents a technical failure at the site of surgical repair. More severe cases involve fibrosis of the pulmonary venous confluence and the origin of the pulmonary veins. The most severe cases involve diffuse retrograde progression of a fibrotic process deep into the pulmonary parenchyma. The pathology can be asymmetric with progression in some veins to complete occlusion while other pulmonary veins are spared. Despite freedom from apparent pulmonary vein stenosis on one side, unilateral stenosis frequently results in pulmonary hypertension.

Because post-repair pulmonary vein stenosis can progress in an insidious fashion, postoperative surveillance is required after repair of total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage. Echocardiography is the exam of choice, as this allows anatomic visualization of the pulmonary veins and the flow patterns of the pulmonary venous effluent. Venous obstruction is typically associated with turbulence, which is easily detected. In addition, progressive stenosis is associated with a transition from a normal phasic flow pattern to an abnormal continuous flow pattern.

Repair of post-repair pulmonary vein stenosis involves anastomotic revision. Conventional techniques involve patch augmentation, typically with autologous pericardium. A more recent ¬ësutureless¬í technique involves incision into the stenotic pulmonary veins extending into the 1st or 2nd order bifurcation within the lung parenchyma. However, in some cases, resection of the stenotic areas (rather than incision) must be done to remove all obstruction. Hemostasis is then obtained by anastomosis of the left atrium to the posterior pericardium along a line remote from the divided pulmonary veins, thus creating a "controlled bleed" into the left atrium. Sutureless repairs are associated with superior freedom from reoperation in patients with post-repair pulmonary vein stenosis. In contrast to stenosis at many other anatomic sites, catheter-based balloon dilatation and/or stenting for post-repair pulmonary vein stenosis has poor outcomes.

critique:
This neonate was cyanotic in the first hours of life, and the hyperoxia challenge helped to focus the diagnosis on cardiac lesions rather than pulmonary issues. The chest film shows clear lung fields, further supporting the suspicion that there is no significant pulmonary pathology. The cardiac silhouette has a narrow base (so-called "egg on a string") that is characteristic of transposition of the great arteries (TGA).

In TGA the systemic and pulmonary circulations are in parallel rather than in series, and survival depends on communications between these two systems. The fully saturated blood in the left ventricle-driven pulmonary circuit must mix with blood in the right ventricle-driven systemic circuit. Approximately 25% of infants with TGA will have a ventricular septal defect, which will allow for sufficient bidirectional mixing to maintain systemic oxygen saturations in a low, but satisfactory, range. Maintenance of ductal patency with prostaglandin E2 infusion is often the first measure initiated in this and other cyanotic heart lesions, sometimes even before a definitive diagnosis has been made. In the newborn, maintenance of ductal patency is predictably established with a low-dose PGE2 infusion. Higher doses may be considered if the ductus has closed, but this is an unlikely situation in the first hours of life. Even in the face of cyanosis, TGA is typically associated with normal or increased pulmonary blood flow, so pulmonary vasodilation with inhaled nitric oxide would not be expected to help. The low saturations are a consequence of inadequate intracardiac shunting/mixing that is characteristic of this lesion. 

However, because pulmonary vascular resistance is lower than systemic, ductal shunting will be predominantly from the aorta into the pulmonary artery. This increased pulmonary blood flow does not necessarily improve systemic oxygen saturation by itself. Left atrial return is increased and drives more oxygenated blood flow left-to-right (and ultimately out to the aorta) through an atrial communication, even one that is relatively small. When the atrial communication is very restrictive or absent, an atrial septostomy can quickly improve shunting and, thus, systemic oxygen saturation. This is a catheter-based procedure that is often performed at the bedside with echocardiographic guidance.

ECMO provides complete cardiopulmonary bypass support, which would stabilize the described situation, but it is complex and risks significant morbidity. An emergency arterial switch operation would also effectively stabilize this child through the initiation of cardiopulmonary bypass, and the underlying anatomic defect would be corrected, but the time needed to mobilize a team to perform such a procedure would dangerously prolong the period of marginal oxygen delivery in this baby.

These native shunting sites are generally not sufficient to provide oxygen to the desaturated blood in the arterial system, and cyanosis is refractory to supplemental oxygen and general supportive care. Ductal flow should be maintained with PGE and early atrial balloon septostomy is indicated to enhance mixing. The latter can be performed at the bedside under echocardiography control or in the cath lab. d-Transposition alone has little net shunt, so pulmonary hypertension is a relatively small risk. Associated anomalies of the pulmonary arteries and unbalanced shunting, however, can be responsible for pulmonary vascular disease.

The history of operative care for transposition is rich. Mustard and Senning atrial switch repairs have been retired in favor of variations of arterial switch operations, which have proven to be superior repairs. Ventricular septal defect is the most common associated defect (up to 80% of patients) and is most often in the subpulmonary position. Other associated defects include pulmonary outflow obstruction and atrial septal defects.

This has led some surgeons to advocate the double switch operation in which the morphological left ventricle is utilized as the systemic ventricle. This operation, typically performed in pediatric patients, consists of an atrial switch, arterial switch, and VSD closure (if present). If pulmonary stenosis is present then an atrial switch, right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery conduit, and VSD closure are performed.

critique:
The early surgical treatment of transposition of the great arteries (TGA) consisted of either a Senning or Mustard atrial switch procedure. The basic principle of these operations is to create a baffle within the atria to direct the systemic venous return into the left ventricle and to redirect the pulmonary venous return into the right ventricle. In the Senning operation native atrial tissue is utilized to create the baffle, but in the Mustard operation pericardial or synthetic material is used. If the LV achieves normal mass, then an arterial switch operation can be done to re-establish the LV as the systemic ventricle. LV retraining has been used successfully in young patients, but results in adults have not been as encouraging.

There is typically a proximal high-pressure chamber and a low-pressure distal chamber divided by the obstructing muscle bundles. There is often an associated ventricular septal defect. The VSD location is variable, but most are proximal to the obstruction. The intra-ventricular gradient may progress if left untreated.

The preferred approach is transatrial through the tricuspid valve. Surgical mortality is low and long-term prognosis is excellent.

question_text: A 12-year-old boy with known bicuspid aortic valve regurgitation underwent a pulmonary autograft (Ross procedure). He had an excellent initial surgical result with trivial autograft valve insufficiency and no stenosis. He was lost to follow-up until a murmur was discovered at a varsity football screening physical five years later. He returned to his cardiologist, to whom he reported no symptoms. He has been engaged in aggressive weight training in preparation for the upcoming football season. MRI images are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan of therapy for him?
critique:
Donald L Ross first described the Ross procedure in 1967. It was then, and continues to be, an attractive option for aortic valve replacement in children and young adults because of the lack of need for anticoagulation and the ability of the autograft to grow with the child. It also has normal hemodynamics, in contrast to every prosthetic option. The early mortality rate is reported to be less than 3% in uncomplicated cases, even in small children. However, significant autograft dilation and/or valvular regurgitation develop in 10-40% at 10 years. The rate of required reintervention is around 80% at 10 years when both autograft and homograft are considered jointly. More optimistic statistics emerge from the most recent analysis of data from the Ross registry, with rates of freedom from explantation of failing autografts of 89% and 82% at 10 and 25 years, respectively.

Despite excellent early- and mid-term results, long-term outcomes are uncertain. This is related to the performance of the autograft valve as well as the pulmonary valve replacement prosthesis. In some patients, the autograft may dilate excessively and produce valvular regurgitation. Pre-Ross aortic valve regurgitation or aneurysm may be predisposing factors. Other risk factors for autograft failure include an abnormality of the native pulmonary valve, root enlarging procedures, and associated VSD repair. The problem of autograft root dilation has prompted some surgeons to use a prosthetic graft for either external reinforcement or to replace the ascending aorta above a minimized autograft root. Each of these options, however, prevents growth. The pulmonary root replacement is less problematic, and the reported incidence of homograft dysfunction is 6-20% at 10 years. In the Ross registry, rates of freedom from pulmonary homograft replacement were 91% and 84% at 10 and 25 years, respectively. 

This patient's images reveal a dilated aortic root (5.5 cm at level of sinuses), moderate-to-severe eccentric aortic regurgitation between right and non-coronary leaflets, probable fenestrations, eccentric dilation of the non-coronary sinus, and moderate pulmonary valve regurgitation. The distal ascending aorta and aortic arch are normal. Heavy isometric exercise is a concern regarding this pathologic dilation, and limited heavy physical activity, especially weight lifting and football, should be recommended. There may be similarity of autograft dilation to the aortic dilation seen in connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome. The efficacy of beta blockers to reduce pressure and dP/dT is unproven, particularly in children, but pulse and blood pressure control seem appropriate goals for this child. Autograft dilation with preserved autograft valve function may be managed by valve-sparing aortic root replacement, but the valve must be free from fenestrations or leaflet prolapse. In the described case the eccentric autograft valve regurgitation makes reconstruction with a prosthetic valve conduit (Bentall) a prudent plan. The regurgitant pulmonary valve also requires replacement.
