question_text: A 14-month-old boy was noted on routine exam to have diminished femoral pulses. Blood pressure was 120/70 in his right arm and 80/40 in his right leg. Echocardiogram demonstrated a discrete coarctation one cm distal to the left subclavian artery with a hypoplastic isthmus and a mildly hypoplastic transverse arch. Intracardiac anatomy is normal. The peak gradient across the coarctation is 50 mmHg. Which of the following is the best management strategy for this patient?
critique:
Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing of the proximal descending thoracic aorta adjacent to the insertion of the ductus arteriosus (ligamentum arteriosum). Coarctation represents 5-8% of all cases of congenital heart disease. A classic presentation of coarctation is hypertension in an infant with diminished femoral pulses. A coarctation with a gradient greater than 20 mmHg should be considered for repair. Median sternotomy is preferred if there are associated intracardiac anomalies that require repair and/or if there is significant hypoplasia of the transverse aortic arch. The coarctation can be repaired by either an extended end-to-end repair or patch aortoplasty using homograft tissue. Isolated coarctation is usually approached via left thoracotomy.

Clarence Crafoord performed the first coarctation repair in October 1944, resecting the narrow aortic segment and performing an end-to-end repair. This has proven to be highly successful when the coarctation segment is short with aorta of normal caliber proximal and distal to the resection. With modern suture and microvascular techniques, an end-to-end repair has a relatively low recoarctation rate when all juxtaductal tissue is excised and when the transverse aortic arch is not hypoplastic. A variation of this is coarctation resection with an extended end-to-end anastomosis. This involves extensive mobilization of the transverse arch and distal aorta with ligation and division of collaterals as necessary. The undersurface of the transverse arch and the lateral aspect of the descending aorta are spatulated, which allows for a wider anastomosis and augmentation of accessible transverse arch hypoplasia. This is particularly useful in neonates and infants.

Prosthetic patch aortoplasty may be required to augment a hypoplastic transverse aortic arch. Such patients need to be followed for possible aneurysm formation and recurrent coarctation. The subclavian artery can be sacrificed and used as an onlay patch over the area of coarctation in lieu of a prosthetic patch. Subclavian flap angioplasty is well tolerated in infants, but it is not done commonly because of concerns about left arm growth and a higher than originally suspected incidence of late recoarctation. Prosthetic interposition grafts allow an excellent repair with a low recoarctation rate in young adults that have reached their growth potential. However, this technique is not appropriate for infants and small children.

critique:
Several potential postoperative complications are associated with repair of coarctation of the aorta. "Paradoxical" hypertension and paraplegia are early problems of great concern. Paradoxical hypertension is thought to result from release of the stretch on carotid artery baroreceptors, with secondary influences by angiotensin and elevated plasma catecholamines. This is usually self-limited and can be managed with beta-blockers. The tendency for hypertension to persist after coarctation repair is proportional to patient age at the time of repair. Approximately one-third of patients greater than 1 year of age at the time of repair will have persistent hypertension. The incidence of paraplegia after repair is approximately 0.5%. Limiting cross-clamp time (preferably less than 30 minutes), ensuring a distal perfusion pressure > 45 mmHg and mild systemic hypothermia (35.5oC) are measures that greatly decrease this risk.

Aneurysm formation, both true and false, can develop if repair is not done. This can also be a late complication after patch aortoplasty, where compliance mismatch between graft and native, abnormal aorta is the likely cause. Pseudoaneurysm and/or aortic dissection occur more commonly following balloon angioplasty than surgical repair.

Residual or recurrent coarctation (> 20 mmHg gradient) has been reported following every type of operative repair and endovascular intervention. Risk factors include operation on infants less than 3 months of age or less than 5 kg, use of silk suture material, residual abnormal juxtaductal tissue, and morphology of the coarctation (e.g., narrow isthmus, long segment). In longitudinal studies of patients after coarctation repair, reduced exercise tolerance and premature atherosclerosis are reported, and these findings are not confined to patients with residual gradients.

critique:
This patient has multiple pathologic features consistent with Marfan syndrome, an inherited connective tissue disorder transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait. Mutations in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) locus on chromosome 15 are responsible for the syndrome. Cardinal features include tall stature, ectopia lentis, pectus excavatum, mitral valve prolapse, aortic root dilatation, and aortic dissection. About three-quarters of Marfan patients have an affected parent, and new mutations account for the remainder. Diagnosis is usually established using the Ghent criteria, which use major and minor characteristics based on clinical observations of organ system involvement and family history.

This child meets the criteria for Marfan syndrome diagnosis based on her positive family history and major cardiac involvement including mitral valve prolapse and aortic root dilation. Musculoskeletal abnormalities including pectus excavatum may be either major or minor criteria depending on severity. Patients with Marfan syndrome typically die from cardiovascular complications. The prevalence of aortic root dilation in Marfan syndrome is as high as 70-80%. While an aortic root diameter of 3.5 cm is not particularly concerning, in a small 11-year-old the z-score of this aorta is > 3 and the rate of growth indicates rapid expansion and a risk for aortic dissection. While medical therapy alone is recommended for most patients with mitral regurgitation, this young patient'¬ís decreased left ventricular function and 3+ mitral regurgitation are strong arguments for mitral repair. Her rapidly enlarging aorta is an independent indication for prompt operation.

If aortic regurgitation or structural valve disease was documented, then this option would be discouraged in favor of a Bentall reconstruction. There is no indication for arch replacement in this young patient.

The patient has aortic atresia, the ascending aorta is 2 mm in diameter, the atrial septal defect is mildly restrictive and there is mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation. critique:
There are three basic therapeutic strategies for palliation of hypoplastic left heart syndrome. Norwood operations (utilizing either aortopulmonary or RV-PA shunts) are designed to palliate the infant in preparation for a Fontan procedure. In contrast, transplantation relies on survival through a variable waiting period with a new heart as destination therapy. The hybrid strategy, utilizing bilateral pulmonary artery banding and ductal stenting, can be considered a palliative procedure in the neonatal period that is a "Norwood alternative" with a Fontan destination or as a temporizing procedure to control pulmonary blood flow and eliminate the need for prostaglandins and thereby minimize attrition during the waiting period prior to transplantation.

Benefits of hybrid palliation prior to transplantation are that transfusions can commonly be avoided and the aortic arch is not reconstructed with homograft. Both of these points are important because limiting donor exposures may improve the likelihood and success of subsequent transplantation. In contrast, Norwood palliation for pre-transplant palliation is associated with relatively high perioperative risk and greater potential for pre-sensitization of the recipient. The hybrid stage I procedure and the Norwood procedure each achieve four critical objectives for neonatal palliation: 

1. Each procedure results in unobstructed systemic cardiac output. In Norwood patients this is achieved through reconstruction of the aortic arch and amalgamation of the proximal aorta and main pulmonary artery into a common ventricular outlet. In the hybrid strategy, unobstructed systemic cardiac output is achieved by stenting the ductus arteriosus. This results in prograde systemic cardiac output to the descending aorta and retrograde flow across the aortic isthmus that reaches the proximal ascending aorta. After the hybrid procedure, care must be taken to closely monitor the patient for evidence of ductal constriction proximal or distal to the ductal stent. Proximal obstruction in patients with aortic atresia (and no prograde aortic flow) can result in critical limitation of all systemic cardiac output. Distal obstruction may result in obstruction to all cardiac output. Depending on the location of the ductal tissue, less severe obstruction results in differential perfusion of the upper and lower extremities.

2. Hybrid and Norwood strategies result in controlled sources of pulmonary blood flow. The hybrid strategy accomplishes this with bilateral pulmonary artery bands whereas the Norwood procedure utilizes aortopulmonary or RV-to-PA shunts. Both strategies lead to a bidirectional cavopulmonary shunt as the second stage procedure. At the second stage, previous shunts are removed, or in the case of hybrid patients, the pulmonary artery bands are removed. Commonly, removal of the bands and dilation of the site of banding is sufficient to provide adequate pulmonary arteries.

3. Both strategies require a reliable source of coronary blood flow. In Norwood patients this is commonly accomplished by side-to-side amalgamation of the proximal main pulmonary artery and the ascending aorta. This creates a short flow path between the systemic cardiac output and the coronary artery ostia. In contrast, the hybrid first-stage procedure in patients with aortic atresia requires a flow path that traverses the aortic isthmus in a retrograde direction and passes through the entire aortic arch and ascending aorta prior to reaching the coronary ostia. A "reverse BT shunt" has been described which can provide a secondary source of blood flow to the aortic arch in patients felt to be at risk for obstruction to retrograde flow across the aortic isthmus.

4. Both strategies require decompression of the left atrium. During the Norwood procedure, an essential task is to resect the atrial septum through the right atrium. In contrast, the hybrid strategy does not always mandate intervention on the atrial septum at initial stage. Many groups perform a balloon atrial septostomy prior to discharge during the initial hospital admission. Careful follow-up is required and repeat septostomy or stenting of the atrial septum is commonly required.

In this patient the most likely cause of inadequate pulmonary blood flow is low systemic blood pressure. Patients with obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection have an exceedingly high rate of postoperative pulmonary hypertension. Acute management of pulmonary hypertension in the pediatric cardiac intensive care unit includes 100% inhaled oxygen, paralysis, hyperventilation, and inhaled nitric oxide. Oxygen and relative respiratory alkalosis promote pulmonary vasodilation. Paralysis helps to minimize vasoreactivity, especially to noxious stimuli such as respiratory suctioning.

Most pediatric cardiac surgery patients have self-limited pulmonary hypertension, but some require longer term medical management. Historically, calcium channel blockers were the mainstay of therapy for pulmonary hypertension, but results were variable. Several new agents, including prostacyclins and sildenafil, have superior efficacy and have supplanted the use of calcium channel blockers. Prostacyclins are administered either intravenous or oral routes. They are potent vasodilators that can also produce profound systemic hypotension and inhibit platelet aggregation. As a result, these agents are often not the first line of therapy in postoperative patients.

Sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, is a potent pulmonary vasodilator and smooth muscle relaxant that is administered orally. Rebound pulmonary hypertension can be a significant issue for patients being withdrawn from nitric oxide. Sildenafil restores cyclic GMP availability and has been shown to be an effective drug to facilitate weaning nitric oxide.

His chest radiograph was unremarkable and a 12-lead ECG revealed left ventricular hypertrophy with a strain pattern. Aortogram and echo frames are shown. A mean gradient of 40 mmHg was measured. critique:
Supravalvar aortic stenosis is a rare form of congenital left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The etiology of this is most often sporadic, but it can be associated with Williams syndrome. Williams syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by a hemizygous deletion or mutation of the elastin gene at chromosome band 7q11. Children with Williams syndrome have supravalvar aortic stenosis, pulmonary artery and peripheral artery stenoses, characteristic facies, hypercalcemia and intellectual and developmental delays.

Supravalvar aortic stenosis is usually characterized by an hour-glass deformity of the sinuses and a luminal narrowing of the aorta just distal to the origins of the coronary arteries. This type is the most common, occurring in 50-75% of patients. Other patients have a fibrous diaphragm just distal to the coronary ostia. Finally, some patients may have diffuse narrowing of the aortic root and ascending aorta complex. The common pathophysiology is proximal aortic hypertension with subsequent left ventricular hypertrophy. Because the coronary arteries are proximal to the stenosis, they may become dilated and tortuous. Diastolic flow in aortic root and the coronary arteries is frequently diminished; this is compounded if coronaries are involved in the fibrous narrowing of the aorta and develop ostial stenosis.

Indications for surgery include symptoms of diminished exercise tolerance, syncope, or angina. Other indications include a systolic ascending aorta gradient greater than 50 mmHg, aortic valve regurgitation, or evidence of compromised coronary artery perfusion. Early operation is usually recommended because of the added risks of coronary malperfusion. Because of the rubbery consistency of the aortic wall, percutaneous angioplasty techniques are rarely effective or durable. The use of stents and stent-grafts in the proximal aorta is not advised.

Surgical repair may be accomplished by one of four methods (see second figure). The first is a single patch technique, described by McGoon in 1961. In this technique an incision and patch of only the non-coronary sinus is carried out. The next is the inverted "Y" patch, reported by John Doty in 1977, in which two sinuses (right and non-coronary) are enlarged with an inverted Y-shaped patch. In 1988, Brom reported the use of a three-patch technique in which all three sinuses are enlarged using prosthetic material. Finally, a three-sinus enlargement technique was described in 1993 by Myers. This technique utilizes counterincisions in the distal ascending aorta in order to avoid prosthetic material. There is no clear advantage of any one technique regarding freedom from re-intervention or survival, but the three-sinus intervention may result in more durable gradient relief.

The ¬ìtetrad¬î of abnormalities includes right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, a malalignment outlet ventricular septal defect, aortic override, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Surgical correction involves VSD closure, relief of the right ventricular outflow tract obstruction by division of muscle bundles, and relief of valvar stenosis if necessary.

In the current era, the preferred approach is to preserve the pulmonary valve if at all possible and to use a transatrial approach for VSD closure. The primary predictor of successful pulmonary valve preservation is a Z-score of -3 or greater. The Z-score is a normalized measure of annulus size based on body surface area. In statistical terminology, a Z-score is a measure of the distance, in standard deviations, of a sample from the mean. A Z-score of 0 (zero) is normal. Positive scores (+1, +2, etc.) reflect an enlarged annulus. Negative Z-scores (-1, -2, etc.) reflect annular stenosis. A recent review of over 100 patients with tetralogy of Fallot demonstrated that pulmonary valve preservation was possible in 80% of patients if the Z-score was > -3.

Many of these patients, however, eventually develop right ventricular dilatation and dysfunction, and pulmonary valve insertion is required later. The modified Blalock-Taussig shunt is typically used in neonates and small infants who have significant hypoplasia of the RV outflow tract or an anomalous coronary artery that precludes a transannular patch. Home oxygen is not indicated because it will not prevent tetralogy spells.

critique:
Blood types (groups) are classified on the basis of the presence or absence of inherited red blood cell surface antigens. These cell surface antigens may be proteins, carbohydrates, glycoproteins, or glycolipids. Some of these antigens are also present on the surface of other types of cells in the body, including the heart. The four blood types are determined by glycoprotein antigens A, B, both A and B or neither A nor B.

Humans naturally have antibodies to the glycoproteins not present on their own cells. For example, potential recipients with type A cells have antibodies to type B glycoproteins. Therefore, a donor with type B blood is not compatible with a type A recipient. Type AB cells lack antibodies to either glycoprotein and are therefore compatible with all donors. Potential recipients with type O have antibodies against both type A and type B cells and therefore require type O donors. Details of this compatibility for each blood type are displayed in the table. Thus, the person with blood type AB is a universal recipient and the person with blood type O is a universal donor.

Traditionally, transplantation of hearts from ABO-incompatible donors has been contraindicated because of the risk of hyperacute rejection. This catastrophe is mediated by preformed antibodies in the recipient against blood-group antigens of a donor. However, ABO-incompatible heart transplantation can be performed safely during infancy before the onset of isohemagglutinin production. This option to expand the use of all donor hearts can markedly reduce mortality among infants on the waiting list.

Echocardiography defines blood flow patterns through the Glenn anastomosis and confirms bilateral pulmonary venous return. Increased central venous pressure suggests resistance to pulmonary blood flow, either from a restrictive Glenn anastomosis or increased pulmonary vascular resistance. Measurement of systemic venous saturation provides useful information about adequacy of cardiac output and systemic oxygen delivery.

Hypoventilation (pCO2 > 45) has been shown to improve oxygenation following bidirectional superior cavopulmonary anastomosis. Improved oxygenation appears to be mediated by hypercarbia-related reduction in cerebral vascular resistance, which increases cerebral, superior vena cava, and pulmonary blood flow. critique:
The Norwood procedure was initially described as therapy for hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). The four anatomic varieties of hypoplastic left heart syndrome are: aortic atresia/mitral atresia, aortic atresia/mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis/mitral atresia, and aortic stenosis/mitral stenosis. Ventricular septation is not possible in the overwhelming majority of these patients because of the mitral valve atresia/stenosis and resultant diminutive left ventricle. Since the left ventricle is not adequate for a two-ventricle repair patients are treated by staged surgical palliation that leads to an eventual Fontan procedure or, less frequently, to cardiac transplantation.

The first stage of the Norwood procedure consists of: (1) atrial septectomy to ensure unobstructed flow from the pulmonary veins across an atrial septal defect to the right ventricle; (2) amalgamation of the ascending aorta and pulmonary valve with arch reconstruction to make the pulmonary valve the systemic semilunar valve (this amalgamation also corrects the arch hypoplasia and coarctation that are features of HLHS); (3) a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt or an RV-to-PA shunt (Sano modification) to provide adequate, but not excessive, pulmonary blood flow as the pulmonary artery is now disconnected from the cardiac structures; and (4) neo-aortic arch reconstruction that ensures unimpeded coronary blood flow.

After the Norwood 1 procedure, the patient will have a functional univentricular heart. The plan will be to perform a bidirectional superior cavopulmonary anastomosis (bidirectional Glenn) at 4-6 months of age and an eventual Fontan procedure between 2-4 years of age.

Bypass was started, but distention of the heart prompted turning on the left ventricular vent during cooling. It was suddenly noted that the vent line, which was previously full of blood, was full of air. The vent was disconnected, but the TEE showed air in the aortic arch. Inspection revealed that the vent was hooked up backwards at the bypass machine. Antegrade perfusion was stopped and retrograde cerebral perfusion was given for one minute via the superior vena cava. The operation was then completed. Postoperatively, the patient awakened and moved all extremities to command, although lethargy was obvious. He then had a seizure and became unresponsive. critique:
Fortunately, massive air embolism during cardiac surgery is a rare event. Measures to prevent this complication include testing vents prior to use, using one-way valves to prevent air from going retrograde, and protocols to ensure proper setup of the vent. Despite such precautions, the complication is well described. Standard reactive recommendations include immediate discontinuation of bypass, Trendelenberg positioning, aortic root aspiration and immediately starting retrograde cerebral perfusion with cold blood and continuous aortic venting. The classic article by Mills and Ochsner on this complication is mandatory reading for all cardiac surgeons. Postoperative symptoms and signs of cerebral embolus include: motor deficits, seizure, air emboli seen in the retina, headache, confusion, disorientation, pupil asymmetry, coma or impairment of respiratory and circulatory centers.

The mechanism of injury from air embolism if believed to be due to direct obstruction from air bubbles 30-60 microns in size along with a secondary inflammatory response. Data on the treatment of such complications are anecdotal due to the limited number of such cases. The mechanism behind hyperbaric oxygen benefit is the reduction in the volume of the individual emboli present in the brain by over 50% at over 2 atmospheres of pressure. Also, at high pressure with 100% oxygen, a large gradient favors absorption of nitrogen from the emboli and replacement with oxygen, which diffuses quicker. There are numerous reports of successful treatment of massive air embolism with hyperbaric oxygen, but the best outcomes are associated with therapy delays of four hours or less from the end of the operation. Obviously, patient safety concerns and availability of a hyperbaric oxygen chamber (see photo) must be considered in this unusual situation, but if patient stability and equipment permit, the use of this treatment should be strongly considered.

Barbiturate therapy has a theoretical advantage of reducing cerebral oxygen demand, but these drugs have not been proven to be helpful for air embolism. Seizures after air embolism are common, but they may not respond to benzodiazepine treatment. Other treatment options that may be helpful include: supine positioning, intravascular volume expansion, and lidocaine. Steroid administration is controversial and not routinely recommended. Intracranial pressure monitoring is appropriate only if signs of increased ICP are evident clinically.

question_text: A patient's symptomatic 3-vessel coronary disease prompted urgent CABG. The preoperative platelet count was 300,000, but three days after surgery it was 120,000. Because of dyspnea and an increased A-a gradient on arterial blood gas a CT angiogram was done. An embolus in a tertiary branch of the left pulmonary artery was identified. The patient is now hemodynamically stable, and the ECG does not suggest right heart strain. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response?
critique:
Heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) results from a complex immune mediated reaction after heparin exposure. Platelet factor 4 (PF-4) binds to the surface of the platelet following activation. Heparin/PF-4 complexes then form. IgG binds to the PF-4/heparin complex. The Fc portion of the antibody then leads to further platelet activation and the generation and release of procoagulant-rich microparticles that result in thrombotic complications (arterial and/or venous).

The diagnosis of HIT requires a high index of clinical suspicion in the cardiac surgical population. Typically HIT occurs within 5-14 days after heparin exposure, but it may occur within hours to days if patient has had a prior exposure to heparin within 3 months ("rapid onset HIT," caused by preformed circulating antibodies). HIT may also occur 9-30 days after exposure and is then called "delayed onset HIT." Any type of heparin exposure may lead to HIT, including LMWH, coated lines, subcutaneous or intravenous administration. Enoxaparin (Lovenox) appears to result in a lower incidence of HIT, but it does not eliminate the risk. Bovine heparin carries a higher risk of HIT than porcine heparin. 

This patient's platelet count drop is significant and an abnormal thrombotic event has been documented. Searching for an embolic source is appropriate, but the immediate response should be to terminate the prothrombotic state. HIT is a clinical diagnosis that requires identified heparin exposure and subsequent thrombocytopenia. Confirmation of the diagnosis by lab testing should be sought in cardiac surgical patients who have a drop in platelet count greater than 50% from baseline or an absolute drop to < 150,000, or thrombotic events. Exclusion criteria for HIT include recovery of platelet counts during continued heparin therapy, obvious other causes of thrombocytopenia, and early thrombocytopenia in a patient without prior heparin exposure.

Laboratory tests for HIT include:
SRA (serotonin release assay) - sensitivity >85%, low predictive value, technically demanding
HIPA (heparin induced platelet activation) - rapid, commonly available, variable sensitivity (30-80%) and is technique dependent.
ELISA (enzyme linked immune specific assay) - high sensitivity, but low specificity with 10% false negative tests, also costly.

Treatment of HIT entails immediate cessation of all heparin exposure (including coated lines and microflushes) and if clinically feasible reduction of thrombin generation by using a direct thrombin inhibitor followed by warfarin. Lone warfarin use after stopping heparin should be avoided. Warfarin-induced skin necrosis is one manifestation of an induced initial drop in levels of Factor VII and protein C with initial warfarin dosing. Cessation of heparin alone without the use of a direct thrombin inhibitor has been shown to result in thrombotic complications in ~ 50% of patients. Despite thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusions in HIT patients should be avoided except in instances of major hemorrhage. Platelet counts should be followed until they recover (typically in ~ 4 days), and monitoring for thrombosis is prudent.

Direct thrombin inhibitors include argatroban (a synthetic direct thrombin inhibitor), lepirudin (a hirudin analog), and bivalirudin (a hirudin analog). Use of direct thrombin inhibitors following diagnosed HIT has resulted in fewer thrombotic complications, but this must be weighed against the risk of hemorrhage in a postoperative surgical patient. These agents bind irreversibly to thrombin, and there are no known agents to reverse their effect. In the United States argatroban is used most often because of FDA approval and its clinical profile of fewer bleeding events.

Heparin antibodies generally disappear within 100 days of the last exposure, and re-use of heparin can be considered after this time if antibodies are absent and if platelet counts are monitored carefully. Thrombolysis is contraindicated in this patient in the early postoperative period.

All pumps have alarms for gas (helium) leakage, but this complication is usually sudden and is most often heralded by the appearance of blood within the catheter. Treatment of balloon rupture is immediate clamping or disconnection of the gas line to avoid a helium embolus. The balloon should be manually deflated and removed as soon as possible, although it may be wise to withdraw it over a guidewire. critique: The intra-aortic balloon pump is a counterpulsation device. Coronary perfusion is increased when the balloon inflates to augment diastolic pressure. When the balloon deflates the left ventricular work required for ejection is decreased. Optimal balloon function requires accurate timing with the arterial waveform. Inflation of the intra-aortic balloon pump should be maintained to maximize augmented diastolic blood pressure, but deflation must precede aortic valve opening and ventricular ejection. Clinically, deflation is usually timed to occur with the onset of the R-wave of the ECG. In the illustration the assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure and unassisted aortic end-diastolic pressure are equal. Balloon deflation extends into the next native ejection, which initially increases afterload and decreases its rate of rise. Late deflation therefore fails to prepare for the next native ejection and impedes ejection and causes increased work. Moving the deflation timing back is necessary for optimal function at this heart rate.

critique:
Besides abnormal baseline repolarization (increased corrected QT interval), other risk factors such as electrolyte abnormalities, heart failure and baseline prolongation of the QT interval may increase the incidence of torsades de pointes. In the preoperative ECG described, the QT interval is prolonged at 510 msec (QT corrected = 517). This patient is at high risk for drug-induced torsades de pointes.

Vaughan Williams Class Ia agents (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) and class III (ibutilide, amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide) are associated with pro-arrhythmic effects such as development of torsades de pointes. Class III agents block potassium channels and prolong ventricular repolarization, thus increasing the QT interval. There are two delayed rectifier potassium channel subtypes: rapid IKr and slow IKs. Inhibition of rapid IKr channels seems to be most associated with pro-arrhythmic effects and torsades de pointes. Class Ia agents such as quinidine inhibit sodium channels and prolong the QRS interval. Quinidine is also a potent inhibitor of IKr channels and it, too, causes QT prolongation. In meta-analyses, quinidine is associated with a 0.5% to 4.4% incidence of torsades. Among class III agents, sotalol is more selective for IKr and exhibits a dose-dependent risk for torsades with incidences of 0.3% to 7%. Ibutilide had a reported incidence of torsades of 8.3% in one clinical trial. Amiodarone is generally classified as a class III agent but it has multiple actions at other channels as well, including inhibition of sodium channels, calcium channels, and beta-blockade. The risk of torsades de pointes associated with amiodarone is less than 1%, which is lower than other class III agents because of its actions on other ion channels.

Sophisticated mapping may be required to differentiate these two flutter descriptions, but in view of a previously successful surgical ablation, the described patient is unlikely to have an atypical flutter.

Typical atrial flutter is managed definitively by percutaneous ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus, and this highly successful procedure is accepted as first line therapy for this diagnosis. Ablative therapies are superior to anti-arrhythmic drug therapy for most regular atrial tachycardias, and secondary drug side effects and anticoagulation risks can be avoided. A pacemaker should not be required if the ablation procedure is accurately done. Electrical cardioversion is not definitive therapy and will not result is sustained control.

Atrial fibrillation occurred on POD #2 and has persisted despite attempts at chemical and electrical cardioversion. He was receiving heparin at 1200 units/hr and recent labs include PTT = 58 sec and INR = 1.0. However, his platelet counts have decreased to 51,000 from 121,000 on POD# 1 (215,000 preop). A lower extremity ultrasound was positive for deep vein thrombosis. Heparin-associated antibody is positive and serotonin release assay is pending. All heparin products were discontinued and argatroban 2 Œºg/(kg*min) was started. The next day, PTT = 56 sec, INR = 2.2 and platelets are 49,000. critique:
Heparin exposure may lead to thrombocytopenia by two mechanisms. Type I heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is non-antibody mediated, is reversible when heparin is discontinued and is not associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism. Type II is antibody-mediated and results in platelet activation and an increased risk of thromboembolism. A test for heparin-associated antibodies (also known as platelet factor 4 dependent enzyme immunoassay or PF4-EIA) has a sensitivity > 90% and a specificity of 50-93% when reduction of platelets occurs more than five days after exposure. Sensitivity increases to 100% with a combination of heparin-associated antibody test and serotonin release assay, while specificity increases to 80-97%. The incidence of heparin antibody formation in post-cardiac surgery patients is higher than other patient populations (as high as 35-65% of patients). The probability of Type II heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and associated thrombosis is high in this patient. He has developed thrombocytopenia with recent exposure to heparin, has a positive heparin-associated antibody, and evidence of new thrombosis. Although the serotonin release assay results for this patient are not known, the clinical evidence for HIT-associated thrombosis is high, and current and future heparin exposure should be prohibited. 

Patients with HIT are at increased risk of arterial and venous thromboembolism due to platelet activation and thrombin generation. Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor that does not crossreact with heparin antibodies. Two clinical trials have evaluated argatroban in the prevention of HIT-associated thrombosis. They reported a relative risk reduction of 44-62% for onset of new thrombosis. While increases in PTT are due to the therapeutic effect of argatroban, increases in INR are due to an assay interference. This interference can mislead clinicians to think there is an alteration in liver function or deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. 

For this patient, argatroban should not be discontinued since he is at high risk for thromboembolism from leg clots. Vitamin K administration is not indicated since the INR elevation is a false result and not an actual deficiency in clotting factors. Giving vitamin K may increase the risk of thromboembolism. Placing an IVC filter is not indicated since the patient does not have active bleeding and leg clot propagation should be prevented by argatroban at therapeutic levels. A filter will not prevent HIT-associated thrombosis. Treating HIT-associated thrombosis with warfarin alone (i.e., no bridging with non-heparin anticoagulant) increases the risk of venous limb gangrene due to depletion of protein C. Consensus guidelines recommend continuted argatroban and initiating warfarin only after platelets have increased to over 100,000. The two anticoagulants should be overlapped for a minimum of five days.

question_text: A 69-year-old man underwent CABG x 4 three days ago. His past history was complicated and included stroke, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and benign prostatic hypertrophy. His creatinine has increased from 0.9 preop to 2.0 and platelets have decreased from 268,000 prior to surgery to 37,000. His current medications include aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, simvastatin, furosemide, omeprazole and a heparin infusion at 500 units/hr. A heparin-associated antibody test was sent and the heparin infusion was discontinued. Which of the following medications is the most appropriate choice for this patient's situation?
critique:
Type II heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is due to formation of IgG antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4) on the surface of platelets. These autoantibodies bind PF4 in complex with heparin, or heparin-like substances, and cause platelet activation. Further studies are necessary to determine if this patient has pathologic clotting, and continued anticoagulation with an alternate drug is prudent.

Enoxaparin is a low molecular weight heparin and is associated with lower immunogenicity and lower risk of developing PF4 antibodies. However, in a patient with existing PF4/heparin associated antibodies, there is a significant risk of cross-reactivity. Low molecular weight heparins should be avoided in patients who have evidence of HIT.

Fondaparinux is a synthetic pentasaccharide which indirectly inhibits factor Xa. While some studies have demonstrated development of in vitro PF4 antibodies with fondaparinux, the actual risk of HIT due to fondaparinux was initially thought to be extremely low. Some case reports have even documented successful use of fondaparinux as a treatment for HIT. However, several recent reports describe HIT due to fondaparinux. Given the risk of possible cross-reactivity and the availability of other anticoagulants fondaparinux is not an appropriate choice.

Argatroban and lepirudin are direct thrombin inhibitors that have no cross-reactivity with PF4 antibodies. Both have been evaluated in clinical trials and are effective treatments to prevent the thrombotic complications associated with HIT. Argatroban is metabolized by the liver and prolonged elimination may be seen in patients with hepatic insufficiency. Lepirudin is eliminated by the kidneys and may accumulate in the face of renal dysfunction. Lepirudin has also been associated with increased rates of bleeding, rare cases of anaphylaxis and the development of lepirudin autoantibodies with prolonged exposure. This patient's renal dysfunction would make lepirudin dosing somewhat complicated and may result in drug accumulation and potential toxicity. Argatroban is a better choice for this patient since he has no evidence of hepatic dysfunction.

critique:
One of the impediments to recovery from major surgical procedures is the inability of the patient to participate in rehabilitation. This can be affected profoundly by the presence of dementia. Dementia is defined as a chronic acquired decline in memory and in at least one other cognitive function (e.g., language, visual-spatial, executive) sufficient to affect daily life. Causes of dementia include Alzheimer's disease (70%), cerebrovascular disease including stroke (30%) and completely reversible dementia such as drug toxicity, metabolic changes, thyroid disease, subdural hematoma, and normal-pressure hydrocephalus (2-5%).

The Mini-Cog screen is a quick, easy to administer screening for dementia (but not for delirium). The test evaluates the patient's short-term memory. Although the test is relative sensitive, it does not pinpoint a cause, which can be organic, vascular or metabolic. The Mini-Cog screen combines an un-cued 3-item recall test with a clock-drawing test (CDT) that serves as a recall distracter. The Mini-Cog can be administered in about 3 minutes, requires no special equipment, and is relatively uninfluenced by level of education or language differences.

 

Administration of the mini-Cog screen:
1. Make sure to obtain the patient's attention. Instruct the patient to listen carefully to and remember three unrelated words and then to repeat the words back to you (to be sure the patient heard them). 
2. Instruct the patient to draw the face of a clock, either on a blank sheet of paper or on a sheet with the clock circle already drawn on the page.  After the patient puts the numbers on the clock face, ask him or her to draw the hands of the clock to read a specific time (11:10 and 8:20 are most commonly used and more sensitive than some others).  These instructions can be repeated, but no additional instructions should be given.  If the patient cannot complete the CDT in ≤ 3 minutes, then move on to the next step.
3. Ask the patient to repeat the 3 previously presented words. 
 
Scoring: 
1 point for each recalled word after the CDT distractor.  Score 0-3 for recall. 
2 points for normal CDT; 0 points for abnormal CDT.  The CDT is considered normal if all numbers are depicted, once each, in the correct sequence and position, and if the hands readably display the requested time.  Add the recall and CDT scores together to get the Mini-Cog Score: 
          0-2 indicates a positive screen for dementia
          3-5 indicates a negative screen for dementia

critique:
Sleep disorders are common in the elderly, particularly after major operations. The hospital environment adds to the problem because of the day and night activities, ambient light all of the time and irregular hours. Simple maneuvers to assist in sleep include keeping regular sleeping hours, turning off lights and keeping nighttime disturbance to a minimum. Long periods of wakefulness in bed is to be avoided, as is napping (or limit to one short nap after lunch). Exercise is important, but should be avoided close to bedtime, and caffeine, alcohol, and smoking should be avoided. Stress management or relaxation therapy may be helpful, especially if the patient is a worrier. Many herbal treatments are available, such as valerian root, chamomile, and melatonin, but they remain unproven. A cup of a warm, noncaffeinated drink before bedtime can be a soothing ritual.

Occasionally, sleep medications may be of benefit over a short period of time. Many medications have adverse effects in the elderly. Trazadone, a serotonin modulator and antidepressant, is often recommended when a drug is required. The long half-life of most benzodiazepines makes their use undesirable. Chloral hydrate is frequently ineffective after a few doses. Ramelteon, a selective melatonin receptor agonist, has an impressive record of efficacy since its introduction in 2005. Zolpidem has many side effects, some paradoxical, and may associated with rebound insomnia when stopped. critique:
The patient described is exhibiting classic signs of acute delirium. Diagnostic criteria adapted from DSM-IV include (1) disturbed consciousness (i.e., decreased attention, environmental awareness); (2) cognitive change (e.g., memory deficit, disorientation, language disturbance) or perceptual disturbance (e.g., visual illusions, hallucinations); (3) rapid onset (hours to days) and fluctuating daily course; and (4) a causal physical condition such as stress of a recent operation. Risk factors include advanced age or comorbid physical problems (especially sleep deprivation, immobility, dehydration, pain, sensory impairment) and dementia.

Evaluation of delirium can be accomplished relatively quickly. The diagnosis can be confirmed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM): both acute onset and fluctuating course and inattention and either disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness. Caregivers should always assume reversibility of dementia unless proven otherwise. Other medical causes should be excluded, including infection, hypoxemia, anemia, and metabolic derangements. The medication list must be checked for any inciting agents such as anticholinergics (e.g., diphenhydramine), tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs, e.g., amitriptyline, imipramine), antipsychotics (e.g., chlorpromazine, thioridazine), anti-inflammatory agents, benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawal, cardiovascular agents (e.g., antihypertensives); diuretics; or opioid analgesics (especially meperidine). This may require a companion to keep the patient oriented and a pharmacologic agent such as haloperidol in small, frequent doses to reach the desired effect. Percutaneous tracheostomy requires a minimum of two (preferably three) operators. One person performs the procedure while assistant(s) at the head of the patient control(s) the airway, anesthesia and bronchoscopy. critique:
de Leval pioneered the use of human factors science in the pediatric cardiac OR. In a prospective study where over 200 arterial switch operations were directly observed by trained human factors observers, he determined that major intraoperative adverse events were directly linked to poor outcomes. Minor adverse events were also shown to be statistically correlated with poorer outcomes.

Recently, much attention has been paid to medical "errors" in American hospitals. Quantitative and qualitative studies have been designed to identify human factors (e.g., teamwork, fatigue, organizational dynamics, authority gradients, shift work, and team performance) that can potentially lead to undesirable outcomes (e.g., near-misses and hospital death). In addition to human factors, latent conditions that may lead to error are evaluated, such as policies, processes, procedures, and cultures. Ultimately, major safety interventions and error reduction strategies can be designed, such as detailed briefing of the entire operating room staff as to incidence and types of human factors in the operating room. Post-intervention reduction in near-misses and hospital deaths can be assessed. Cisplatin or platinum-based chemotherapy for NSCLC is the most effective current agent in clinical trials for treating lung and esophageal cancer. Cisplatin is classified as an alkylating agent, and it is most active in the resting phase of the cell cycle. Drugs in this class are cell cycle non-specific. There are several types of alkylating agents, but cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin are "metal salts."

The following side effects occur in greater than 30% of patients receiving cisplatin:
- nausea and vomiting: Nausea may last up to 1 week after therapy. Anti-nausea medication is given before the infusion and continued as needed later.
- kidney toxicity: Effects on kidney function are dose related, observed 10-20 days after therapy, and are generally reversible.
- electrolyte abnormalities (low magnesium, low calcium, low potassium)
- anemia and leukopenia: Marrow suppression is predictable, with onset after 10 days, nadir between 14-23 days, and recovery after 21-39 days.

When these compounds are compared to non-platinum-based drugs there are no significant differences in the rates of neurotoxicity, febrile neutropenia, or death due to toxicity.

question_text: A 76-year-old man has respiratory compromise and increased work of breathing the day after a "routine" right upper lobectomy. Oxygen saturation is 90% on a non-rebreather mask (FiO2 = 1.0) and breath sounds are diminished on the right. The chest radiograph shows significant atelectasis on that side. With a combination of IV lidocaine and topical benzocaine an awake bronchoscopy is done and a mucous plug is removed from the right mainstem bronchus. Air exchange and oxygenation improve, and FiO2 is reduced to 0.5. However, 10 minutes later the patient is cyanotic, the O2 sat is 68%, and it is unresponsive to increased oxygen administration. Breath sounds are still heard on both sides. The next step in this patient's management should be to
critique:
While retained mucous may still be an issue, the exam suggests that aeration is improved. Repeating the bronchoscopy is unlikely to result in sustained improvement and ECMO and reoperation are overly aggressive. If the patient's air exchange is reasonable on both sides and administered oxygen concentration is high, an additional benefit from intubation is not assured. If oversedation is ruled out this patient may be suffering from methemoglobinemia. Topical anesthetics such as benzocaine can induce significant oxidative stress that oxidizes iron in hemoglobin from the ferrous (Fe2+) to the ferric (Fe3+) state. The resulting hemoglobin is unable to transport oxygen and hypoxia and cyanosis result. Methemoglobin levels of up to 20% are often tolerated without incident. Lidocaine is a rare cause of methemoglobinemia by itself, but the combination of IV and topical anesthetics used for this patient's bronchoscopy should raise suspicion of this iatrogenic complication. 

The clinical findings of methemoglobinemia can be subtle or profound with cyanosis, dyspnea, lethargy, headache, dizziness, deterioration of mental function, or stupor. The easiest test is to examine grossly a blood sample. Finding a classic brown color that fails to change color (turn red) upon exposure to atmospheric oxygen is pathognomonic. Methemoglobin levels are accurately determined in the laboratory, and a level greater than 1% is considered abnormal and should be treated. Treatment includes oxygen administration and intravenous methylene blue (1-2 mg/kg up to 50 mg/dose in adults) as a 1% solution over 5 minutes. However, methylene blue should not be administered to patients with G6PD deficiency (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency) because it will not work well, it may result in severe hemolysis (which can negate the test for G6PD deficiency), and because some of these patients will have paradoxical worsening of the methemoglobinemia.

critique:
Transfusion-related acute lung injury, or TRALI, is an acute lung injury pattern that occurs during or within six hours after a transfusion. All blood products can cause TRALI. Although the mechanism is not precisely defined, the problem resides in the donor. Suspected cases of TRALI should trigger notification of the blood bank to investigate the donor, as other potential recipients are at risk. Blood products from multiparous donors appear to confer the highest risk for inducing TRALI. Of note, the recipient does not appear to be at increased risk for TRALI from future transfusions, although re-exposure to the same donor would cause similar problems. Mortality for TRALI is estimated at 5%, which is much more optimistic than ARDS.

The transfusion in this case was elective and the starting hematocrit was not critically low. Care for the patient during and after this complication is supportive. Intubation may be necessary, but resolution is usually rapid and most patients are extubated within 48 hours. Ventilator management is guided by the same principles used in ARDS, i.e., a lung-protective ventilator strategy. A trial of diuresis can help distinguish between volume overload and TRALI. Although steroids have been used anecdotally, they have not been studied prospectively and are not recommended. The use of erythropoietin has been shown to increase hemoglobin concentrations in critically ill patients, but it does not effect the average number of PBCs used or the number of patients who receive a transfusion. Erythropoietin use is associated with an increased number of thrombotic events.

While the nurse was giving final discharge instructions, the patient fell back into his bed and was unresponsive with no pulse. CPR was initiated and ventricular fibrillation was documented. After defibrillation it was not possible to administer medications because IV access could not be obtained. Femoral line placement was unsuccessful due to the patient's nephrogenic fibrosing dermopathy. The patient was orally intubated. critique:
Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) guidelines (see reference) advocate intravenous administration of medications when possible. The advantages of peripheral access are ready access in most patients and simple catheters that do not require interruption of CPR. If return of spontaneous circulation does not occur after the first several minutes, central access should be obtained to ensure delivery of medications and to facilitate blood draws for labs. The 2005 guideline specifies access route priorities, and administration via an endotracheal tube was downgraded to third line and intraosseous administration was recommended as second line, after intravenous administration. Intraosseous administration of medication utilizes the same dose as intravenous administration and achieves the same plasma concentrations as central administration. However, specialized needles and training are needed for providers to secure intraosseous access. Because this may not be feasible for most institutions or providers, endotracheal administration must be considered in certain situations.

In this case, intravenous access was attempted without success. Another attempt at central venous access with cut-down may succeed, but the delay for setup is undesirable, and CPR interruption is required. The endotracheal tube (ETT) offers immediate access, but not all medications may be safely administered, and dosing for some drugs is different to achieve the same plasma concentrations as IV administration. The acronym NAVEL may facilitate recall of common medications that may be administered via ETT (NAVEL= naloxone, atropine, vasopressin, epinephrine, lidocaine). Studies have shown conflicting results about the optimal endotracheal dose of medications. For epinephrine and lidocaine, the recommended dose is 2 to 2.5 times the IV dose diluted in 5 or 10 ml of normal saline. For vasopressin, the recommended endotracheal dose is 40 units, the same as the IV dose, but diluted in 10 ml of normal saline. After the medication is instilled via the ETT, CPR should be briefly stopped and bagged breaths given to distribute the medication throughout the airways. Bicarbonate, calcium and amiodarone, however, should not be administered via ETT. Amiodarone is a highly lipid soluble drug with somewhat irregular absorption through the lungs. Potassium and magnesium repletion are clearly indicated. Optimal drug treatment for conversion and maintenance remains controversial, and antiplatelet and anticoagulant strategies remain the best strategies for many patients with this complication. Mechanisms for this finding are hypothesized to be tachycardia-induced atrial cardiomyopathy, cytosolic calcium accumulation, and/or atrial hibernation. Third degree heart block with a ventricular rate of 50 has been present for three months. The patient was without symptoms until recently, although the slow heart rate and occasional pauses were noted. A transesophageal echocardiogram was done yesterday and showed vegetations on the mitral and aortic valves and a large paravalvular abscess. The patient had a witnessed cardiac arrest this morning. The initial rhythm was thought to be ventricular tachycardia, possibly polymorphic, that degenerated into ventricular fibrillation. critique: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a type of irregular wide complex tachycardia. While patients may not be unstable with this rhythm, there is a high risk of degeneration into ventricular fibrillation, as in this patient. To assess polymorphic ventricular tachycardia the ECG should be evaluated and the QT interval determined. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in the presence of a normal QT interval is often due to acute ischemia. A diagnosis of ¡torsades de pointes can only be made when the QT interval is prolonged, either due to congenital or acquired causes. This patient has a long QT interval on ECG. The Bazett formula for corrected QT (QTc) is the QT interval (0.55 msec) divided by the square root of the R-R interval (0.88 msec) = 0.58. The upper limits of normal for men and women are 0.39 and 0.41 respectively. In this case the QTc is markedly prolonged and torsades may be triggered by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, hypothyroidism, drugs that prolong repolarization (including several antibiotics) and severe malnutrition. The common mechanism for drug-induced torsades de pointes is inhibition of a specific repolarizing potassium current, I(Kr). This patient has AV dissociation and bradycardia with noted pauses. Transvenous pacing and isoproterenol can be used temporarily to increase the heart rate and shorten the QT interval (i.e., overdrive pacing). Magnesium has been shown to be effective in terminating torsades in patients with a prolonged QT interval, and large IV doses (several grams) should be given. Lidocaine can prevent polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and it does not prolong the QT interval. Amiodarone is not an appropriate choice given its potential to prolong further the QT interval and to slow the heart rate due to its beta blocking effect.

It should not be used alone for therapy since resistance develops rapidly. In contrast to native valve endocarditis due to MRSA in which gentamicin is recommended for only 3 to 5 days, therapy for prosthetic valve endocarditis should include therapy with gentamicin or another aminoglycoside for 2 weeks. Recommendations for prosthetic valve endocarditis due to methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) include combination therapy with nafcillin for at least 6 weeks, plus rifampin for at least 6 weeks, plus gentamicin for two weeks.

It is bacteriostatic against staphylococci and enterococci and bacteriocidal against streptococci. Linezolid is effective for bacteremia, urinary, skin and soft tissue infections caused by methicillin susceptible and resistant Staphylococcus aureus, penicillin susceptible and resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae and vancomycin resistant Enterococcus faecium. A.  The physician expert witness must have had a current, valid, and unrestricted state license to practice medicine at the time of the alleged occurrence.
B.  The physician expert witness should have been a diplomate of a specialty board recognized by the American Board of Medical Specialties at the time of the alleged occurrence, and should be qualified by experience or demonstrated competence in the subject matter of the case.
C.  The specialty and experience of the physician expert witness should be appropriate to the subject matter of the case.

E.  The physician expert witness must be familiar with the subject matter of the case and the relevant standards of care at the time of the alleged occurrence and must have completed training and have been actively involved in the independent clinical practice of the specialty at that time.
F.  The physician expert witness should be able to demonstrate evidence of continuing medical education relevant to the specialty and the subject matter of the case.
G.  The physician expert witness should be prepared to document the percentage of time spent in serving as an expert witness.  In addition, the physician expert should be willing to disclose the amount of fees or compensation obtained for such activities and the total number of times the physician expert has testified for the plaintiff or the defendant.

Isolated lung ventilation (ILV) may be considered for anatomic or mechanical indications, such as support during massive hemoptysis or to manage copious secretions. While individual lumen size is suboptimal, flexible access to each lung is assured. Other applications may include optimal management of a bronchopleural fistula or for differential lung ventilation following a single lung transplant. Asynchronous ventilation of separate lungs is technically easier than synchronized ventilation and is associated with no adverse effects. ILV can be performed with a double lumen endotracheal tube or an endobronchial blocker. The small airway size of a pediatric patient may not accommodate the smallest commercial double lumen tube (approximately 10 mm outside diameter). Using an endobronchial blocker, therefore, is the only alternative for infants and many children. The right mainstem bronchus is short, and secure placement of a right-sided double lumen tube is difficult. The risk of right upper lobe obstruction is high (89%) and many patients will not tolerate ventilation of right middle and lower lobes only. Therefore, most surgeons and anesthesiologists favor routine use of a left-sided tube unless stenosis or aberrant anatomy precludes its use.

distractor_a: It appears that the patient cannot understand the details of a proposed procedure.
distractor_c: The patient states he/she does not want to hear a discussion of risks.
distractor_d: The physician believes the patient may be mentally harmed by disclosure of risks.

question_text: Informed consent may be waived in each of the following situations EXCEPT
critique:
Complex patient situations may require special efforts to obtain informed consent. Properly obtained informed consent for treatment involves three phases, each of which involves doctor-patient communication as a part of patient education:
1. Details of a treatment or procedure must be explained including potential benefits, serious risks and feasible alternatives. The most likely outcomes of treatment should be offered to the patient.
2. The practitioner must evaluate whether or not the person has understood what has been said, must ascertain that the risks have been accepted, and that the patient is giving consent to proceed with the treatment with full knowledge and forethought.
3. The patient must sign a witnessed consent form, which documents in generic format the major points of consideration.

There are four recognized exceptions to the informed consent requirement. When any of the following are applicable to a clinical situation, the physician need not obtain conventional informed consent:
1. Emergency exception: When immediate treatment is required due to a condition which constitutes a significant danger to the life or health of the patient, a physician may forego the informed consent process. Before invoking this exception the physician should be certain that the clinical circumstances are truly life threatening, and that action is necessary to prevent immediate injury to the patient or is necessary to relieve pain and suffering. The emergency exception is met when "time is of the essence" and the possible harm to the patient is more than trivial.
2. Therapeutic privilege: There is a small number of patients who will be mentally harmed by the disclosure necessary to obtain informed consent. Although the law does not provide clear direction with regard to the degree of harm necessary to trigger the therapeutic privilege, a physician performing a procedure may invoke it in selected clinical situations when he or she believes it is in the best interests of the patient.
3. Waiver: A patient may elect not to be advised of certain elements normally disclosed during the informed consent process, as herein described. In such a case, the duty of the physician performing the procedure to obtain informed consent is in effect "waived" by the patient. When the waiver exception is relied upon, the physician performing the procedure should be certain that the patient has full knowledge and understanding of his/her right to the informed consent process and that he/she voluntarily relinquishes it. As with the application of any of the exceptions, appropriate documentation is essential.
4. Under rare circumstances a court may order a procedure to be done on a patient, in which case informed consent is waived. The court order mandates that the intervention be completed, even if it is against the patient's will.

Actual laws and guidelines for informed consent vary slightly within the United States, and state law is guiding. Consolidation of guidelines, however, is a goal of CMS, which has issued "Hospital Interpretive Guidelines for Informed Consent." In this document the only acknowledged exception relates to emergency circumstances. Integrating the informed consent process into the electronic medical record has considerable support, as the approach is consistent, application can be global, guidelines can be addressed and several business issues (intake efficiency, charge capture) may be improved. In any case, when a patient seems not to understand the discussion the surgeon should seek participation of that patient's next of kin, caretaker or representative. When the issue is patient competence, it remains imperative that understanding and consent still must be achieved preoperatively. The reference internet link points to resources compiled by the American College of Surgeons.

question_text: Each of the following statements about postpneumonectomy syndrome is correct EXCEPT
critique: Postpneumonectomy syndrome (PPS) is an uncommon syndrome that occurs as a result of progressive rotation and shift of mediastinal structures after pneumonectomy. The consequence of this shift is bronchial obstruction. Although it can occur immediately following pneumonectomy, it is more common much later and is also more common in the pediatric population. It is more common after right pneumonectomy, with an average of 7.5 years before operative intervention was necessary. Long-standing PPS has been associated with tracheomalacia. The diagnosis of PPS is suspected by history, and it is confirmed by CT scan and bronchoscopy that shows narrowing from twisting and/or external compression. The surgical management of PPS is based upon three basic principles: direct repositioning of structures, mechanical airway support, and increasing the volume of the post-pneumonectomy space. Repeat thoracotomy on the original side, with freeing of the retrosternal space and mediastinum are initial goals. The importance of extensive dissection of one "tethering point," the origin of the bronchial stump and surrounding structures (distal trachea, vertebral bodies) is emphasized by some authors. Most patients improve substantially after reoperation, in which breast implants, lucite balls or other prosthetic materials are used to limit the volume of potential mediastinal shift. Suturing scar or pericardium to the posterior sternum and phrenic nerve division are not necessary if volume fixation by implants is done. The use of endobronchial stents for this benign condition is not advised because of their long-term shortcomings.

question_text: An 86-year-old man with a history of CAD had a drug eluting stent successfully placed for a circumflex marginal lesion three years ago. Follow-up revealed severe mitral regurgitation, and MVR with a 29 mm bioprosthetic valve and PFO closure were performed. He was transferred to the ICU on dexmedetomidine and sodium nitroprusside infusions. critique:
When tissue factor is exposed, such as on injured endothelium, circulating activated factor VII (factor VIIa) binds to form a complex which activates factors IX and X. Factor Xa then activates factor V and the complex of Xa-Va-tissue factor is responsible for generating a small amount of thrombin from prothrombin. Factor VIII, V and platelets are then activated by this small amount of thrombin. Activated factors IX and X form a complex that subsequently generates large amounts of thrombin. Platelets are an important component in the coagulation cascade since factors Va and VIIIa are bound to the platelet surface. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin by thrombin and is necessary for development of hemostatic plug formation.

Administering pharmacologic doses of activated factor VII results in significant thrombin generation by directly activating factor X without first activating factor VIII or IX. Studies have demonstrated that the activity procoagulant activity of factor VIIa is significantly impaired in the setting of low platelets, acidosis and low fibrinogen. While hypothermia does not directly impair the activity of factor VIIa, it impairs the activity of platelets and other coagulation factors. A multidisciplinary task force developed guidelines for recombinant factor VIIa use in massive bleeding due to trauma. This document recommends that the following conditions be met prior to factor VIIa administration: platelet count > 50,000 (preferably > 100,000), fibrinogen > 50 mg/dl (preferably >100 mg/dl), and pH > 7.2. Warming of the hypothermic patient is recommended to prevent impairment of other clotting factor activity, but within physiologic range temperature does not directly impact the activity of activated factor VIIa itself.

question_text: Each of the following statements regarding practice guidelines is true EXCEPT
critique:
Clinical practice guidelines offer an important means of applying available evidence to clinical care. Major recommendations developed from practice guidelines are usually classified into three categories: Class I (recommended), Class II (may be useful), and Class III (not recommended). The evidence used to support the Class of recommendation is also graded into three categories: Level A (multiple randomized trials and/or meta-analyses), Level B (few randomized trials with some observational or retrospective studies), and Level C (expert consensus based on limited experimental data). Multiple sources of evidence are used to develop practice guidelines including literature searches of databases such as PUBMED. It is important to realize that only about 30% of important medical literature can be found in these large computerized databases, so careful searching of the so-called "fugitive literature" is a necessary step in practice guideline development. Examples of "fugitive literature" include government reports, consensus documents from expert panels, and negative studies that were not published in peer-reviewed literature but were recorded as clinical trials in a national registry of clinical trials.

The guideline development process often uncovers areas where knowledge is lacking and, hence, can be hypothesis generating. An example is the management of patients on clopidogrel who need urgent coronary revascularization. A randomized controlled trial to answer this question is not currently available -- this is apparent upon scrutiny of the literature to develop blood conservation guidelines. Evidence-based guidelines attempt to reconcile conflicting lines of evidence, and they give greater weight to evidence derived from more methodologically rigorous studies and those for which the overall weight of evidence is most convincing. Evidence-based guidelines must be viewed as recommendations, not absolutes. Consequently, they are not legal instruments and should not be considered as unassailable.

Reluctance to adopt clinical practice guidelines is pervasive among both caregivers and patients. Regardless of recommendations from trusted sources, patients continue to act in ways contrary to their best interests and physicians limit their adherence to guideline recommendations. A familiar example is lack of smoking cessation in populations at risk. Barriers to guideline implementation include: (1) widespread adherence to customary, accepted practice patterns ("natural validity") despite evidence that a different practice is better; (2) failure of physicians to appreciate that a guideline recommendation is a change for the better; (3) failure of the guideline to persuade physicians or patients that its background evidence is unconvincing; (4) an ill-defined and/or ill-chosen target audience for the practice guideline; and (5) conflict of the recommended practice with established norms.
